paragraphs.text: Oh, hello. Welcome to our home. I’m Jo March and I’m here to share with you a little about the story you are going to read.

As you may know, it is entitled Little Women . It’s a story about my family─well, more specifically, about me and my three sisters: Meg, who is the oldest; Beth, who is a couple of years younger than me; and the baby of the family, Amy. Our story is based on the true-life story of the author, Louisa May Alcott, who also had three sisters.
Louisa May Alcott was born on November 29, 1832. Like me, she was the second daughter in a family of four girls. Louisa grew up in Concord, Massachusetts, USA.

From a young age, Louisa loved to write. She wrote poetry and even several thrillers, believe it or not. She was also an avid reader, fueling her imagination with works from Shakespeare to Charlotte Bronte.

As you read Little Women , you may see a strong resemblance between my character and Louisa. In fact, according to Louisa, she did indeed base my character on herself, while her real sisters─Anna, Lizzie, and May─are depicted by Meg, Beth, and Amy respectively.
Little Women was published in 1868. The story is set during the American Civil War.

Father is away at war, not as a soldier, but as a chaplain. He is a very thoughtful, kind man, who instills in us, his daughters, a strong sense of morals and family values. At one time Father used to be very rich but now, after the war, our family is struggling financially.

Mother is the most loving, caring person in the world. She is not perfect, but she makes every effort to help us girls learn life’s important lessons, as well as treasure the moments we share together as a family.

My sister Meg is a lovely person who has a strong sense of responsibility and looks after her younger sisters. Meg does have her faults, though, and one of them is vanity. She longs to have fashionable, pretty things, as most girls do. But what can one do if family finances don’t permit such treats?

Next comes me. As I mentioned, the author Louisa and I share many traits. I am also a writer and I love to read. I’m not pretty like Meg or gentle like Beth, but I have a very strong personality, as my family will tell you.

My biggest weak point is my short temper and I often lose control of it. It gets me into many arguments and sometimes causes mishaps. But I’m loyal and true to my family and friends. I will do anything for them. I’m a bit of a tomboy, which means I act like a boy. In fact, I’ll admit I sometimes wish I were a boy. This kind of thinking also gets me into trouble.

Beth is my darling little sister. I have a soft spot for her as she is the most gentle and shy creature you will ever come across. Like Mother, Beth is very caring and she holds nothing back when it comes to helping others. Beth never complains or upsets people and she would rather do something herself than be a bother to others. She loves music. Her voice is as angelic as her personality.

Finally, there’s Amy, the youngest of our clan. I suppose Amy and I are the pair of sisters who argue the most. Just between you and me, she irritates me so. However, I admit Amy does have her good traits. One of them is her beauty. She is like a porcelain doll. When she smiles at you, you forget all your troubles. She is also a very talented artist.

I wouldn’t be surprised if she became a famous painter one day. One of Amy’s weaknesses is her selfishness. She’s the youngest so I can understand this somewhat. But this characteristic gets her into several scrapes, which Amy thankfully learns from.

So now you know a little about my family and something about Louisa May Alcott. As I mentioned before, our family lived during the American Civil War. Life at that time was quite different from what it is like for you today.
For example, look at my clothes.
Not only did we have to wear these long dresses, but when a woman went out, she was expected to wear gloves and carry a parasol.
Given that I’m a tomboy, can you imagine how difficult it was for me to wear such things? My sisters had to remind me every time I wasn’t dressed in a "ladylike" way.

At this time, women were expected to behave in a certain manner as well. For most women, their purpose in life consisted of finding a marriage mate and having children. I resisted such notions and got myself into a lot of trouble for it. But I, like Louisa, am a firm believer that women should have their independence.

Another thing you might find unusual is our way of life. It was common in our time to have servants and housekeepers. My family, as well as Louisa Alcott, hated the idea of slavery. We would never regard our beloved Hannah as a slave. She is trusted and loved and is a great help to our family.

Something else you may find peculiar is how the young men and women interact. In my day, society was much more conservative. It was not considered proper for young people to date or go out unless they intended to marry. It’s true that many married at a young age, but we had strict rules that allowed or did not allow certain behaviors.

Time is constantly changing and that can’t be helped. Fashions, manners, customs, and traditions change, too. Some things, however, are timeless: learning how to grow up, learning how to deal with family issues, learning to love and respect others, and of course─most important of all─learning who you are.
Little Women is a story about just those things. Even though it was written more than a hundred years ago, I hope that you will find lessons you can learn from and apply in your life today.
The crackling from the fireplace gave the impression that all was well in the March home. Another crackling sound, that of Jo pushing down on her knuckles, told a different story.
"I wish this bothersome snow would stop." Jo banged the window as she watched the gigantic snowflakes silently piling up on the ground.

"Jo," shrieked Amy, "that's so unladylike!" Amy smoothed her dress and caressed her curls. She could not stand it when her older sister acted like a boy. Jo, on the other hand, wished she could be a boy. She often complained: "Why do I have to wear this confining dress? Why can't I wear trousers and kick my legs up and gallop around freely, like a horse?"
Whenever Jo said such things, her older sister Meg would gently shake her head and say: "Because whether you like it or not, you are a girl. And girls should behave as such."
On this cold winter day, however, Meg did not scold her tomboy sister. In fact, she agreed with Jo about the endlessly falling snow.
"It's so cold and miserable," Meg lamented. "When we were rich, we could warm up every room in the house."
Now the only room that was heated was the living room in which they sat.
"We didn't have to wear these unbecoming sweaters." Amy turned up her nose as if her sweater had a funny smell.
"Now our concerns are about how Father is faring under these treacherous conditions," added Jo. She stomped over to the fireplace and rubbed her large hands together vigorously.

Being over the age at which men could enlist in the army, Father had volunteered his services as a clergyman. The girls were too young to understand or to care what the Civil War was about. They only wanted it to end so Father could return home.

At one time, the March family had been very wealthy. Meg and Jo, the two oldest girls, could remember a time when they received many gifts all year around. Now they didn't have enough money to buy even Christmas gifts for each other.
"If you had five dollars . . ." Jo began. (At this period of time, five dollars was a lot of money.) "If you had five dollars," Jo repeated, "what would you buy?"
The girls fell silent as their eyes grew bigger with fanciful thoughts.
"I know what I would buy," Amy gushed at last.
Her sisters turned to her.
"Go on," urged Jo.

Amy's cheeks got pink and she pressed her hands together excitedly. "I would buy a new set of watercolors," she said. "And then I would buy two new hairpins: one red with silver butterflies, like my best friend Kitty has. And the other blue like my eyes."

"As for me," Meg said, "I would buy beautiful silk material for a new dress. Maybe I would have some money left over for gloves since I desperately need new ones." Meg held up her lovely hands, which were now pinkish red from the cold. Meg had many vanities but she took special pride in her hands.

"I," Jo blurted in a loud, comical voice, "would buy four bottles of black ink, a case of pens, twenty rolls of paper, and three hundred . . ." she paused for dramatic emphasis. "Three hundred," she repeated again, "leather cases for all the books I am going to publish."
Jo dreamed of being a writer. Nothing suited her more than to sit at her desk and enter a world of make-believe and fantasy.
"You can't afford that many leather cases with only five dollars. That's ridiculous," Amy pointed out.
"Well, so is this game," Jo retorted, "because none of us actually has five dollars!"
"Girls," Meg said in her "motherly" voice. "Do stop arguing. You're behaving like children. Now, Beth, let's hear what you would do if you had five dollars."
Beth had a faraway look in her eyes. She was smiling.
"First of all, I'd buy a new pair of slippers for Mother. I noticed her old ones have several small holes in them," Beth said in her gentle, quiet way.
The other girls glanced at the familiar slippers next to the sofa. They all felt rather guilty when they saw that the well-worn slippers did, indeed, have many holes.

"And then I would buy Father a new scarf and hat in his favorite color," Beth continued. "If I had money left over, I would get each of you girls a handkerchief with your name on it. And one for Hannah, too."
Of the four girls, Beth was by far the kindest and most loving. She never said a bad word about anyone nor did she ever complain. She had a positive view of everything and everyone.

"Oh, Beth!" Jo ran over and wrapped her arms around her sister. "You make me feel so ashamed! Here I am thinking of myself, but you─" she sniffed, for Jo was a very emotional girl,"─you even thought of Hannah, our housekeeper."
Meg and Amy also gave Beth a hug. They, too, were feeling a little embarrassed about their selfishness.
Even though the sisters had different personalities, they were very close and loved one another very much.
"Girls, what is going on?"
The girls had not heard Mother come home.
"Mother!" they cried and ran to give her a hug.
Mother's hands and cheeks were cold from the air outside, but her hugs and kisses warmed the girls up instantly.

Meg quickly removed Mother's heavy coat. Jo ran to get more wood for the fire. Amy grabbed Mother's sweater, which was folded up on her chair, and gave it to her. Beth quietly brought Mother's slippers to warm her feet. As Mother sat on her chair and rubbed her hands in front of the fire, Jo told her what they'd been talking about.
"We were so selfish, Mother," admitted Jo. "Except for Beth. She only cares about other people."

Mother smiled affectionately at each daughter and said: "I'm glad that you discovered your fault, girls. But finding out our faults is only the first step. What we do with this knowledge is more important."
That evening, after a simple dinner, Mother and Hannah took inventory of the food pantry while the girls sat around the fireplace talking again.
"I have some money saved up," Jo began. "It's only a little bit . . . but, well, I wanted . . . Mother . . . a little gift . . .," she stammered.
"Oh, Jo! What a lovely thought!" Beth understood right away what her sister was trying hard to express.
"What's a lovely thought?" Amy asked irritably. Unlike Beth, she had no idea what Jo was trying to say.
"This Christmas none of us has much to give," Beth explained. "But with what we do have, Jo suggests that we should all give something to Mother." Beth smiled at Jo, who nodded enthusiastically.
"That's exactly what I wanted to say, Beth," she said gratefully.
Meg and Amy both agreed it was a splendid idea. They spent the rest of the evening discussing what Mother needed and what they could give her.
Although the girls would not receive gifts themselves, they were quite happy to learn the true meaning of giving.

On Christmas morning, the March sisters awoke early because they wanted to surprise Mother with their gifts. Jo reached under the bed and pulled out a wooden box where the gifts for Mother were hidden.
"I hope Mother likes this," said Jo. She held up a wrapped parcel close to her heart. Jo had penned a poem just for Mother.
Beth fingered her gift to Mother: two handkerchiefs with daisies. She had spent all night making them. Although some of the daisies looked like uneven yellow spots, Beth hoped Mother would love them.
"Smell how lovely that is." Amy pressed a small box under Meg's nose.
"Did you get lavender? It's Mother's favorite," Meg said knowingly.
Amy had used her savings to buy a bottle of cologne for Mother.
"Of course it's lavender, though my personal preference is roses," said Amy.
"Meg, where is your gift?" Jo lifted the wooden box and shook it hard.
"Oh, I have it here," said Meg. From her pocket she pulled out a bundle wrapped in a silk handkerchief. Inside was a pair of white silk gloves.
Jo squeezed Meg's hand. She knew that Meg had saved her hard earned money to purchase those special gloves.
"They will fit Mother's hands perfectly," Meg said as she lovingly placed them inside the box.
The girls crept quietly downstairs to the living room.

Mother usually reclined in her chair sipping her coffee before the girls scurried in for breakfast. So, in order to surprise her, the girls tiptoed across the hall and stood quietly outside the living room entrance. Amy had a fit of giggles.
"Shh!" Jo hissed at her.
"Girls, on the count of three," Meg whispered. "One, two . . . THREE!"
The girls flew into the room and shouted simultaneously: "Surprise, Mother! Merry—!"
But before they could finish their greeting, the girls noticed Mother's chair was unoccupied. Instead Hannah had just strolled in with a tray full of cakes.
"Ah!" Hannah screamed as she almost flipped the tray over.
Meg ran over to help their beloved housekeeper.
"Oh, girls!" Amy clasped her hands, her eyes growing big as she looked at the dining room table.
The table was covered with heaps of food. There were sausages, eggs, fresh juice and butter, and cakes adorned each corner.
"Your Ma wanted to surprise you girls with a Christmas feast," said Hannah, still clutching her chest and breathing deeply.
The girls were so touched by their mother's loving act.
"But where is she?" asked Jo.
Before Hannah could answer, Mother walked in through the front door.
"Good morning, my darling girls!" Mother opened her arms wide to embrace her daughters.
"Where did you go, Mother?" Meg asked.
"I went to see the Hummels," replied Mother.

The Hummels were a very poor family with many small children. Mr. Hummel had been drafted into the army, leaving his pregnant wife and six small children to fend for themselves. Since Mother worked as a volunteer to help unfortunate people in the community, she knew the Hummels' situation very well.
"How are the children?" asked Beth gently.
"Not very good, I'm afraid," Mother answered gravely. "They have no heating or . . . food." Her voice trailed off as she looked at the feast on the table.
The girls knew what Mother was thinking, but except for Beth, the other girls were reluctant to part with their Christmas meal.
Meg reasoned to herself: "We don't get any gifts. We should at least get a decent Christmas meal."
Jo was thinking: "I'm starving! And those sausages look so appetizing!"
Amy contemplated: "Maybe we can eat first then give the rest away to the Hummels."

Mother smiled at them as if she could discern their very thoughts. But she said kindly: "I just want to say that this meal is a gift from me and Hannah to you. However you want to use your gift is entirely up to you. I will love and respect you whatever you decide."
Meg spoke first. "Mother, the girls and I would be honored if the Hummels could enjoy this lovely meal."
Jo and Beth nodded in agreement. A moment or two later, Amy nodded too.
"My girls, I am so proud of you," Mother said.
"Let's all go together to visit the Hummels," suggested Beth.
So the girls sprinted upstairs to change their clothes.
Within a few minutes, the food was all wrapped up and ready to go. The girls got into their boots and coats and ventured out. Each of them carried large baskets filled with food.

As the Hummels did not have any heating, Jo hauled a sack of wood as well. None of the girls felt regret or resentment. Deep in their hearts, they knew the Hummels would relish the meal much more than they would.
As they passed the old mansion next to their house, Jo happened to look up. From the third floor, a dark-haired boy peered down at them as they trudged along.
"Look! There's old Mr. Laurence's grandson!" Jo called out to her sisters.
"Jo!" reprimanded Meg. "Stop staring at him. It isn't proper for a young girl to stare at a boy!"
"Don't be such a granny, Meg," snorted Jo. Since both her hands were full, she lifted up her foot and wiggled it at him as an alternative to waving.
"Jo! You're so shameless!" said Amy in rebuke.
From the window the boy also lifted his foot and wiggled it at Jo. Jo let out a loud, hearty laugh.

No words could describe how grateful the Hummel family was for the generous gift. Jo expertly got a fire going in no time while Meg and Amy set up the table and filled it with food. Beth and Mother took care of the sick children.
"Did you see how happy those children were?" Amy said, as the girls walked back home, her footsteps light and perky.
"Mrs. Hummel could not stop crying," remarked Jo. "I felt so sorry for her."
"Hopefully Mr. Hummel will be able to return home soon," said Mother.
Silently, all the girls prayed for their father to do the same.
As the girls got nearer to their house, something made them stop.
"Is that our house?" asked Amy.
"Well, I think so, but it looks different somehow," replied Meg.
There was a warm glow to the house as if each room was emitting heat.
"What if the house is on fire?" Jo shouted.
She tore across the field, her hair flying out of its bun, and threw open the door.
What a sight to behold! The entire house was cozily warm, a fire burning brightly in each fireplace. The bare dining room table was once again crowded with all sorts of delights.
"Hannah! What is this?" Mother demanded to know.
Choking back tears, Hannah could produce no reply but simply pointed to the mansion next door.
"You mean Mr. Laurence sent this?" asked Mother.
Hannah nodded, overcome by a fresh wave of tears.

"Here's a card!" Jo waved a small piece of paper in the air: Dear Mrs. March and all her lovely daughters, Jo read: My grandson and I would like to give a gift to you as you so generously give to others. Your neighbor, Mr. Laurence.
The girls all grabbed hands and started to dance around the table. Never had they been so surprised.
"You see, girls," Mother said happily. "When you think of others, others are also thinking of you."
After indulging themselves to their hearts' content, the girls concluded the Christmas feast as they always did—with a cup of hot tea and words of affection from Mother.
"This has been a trying year for all of us," Mother said. "So thank you, my little daughters, for gracefully yet courageously bearing our burdens."
Because of everything that had happened that day, the girls had been unable to present their gift to Mother. Therefore they were planning to give it to her now.
"Mother, we have something for you," said Jo as she signaled Amy with her eyes.
Amy, meanwhile, was tugging and yanking at a knot in her curls.
"I shouldn't have allowed those children to touch my hair," Amy complained, recalling the two little Hummel girls who had played with her beloved hair.
"Amy!" Jo barked sharply, as she tilted her head to indicate the box hidden behind her. The girls had agreed that the youngest should bestow the gift.
"Oh!" Amy flushed as she stood to carry out her duty.
Mother delicately took out the gifts one by one without uttering a sound, yet her eyes conveyed the depth of love and appreciation she felt for her girls.
Clutching each gift tenderly, she simply said: "My little women."

Bright and early the next morning, Jo slipped upstairs to her sanctuary in the attic. There she had pushed an old oak desk near the oval window, along with a shaky chair and large wicker basket. That basket housed what Jo the writer called "the dregs." All her incomplete, meaningless, and undesirable thoughts were discarded there.

The family knew better than to disturb Jo when she was in her creative mode. Those foolish or fearless enough might encounter one of Jo's infamous temper tantrums. Meg, at this moment, chose to take that risk, as she charged in, waving a card in her hand.
"Jo! You'll never believe what this is!" Meg cried.
Jo crumpled the paper she had been writing on and tossed it into the dregs.
"If you don't tell me soon, that is going to end up in there!" Jo said menacingly as she pointed a threatening finger at the paper in Meg's hand and kicked the wastebasket with her foot.
"The Gardiners have invited us to a New Year's ball!" Meg could hardly contain her excitement.
"A ball?" Jo shrieked. "Who cares about some stupid ball?"
Meg narrowed her eyes and said in a cool tone: "I do. How else are you going to meet your future husband?"
It took all of Jo's might to restrain herself from losing her temper.
"There are more important things in life, Meg, than to be married," Jo replied in a calm voice.
"Well, I want to go," said Meg, ignoring Jo's growls and grumbles.
"And Mother says I may," she paused, "only if we both go."
Meg finally looked at Jo with an almost desperate gaze. Immediately Jo's stubborn heart softened at her sister's silent plea.

To Jo's dismay, the day of the ball arrived more quickly than she expected. Although she was secretly praying for a severe snowstorm or some other incident that would force the ball to be canceled, outwardly Jo put on her happy face and got ready for the event.
"What gloves will you wear with your dress?" Meg glanced at Jo's maroon frock hanging on the door.
"I don't have any," was Jo's curt reply.
"You must wear gloves," Meg insisted.
"Gloves are so . . . so . . . silly!" Jo blurted out.
"A true lady must wear gloves," Meg said, her voice rising.
Jo bit her lip to stop herself from saying something nasty to Meg. Instead, rolling her eyes, Jo said: "Then I'll just have to borrow a pair of yours."
"Absolutely not," was Meg's curt reply. "Look at your big hands. You'll stretch mine out."
Like all mothers, Mrs. March had a good sense of timing. At that instant, she waltzed in with a pair of her own gloves, preventing another one of Jo's explosions.
"I thought you might need these." Mother smiled as she handed Jo the gloves.
Finally, after more shrill cries and minor mishaps, the girls were ready for the ball.
"You both look beautiful," praised Beth when she saw her sisters in their ball dresses.
"Like two princesses! Just remember to find a handsome prince!" giggled Amy.

The Gardiners were a wealthy family who often entertained guests at their mansion. Sallie Gardiner was Meg's good friend. The young girls knew each other since childhood and remained close friends even after Meg's father lost his fortune.
"Isn't this sublime, Jo?" Meg called out happily as she and her dancing partner glided past Jo, who sat tugging her tight dress collar.

"Lovely," mumbled Jo. She looked longingly outside at a group of young men kicking a ball around. It was so unfair. Jo hated living by rules that told her young women had to look pretty, giggle, and be ladylike. Meanwhile, boys could do as they please.
"Why can't I do that?" she said aloud.
"Do what?" a voice asked from behind.
Jo whipped her head around and came face to face with the Laurence boy.
"That's very rude of you," she scolded, wagging a finger at him.
"What is?" he retorted.
"Creeping up behind a lady and frightening her out of her wits," Jo said, dramatically placing a gloved hand over her forehead.
"I beg your pardon." The young man bowed deeply then continued: "Then I shall leave the lady to her wits."
"Wait!" Jo called out. "You can stay as long as you don't bore me like this party."
"So you don't like balls?" the Laurence boy asked with a twinkle in his eye.
"I can't stand them. Look at those silly girls. Their dresses are so tight, it's a wonder they're still breathing!" Jo tugged her collar again, reminding herself of her own discomfort.
"I don't fancy these sorts of things either," replied the young man.
"What are you doing here then?" asked Jo.
"My grandfather made me come," he replied, frowning.
"Oh, which reminds me," Jo exclaimed suddenly. "Thank you for the lovely Christmas meal."
The Laurence boy shrugged and said casually: "Grandfather sent it, not me."
Jo elbowed him in a very unladylike manner and said: "But I know it was you who told him."
"Do you have a name?" he asked, his cheeks flushing.
"Jo," she replied.
"That's not a very girlish name," he pointed out.
"It's short for Josephine. But if you call me that, I won't ever speak to you again."
Laughing, he said: "I'm Laurie."
Jo's loud laugh caused many people to glance their way.
"What kind of a name is Laurie Laurence?" she said, struggling to resist bursting out in laughter again.
Laurie pretended to be offended.

"My real name is Theodore but I prefer to be called Laurie. If you have a problem with that," he paused, adding with a wicked glint in his eyes, "Josephine, then I won't ever speak to you again either."
Jo punched him playfully and let out another hearty laugh.
Nearby, people shook their heads and commented on that ill-mannered, noisy young woman.

The more Jo got to know Laurie the more she liked him. She found that her preconceptions about his privileged upbringing and the behavior she expected from someone so wealthy were quickly shattered. For Jo had never met anyone as down-to-earth, sincere, and witty as Laurie. However, what happened later on that evening really clinched their friendship. The two young people were exchanging jokes and laughing rather loudly when Meg, who had been dancing almost the entire evening, limped over to where they sat.
"Jo," Meg whispered, her face pinched with pain.
"Meg! What's the matter?" Jo exclaimed, alarmed.
"I've hurt my ankle," answered Meg, tenderly massaging the swollen area.
"Oh, dear, what are we going to do?" Jo cracked her knuckles.
"Jo! Don't do that! That's so ill-mannered!" Meg, in her agony, still worried about how others might perceive them.
"Can I help in any way?" Laurie gallantly interrupted.
"No, silly boy," Jo brushed him aside. "It took us twenty minutes to walk here," she calculated to Meg. "If I carry you, we may be able to get home in less than an hour."
"No!" Meg and Laurie cried out simultaneously.
"We can't afford to hire a carriage, Meg," said Jo decisively, "so unless you want to ask Sallie whether or not they can accommodate you for the night, then I don't see any other way."
Indeed, Jo spoke truthfully, since the Marches no longer had a carriage and the girls certainly did not have enough money to hire one to take them back.

"Well, I was planning to return home soon," said Laurie, clearing his throat then continuing, "and I have a carriage. If you would do me the honor of escorting you back home, then I shall be the envy of all the lads here tonight."
Jo appreciated Laurie's tact and kindness. The two sisters heartily accepted Laurie's offer and they rode home in luxury and comfort.

The following day was their last day of freedom, as Jo put it. The winter holidays were coming to a close and the girls would be returning to their normal activities. For Meg and Jo, that meant going back to work.

Meg worked as a governess for the King family and their children. Although she took great pleasure in making her own living, Meg sometimes found it a challenge to be surrounded by wealth and luxuries that she knew she would never possess. "It frustrates me how wealthy some families are, while others are so deprived," she often complained upon returning from her place of employment.

As for Jo, she worked as a companion to their rich old Aunt March. Every morning when Jo arrived at the mansion, Aunt March presented her with a list of things to do that day. Often the list included petty things like brushing Polly, the pet parrot, and feeding her crackers, or changing the order of the cushions on the sofa. Of course, one thing Aunt March always wrote down was for Jo to read to her from a book of the old lady's choice. Needless to say, Jo's favorite part of the day was when she could escape into the pages of an imaginary world.
"At least you girls get reimbursed for your diligent efforts," whined Amy.

Though it was a holiday period, Mother made sure the girls had plenty to do around the house so they did not become lazy. Meg was shortening the hem of some of her old dresses so Amy could wear them to school. Jo was sitting and darning some old socks. What little silverware the Marches had, Amy was polishing. And Beth, who at the age of thirteen still loved her dolls, was mending some button eyes on one of her "children."
"What do you mean, Amy?" Meg asked lightly as she adjusted the cushion under her injured ankle.

"I am forced to learn things I have no interest in," Amy began, her cheeks flushed pink. "Girls tease me all the time about my dresses or ribbons. And I don't get paid for any of the abuse I suffer daily like you do."
Jo rolled her eyes and said, "No one gets paid to go to school. And besides," she added, using her needle to point to Meg and herself, "we had to go to school just the same as you."
Meg put her sewing down. "If only our lives were different, girls."
"What would you change, Meg?" asked Beth. She had finished "surgery" on one doll and was moving on to replace a torn-off limb on another worn-out one.
"Well, I wouldn't work for the Kings," Meg said after a while. "I would find an agreeable job, perhaps as a seamstress so that I might design beautiful gowns for ladies to wear."
"But you wouldn't be able to wear them yourself," said Jo candidly.
Meg gave her a hurt look and continued, "There might be some material left for me to make my own dress."
"Then you would look like Beth's doll there," Jo laughed, pointing to one doll who wore an ugly dress made out of different scraps of fabric sewn together.
"That's mean, Jo. I just want a better life for myself and my family," was Meg's tearful reply.
"Sorry, Meg," apologized Jo. "As for me, I'd be happy if Aunt March took longer naps."
The sisters shared a hearty giggle over this as they knew how cranky and bossy their old relative was. Jo often blamed Aunt March's bad moods on her lack of sleep.
"What would you do while she's sleeping?" asked Beth.
"Go to her library, of course, and read every single book," was Jo's matter-of-fact reply.
"Well," Beth said in her soft and mild manner, "if only I wasn't so shy I would love to earn some money and buy a piano."
Her sisters gave her an encouraging nod for they knew how Beth's shyness hindered her from the everyday activities others took for granted, like going to school.

"If only I didn't have to go to school," whined Amy. "I wouldn't have to hear those degrading remarks about my attire." Though she moaned about school all the time, Amy never missed an opportunity to use new words she had learned there or to tell her sisters something interesting she had just been taught.
"Your dresses are lovely," chirped Meg, since they used to belong to her at one time.
"But they're so outdated," retorted Amy, adding, "although some girls do say rather pleasant things about my hair." She fluffed and patted her curls.
Her sisters silently chuckled at Amy's open vanity about her beauty trademark.
"And if only I had a straight elegant nose," Amy complained, pinching the ridge of her nose and tugging at it as if that would restructure it.
"As much as we would all like our 'if only' stories to come true," broke in Meg, "the reality is that tomorrow life will return to just as it was a few weeks ago."
"And there is not much we can do about it," concluded Jo.
The sisters harmoniously let out a wistful collective sigh and resumed their work.

"Normal" life for the March girls began bright and early the next day. Unfortunately, neither Meg nor Jo was in the best of moods. Like most siblings, they did what they always do when things are annoying and irritable: they took it out on each other.
"Hurry up, Jo," snapped Meg as she put on her thick winter coat.
"Why? Are you so anxious to see your precious King children?" Jo retorted nastily.
"Must you doodle at your desk every morning? For once can't you keep an eye on the clock?" Meg spat back.

Jo woke up at the crack of dawn every morning and rushed up to her sanctuary where she "doodled" on her latest story. She called it her "pre-day exercise" and often forgot the time until one of the others had to go up and remind her.

"Girls, do you think it's wise to start the New Year off like this?" Mother gave the girls a quick kiss and hug. As she did every cold winter day, she had baked two buns for them, not for eating but to keep their hands warm from the frigid temperature. She slipped one inside each of the girls' coat pockets. Immediately the girls felt a surge of warmth spread across their stomachs. Perhaps it was that or Mother's gentle smile that made Meg and Jo stop arguing.
"We'll try harder, Mother," promised Meg.
"It's my fault and I apologize, Meg," admitted Jo.

The sisters started out on the path toward the street. As part of their routine, they looked back before turning the corner, for Mother was always at the window, smiling and waving at them. No matter what happened or whatever mood they were in, that small gesture filled their hearts with love and hope.
Today Jo caught a glimpse of someone else looking out a window next door. It was Laurie, looking pathetically tiny in comparison with the massive house he lived in.
"There's Laurie!" Jo cried excitedly. She held up her foot and wiggled it at him. He promptly returned the greeting.
Then to Jo's astonishment, Meg also lifted her foot and waved it.
"Meg!" cried her astonished sister.
"I'm only showing him that my ankle is better now, thanks to him," was Meg's explanation.
Giggling and linking their arms to stay warm, the sisters hurried along the street.

After a particularly trying day at Aunt March's, Jo dragged her feet home, eager to curl up on the sofa and read her book. As she approached the familiar grounds, something made her lift her head up in the direction of the Laurences' mansion. In the same window he had appeared in that morning, there stood Laurie, wearing what seemed to be the same attire as well.
"That lazy boy hasn't changed all day," Jo remarked.
"Hello, Jo!" Laurie opened his window and shouted down at her in a hoarse voice.
"Are you sick?" Jo yelled back.
The sudden cold air from the open window set Laurie off in a coughing fit.

"Don't bother answering that question," Jo replied firmly. "I can see you're not well. Just stay put. I'm coming over!" If anything, Jo was loyal to her friends. If they were sick in bed, she would make any sacrifices necessary to cheer them up. Forgetting her own fatigue, Jo sprinted inside her house to change and gather a few things for her sick neighbor.
Of course Jo had to get Mother's permission first. When Mother heard how sick Laurie was, she got Jo to take over some homemade soup.
Jo did not often lack words to express anything but when she stepped into the Laurence mansion a few minutes later, she was speechless.

Dark, exquisite furniture decorated the foyer, each piece intricately carved in exotic Asian wood. A massive crystal chandelier hung stately in the center of the hall. Large oil paintings of the Laurence men hung on the walls. There was one of a younger man who had the same mischievous grin as Laurie. Jo concluded that he must be Laurie's deceased father. She recognized the painting right next to that as old Mr. Laurence.
"Does he frighten you?" a scratchy voice called from the top of the stairs.
Jo looked up to see Laurie, in a maroon silk dressing gown, gazing down at her with a teasing grin.

"I don't get frightened of anything or anyone," Jo stated overconfidently. Inside, however, she admitted to herself that if she came across Mr. Laurence face-to-face, she might feel a little bit intimidated.
"Don't just stand there staring," Laurie's cheerful voice broke into her thoughts. "What did you bring for the sick boy?"
Jo had almost forgotten about the basket of goodies. "Mother made a fresh pot of soup. When I told her about you, she sent it over immediately."
Lowering his eyes, Laurie said quietly, "I wish she was my mother. In fact, I have a secret to tell you."
Jo, who loved secrets, urged him to tell her.
"But you have to promise you won't laugh," he said solemnly.
"Okay," Jo said with uncertainty, for she found it very hard not to laugh when she thought something was truly funny.
Laurie came down the stairs and stood next to Jo. Jo did not realize how tall he was until that moment.
"I have often watched you and your sister play. From the window in my room, I can look into your living room," he said shyly.
"Oh, you naughty boy! You were spying on us!" Jo exclaimed.
"No, no!" protested Laurie. "I wasn't spying. I was merely curious and," he paused, "a little jealous at how happy your family always seems to be."

Jo and her family knew of Laurie's misfortunes, though not in detail. His parents had died in a tragic accident when he was a small boy. Having no other relations except for his grandfather, Laurie had been sent to boarding schools abroad. Then last year, his grandfather had brought Laurie over to live with him.
"I've always wanted a big family," he said wistfully.
Something tugged at Jo's heart and she longed to give him a big hug just as she would have with her sisters.
"Well, you have my permission to watch us whenever you like," she replied. "In fact, I need to ask Mother first, but I'm sure she will be more than happy to have you visit."
"Thank you, Jo," he said sincerely. "I would really like that. Now, perhaps I should test that soup out to see whether it has gotten cold or not."
So the two friends walked to the kitchen, laughing all the way. Laurie and Jo chatted away like two old friends with so much in common. Jo told him all about her sisters.
"Well, now I'm happy to know who Beth is and who Amy is," said Laurie, who had been confused about the younger girls' names.
"By the way, Beth sent this over to you," Jo said, taking out an old rag doll that Beth treasured. "Whenever she feels sick, Lucy," Jo pointed, indicating the doll's name, "makes her feel better."
Slapping his knee, Laurie nearly tumbled off his chair, but stopped suddenly when he caught sight of someone standing in the doorway.
"Why aren't you in bed resting, Theodore, instead of acting like a silly monkey?" the old man said in a dangerously low voice.
Old Mr. Laurence was home and he was not happy.
Although they were doing nothing wrong, Laurie and Jo felt like two very naughty children. Sitting up straight, hands folded in their laps, neither young one dared to utter a sound.
"You say you are too ill to have your lessons with Mr. Brookes," Mr. Laurence began.
"My tutor," Laurie whispered under his breath to Jo.
"Did you say something, boy?" Mr. Laurence stood menacingly in front of Laurie.

"No, sir," squeaked Laurie, "I mean, I was telling Jo, who's our neighbor . . . you know that lovely family with all those girls, and Jo, here, being the second eldest . . . well, I was telling her who Brookes was, I mean, Mr. Brookes, sir."
Jo felt a giggle in her throat as poor Laurie rambled on.
"What's so funny, girl?" Mr. Laurence moved over to where Jo sat.

At that moment, the whole situation seemed oddly hilarious. Holding back the laughter that bubbled inside was causing Jo physical pain. She could no longer do it. "Oh, I'm dreadfully sorry, sir," roared Jo, wiping the tears from her eyes.
Both Laurie and his grandfather were shocked at her outburst.

"Well, Laurie looks horribly sick and that ugly doll he's holding . . . " Jo's voice cracked but she continued, "As for me, I should be ladylike and not laugh out loud. And you . . . " Jo stopped herself before she did further damage.
But to her astonishment, the old man looked at her with a twinkle in his eye and said, "Please continue. I'd like to know what is so funny about me."

Ignoring Laurie's kicks from under the table, Jo cleared her throat and went on: "Well, you're like a schoolmaster who has just caught his two most naughty pupils doing something terrible but he doesn't know what. So you're frowning and grunting and trying so hard to look upset but . . . but . . . ," Jo gasped for breath, "to me, sir, it's absolutely comical."

Still chuckling, Jo stood up and gathered her things. "But I understand that I was completely out of line. My sisters tell me that I am so boorish, that's what the youngest, Amy, says, and I'm sure the others agree, though Beth, being so sweet and gentle, would never tell me that to my face, but I do cause so much embarrassment to our family. So before I do any more damage, I had better leave," Jo babbled. She caught a glimpse of Laurie bowing his head lower and his shoulders quivering.

"That boy is laughing at me," she said to herself. Resisting the temptation to give Laurie a playful punch, Jo, instead, took a deep breath, faced the old man and said, "Sir, may I speak freely one last time?"
"You've been saying whatever you like until now. Why stop?" Mr. Laurence said in a teasing voice.
"Well, in my opinion, sir, I think Laurie is a splendid boy. And what he really needs to feel better is some warm love and lots and lots of laughter," said Dr. Jo.
Mr. Laurence was a shrewd man. He had already noticed how different Laurie seemed when he was with Jo. The change in his grandson was a pleasant one.

"Then maybe you'd better stay and make sure he gets well," was the old man's surprising remark. He smiled warmly at Jo and then at his grandson. Later on she described Mr. Laurence's transformation to her sisters this way: "It was as if another person took over his body and he suddenly turned into the kindest man in the world."

From that moment on, Laurie became the daily visitor to the March home. During the day he had his lessons with Mr. Brookes, a handsome intelligent young man employed by Mr. Laurence to help with his grandson's studies. Left with no choice after Laurie refused to attend boarding school, his grandfather finally agreed to let him receive home-schooling until he went off to university the following year.

Even during his lessons, Laurie had one eye on the time. As the hands of the antique grandfather clock in the library inched toward four, Laurie's ears strained for the now-familiar sounds of his neighbors returning from their day's activities. Amy would come home first. Laurie recognized how she slammed the door in her impatience to shut out any memory of the school day. Then she would call out in a childish shrill, "Hannah! Can I have a snack? I'm so famished!"

Meg and Jo came home around the same time but their entrance was completely different. Laurie never knew when Meg returned home exactly because he would not hear her going into the house like Amy. But from where he sat, he could see Meg walk into the kitchen, say hello to Hannah, put on her apron, and help the housekeeper prepare dinner. Thinking about his friend Jo brought a smile to Laurie's lips. Jo, knowing that Laurie would be watching out for her return, would make all kinds of noises to let him know she was home.

One time, she started to hum a funny song as she walked up the path to their door. Laurie had burst out into laughter, alarming and troubling Mr. Brookes, who was in the middle of explaining a rather dismal subject. Then, on another occasion, Mr. Brookes was explaining a tricky mathematical problem on the blackboard when he was interrupted by a strange barking noise. Looking out the window, Mr. Brookes could not see any canine in the area, but he did happen to catch a glimpse of a girl hastily shutting the entrance door over at the March home. Of the four girls, Beth stayed home all day but Laurie could not make out any sounds that alerted him to where she was. Once, he thought he heard very soft singing, but Laurie could not be sure if it was Beth, who he knew loved to sing, or if he had imagined it.

"As your attention has already left the lesson and moved on to the affairs in the other house," Mr. Brookes declared, closing his book, "you may be excused now." Giving him a mock salute, Laurie sprang up, and leaped out of the library.

Nothing was ever boring at the Marches' home. The girls always had plenty to keep themselves occupied and there was never a shortage of things to talk about. On this particular evening, the conversation ranged from spiders to dinner invitations.
"Grandfather would love for all of you to come for dinner tomorrow," Laurie said.
Although Mr. Laurence had extended the invitation on several occasions, Mother was delaying accepting it until Beth felt comfortable enough around Laurie to venture over to the unfamiliar house.
"That's very kind of him," Beth replied in her soft way.
Laurie and Jo stopped playing cards to stare at her.
"Does that mean you'd like to come to my house?" asked Laurie.
Beth smiled shyly at Laurie and said: "To me, you're more than a neighbor, Laurie, you're our dear friend."

As Jo anticipated, her sisters were in awe of the Laurences' impressive estate. Even Mother paused to admire the elegant designs on the rugs as well as contemplate the splendid display of antiques in each room.
"We are grateful for your hospitality," Mother thanked Mr. Laurence.

The Marches were served an eight-course meal, of which they now enjoyed the final portion: a decadent chocolate cake with tea exported from India. Meg and Amy ate petite bites of the light, fluffy dessert, making sure not to show their teeth when they pulled the silver fork away from their mouth. With straight lady-like posture, they delicately patted the corners of their mouths after each nibble. Beth, who usually did not favor desserts, seemed to savor this particular one. Jo, unlike her more refined sisters, could not resist groaning in delight after each bite, causing Laurie to roll his eyes and make monkey faces at her. She returned the gesture, resulting in blasts of laughter from both parties.
Shaking his head at Laurie but smiling, Mr. Laurence replied to Mother, "I am the one who is grateful. Friendship with your daughters has changed my grandson immensely."
To Mother, Laurie had become the son she never had. "He is a sweet, dear boy. You must be proud of him," she said.
Perhaps it was Mother's sincerity and kindness that moved Mr. Laurence to speak openly about his most devastating losses in life.
"Theodore, or Laurie, as he likes to be called, reminds me of his father. They both have the same mischievous attitude, the same rebellious streak, and the same talent for the arts.

I also had a little girl—the mildest, most adorable daughter parents could hope for.Your Beth reminds me of her so. My darling girl had a love for music, especially the piano, and she would play for my wife and me every evening. How I would look forward to returning home to the sounds of music coming from the conservatory.

"My son, after he became a young man, went against my wishes, and followed his heart to Italy where he fell in love with a beautiful young woman. She was also an artist. They traveled across Europe with their small child, Laurie, living like gypsies—no permanent home, no decent food or clothing. I was furious, of course, and refused to support them financially unless they returned here and lived like normal folks.
"Tragically, they died in an accident, leaving Laurie an orphan entrusted to my care."
"You've raised a wonderful boy, Mr. Laurence," said Mother comfortingly.
Mr. Laurence smiled sadly and said, "Although I may not say it to him enough, I am proud of my grandson."
"What happened to your sweet daughter?" Mother gently inquired.
Mr. Laurence's face was masked in pain. "She developed an illness when she was young and died of it."
Mother remained silent as she looked at her girls, grateful that they were all in good health.

"Grandfather?" Laurie broke the awkward silence. "Jo tells me that one of her sisters here has magic fingers. Apparently they glide effortlessly across the piano, creating the most beautiful melodies to the ears. Ouch!"

Jo had just given Laurie a good strong kick to let him know how she felt about his unauthorized comment. As for Beth, she flushed pink as she slid lower into her chair and avoided eye contact with everyone.

Mr. Laurence, already detecting Beth's shyness and reluctance to be in the spotlight, discreetly remarked, "I'm sure each young lady has a special talent of her own. Whether she chooses to show off that ability is her choice entirely. Now, I suggest we all go to the conservatory to relax."

Everyone stood up and followed the master of the estate to his most beloved room. The conservatory room offered delights for everyone according to individual tastes. For Meg and Amy, a most exotic arrangement of flowers and plants greeted them.
"What an exquisite piece of creation!" exclaimed Amy, bending down to smell a lavender flower.
Meg and Amy strolled around the room, whispering, and nodding their heads in approval at the enchanting display.
For Jo, a shelf full of books prompted her to squeal like a little girl. "Have you ever seen anything so glorious?"
"What's so glorious about an old bookshelf with smelly books?" Laurie asked humorously.
"It's what is inside them that makes them special!" said Jo as she ran her hand across the books' spines.

However, it was Beth who felt the greatest pleasure of all. In one corner of the conservatory stood a stately grand piano, its lid rolled back as if to invite someone to touch its polished keys. As much as Beth's heart yearned to sit on the plush velvet stool and feel the ivory keys, she was too timid to act upon her desire. Her eyes never leaving the magical instrument that called to her, Beth inched away to the opposite side of the room.

"This is my favorite room of the house," Mr. Laurence began in an unusually loud voice. "Unfortunately, during the day, nobody is around to enjoy it. Even the servants don't come in here unless I give them permission. Everything here, especially that piano, is longing for some company. Too bad no one can give it the proper attention it deserves."
Mr. Laurence shook his head regrettably. Out of the corner of his eye, he caught sight of Beth moving out slowly from behind a large armchair.
"Could I perhaps impose on the kindness of your family?" Mr. Laurence continued, pretending that he didn't notice Beth's obvious interest.
"Of course, Mr. Laurence," replied Mother, already discerning what the wise old man was about to suggest.

"Would one of you be so kind as to come here once a day to make sure everything is in order? And perhaps, play on the piano keys so they don't get stuck or dusty?" Mr. Laurence pleaded, his eyes lingering on Beth.
"Would you allow one to play the piano?" Jo asked innocently.

"You could do as you like," the old man replied with a wink, "because when the conservatory door is closed, no one can hear anything. No one will be around to watch or bother you in any way. You will be completely alone."
"Well, I would love to help you, Mr. Laurence," Jo replied heroically, "but I am working during the day, as is Meg. And Amy attends school."
"Maybe I could help, sir," Beth spoke so softly no one heard her at first. Then she repeated it in a slightly louder voice.
"Oh, would you, Beth, dear? Are you sure?" Mr. Laurence intentionally walked over to the piano and tapped his fingers on the keys.
"Look at the sly fox," Laurie muttered to Jo.

Jo nudged Laurie in agreement but kept her focus on Beth, whose footsteps directed her to the piano, as if a strong magnetic force was pulling her. Her trembling fingers reached out and lightly tapped the piano. Then with more boldness, she brushed it much like stroking a cat.
"It would be my pleasure, sir," Beth replied honestly, giving the old man a soft, grateful smile.
Every morning was eventful at the March home, today being no different. Amy had overslept and was very cranky. Her hair, her most precious asset, looked limp and lifeless.
"May I please be excused from school? I’m just not happy today," she whined, munching on a piece of dry bread that would have been warm and soft if she had gotten up in time to eat it.
"Well, then we should all stay home. I’m not happy and neither is Meg," Jo shouted sarcastically from the foyer.
Late as usual, the two older girls were hastening to get out the door, but Jo couldn’t find The Pirate’s Enigma , a book she had borrowed from Aunt March.
"Where could that stupid book be?" Jo yelled in frustration.
"Jo! Mind your tongue and mind your temper!" Mother rebuked as she yanked at Amy’s knots.

"I’ll look for the book," Beth offered in her timid manner. "Pray for me that Aunt March won’t have an urge to hear that story read to her today. I’ll just pretend to be deaf or have a sore throat if she does," Jo remarked, shoving her arms into her thick coat, and finally stepping outside the door.
Blowing kisses at everyone, Meg and Jo began their trek to work.

When Mother went to the window to wave at her girls, Amy reluctantly gathered her school books, got her lunch pail from Hannah, and dragged her feet to the foyer. "You’re so lucky you can stay home all day," Amy said wistfully to Beth.
At other times when Amy said this Beth would shake her head and say, "You’re the lucky one. I wish I could go to school."
Today, however, Beth did not say anything because inside she was feeling very lucky. Today she had something very special to look forward to.
It seemed to take an eternity before everyone was finally gone. Beth was all by herself.

The kitchen door of the March home faced the Laurence mansion, in particular the conservatory, where the object of Beth’s desire was. Beth, however, had a major obstacle to overcome first: her fear. "What if Mr. Laurence suddenly walks into the conservatory?" she said to herself. "What if Laurie hears me play and thinks I’m horrible. Then what if he tells Jo? What if the door locks after I’m inside and I can’t get out?"

But no matter how many "what ifs" Beth could think of, her fear did not hold her back from the beautiful instrument inside. Taking a deep breath, she opened the kitchen door. Sticking her head out and checking to make sure no one was around, she took one brave step forward. Then, like a frightened field mouse, she scurried across the yard onto the stone pathway that led to the mansion.

Pausing to cool her flushed cheeks, Beth felt like an intruder, as if she were entering a home not her own. Mr. Laurence, of course, had given his permission; yet, it was an odd sensation as Beth pushed open the glass doors to the conservatory.
As Mr. Laurence had promised, the room was empty, and as before Beth caught her breath when her gaze fell upon the beautiful piano.

"Hello. I’m Beth." The magnificence of the musical instrument impelled her to introduce herself. Giggling, she continued, "Mr. Laurence says I must come every day and look after you." She lightly stroked the keys. "He doesn’t want you to get dusty or for your keys to get stuck." Even with Beth’s amateur touch, she knew none of the polished keys ever got stuck.
"But just between you and me," she leaned closer to the piano, as if she were whispering a secret, "I was hoping he would ask so I could come and play music on you."
Pulling the stool out, Beth carefully sat down on the soft velvet cushion. "Oh, look!" Beth reached out to open an old leather book resting on the stand.
Inside was a collection of sheet music, many of them songs that Beth knew. "You even prepared music for me to play. How kind you are!" Beth lovingly patted the top of the piano.
After taking a moment to select a song, Beth clenched and unclenched her fists, as she’d seen pianists do. Then, ever so cautiously, she began to play.

At first, the sounds were timid, like Beth, and unsure, lacking confidence and power. However, as she practiced and became more acquainted with her new friend, she felt comfortable enough to open her soul. Oblivious to the passing of time, Beth fell into a world of sound and harmony. True to her word, Beth visited the conservatory every day.

Even though Hannah scolded her for not eating properly or practicing so long that her bones were stiff and numb, Beth felt that nothing could give her greater happiness than the time she spent playing music.
Unknown to Beth, she already had a couple of secret admirers who also were finding joy and comfort in her melodies.

One of them should have been paying closer attention to his lessons, but found himself straining his ears to hear Beth’s music. After Laurie discovered he could hear Beth playing downstairs, he deliberately opened a window in the library in order to hear the music more clearly.
"Must you keep that window open? It’s freezing in here," Mr. Brookes complained to his young pupil.

Mr. Brookes was not amused since the temperature outside was way below zero. The other admirer chose to sit in his study, lean back in his chair, and remember the time when his own little girl’s music could be heard through those very walls.

Since everyone was home on the weekends, Beth could not practice her beloved piano in the conservatory, but she continued to play the music in her mind wherever she was. One Saturday, after returning from the grocer’s with Hannah, Beth found herself encircled by her sisters, all of them shouting with excitement at once.
"You’ve got a gift, Beth!" screamed Amy.
"A gift?" Beth asked, confused.
"Come see it. Come!" Jo took Beth’s arm and led her to the living room.
As she stepped into the familiar room, Beth’s eyes immediately went to the corner where something new stood. It was a beautiful solid oak piano.
"Is this really for me?" she whispered, her voice trembling.
"Look at this card, Beth!" Jo swung a white envelope in her face.
"Read it! Hurry, Beth!" Amy pleaded.
"I can’t. I’m too nervous. Jo, can you read it for me, please?" asked Beth.
Jo ripped the envelope open and read in a loud voice.
My dearest Beth,

I’m afraid you may not like what I am about to say. But I must confess that I have been listening to your beautiful music from my study. You may not realize it but your lovely melodies have brought much happiness back into my home. Therefore, as a token of my deepest appreciation, please accept this gift, which, at one time, belonged to my own daughter. May it bring much music and joy to your home and hearts, as it has done to mine.
Your greatest admirer,
Mr. Laurence
The March girls never lacked ideas about how to keep themselves entertained at home. And having a piano in the house only added to the fun.
"Beth, can you play this one next?" Amy asked about an old folk song she had liked as a little girl. "It reminds me of my childhood," the 12-year-old girl recalled fondly.
Mother turned away, hiding a smile, while Jo rolled her eyes and said in a teasing tone, "And now that you are so old, you want to relive the days of your youth, do you?"
"You don't know how hard my life is right now," Amy started to protest.
Before a quarrel could start, Beth hastily began playing Amy's request.

It was true what Amy said. School had changed quite a bit since her older sisters had attended. Nowadays, girls Amy's age were more outspoken, bold, and daring. As a result, some girls pressured others to do things they would not normally do. Wanting to please and be accepted, sometimes they gave in to the pressure, as Amy did today.

The day started off like any other day: Meg and Jo were running late as usual, thanks to Jo. Beth was dressed and ready to leave for Mr. Laurence's. Mother and Hannah had faithfully prepared everyone's breakfast and packed Amy's lunch. Amy, on the other hand, was unusually quiet. Noticing her sister's odd behavior, Meg asked, "Is there something the matter, Amy?"
Dramatically shaking her head, Amy sighed, then lamented, "Yes, there is."
"Won't you tell me what it is?" Meg further inquired, keeping one eye on Jo, who had come downstairs just a second earlier but then stomped back up muttering under her breath.
Amy brushed her golden curls, lowered her eyes, and said in a soft, pitiful voice, "Today is my turn to buy limes for the girls but I haven't got any money."
"Limes? What for?" Meg asked, surprised.

"Well, Christina, Katy, Mary, and Julia . . ." Amy named the most popular girls in her school and continued, ". . . started the most marvelous game. Each week a girl buys a bag of limes and gives one to her true friends. If you are given a lime, that means that you are considered a friend. And the girls have all been so kind to me. I never knew I had so many friends!" Amy cried modestly.
"So today you are the one handing out the limes," Meg stated.
Nodding, Amy exclaimed, "Oh, dearest Meg! Could you help me out? I don't even have a penny! What will the girls think if I don't have any limes to give them?"
Sweet understanding Meg merely opened her purse and took out a quarter. (Now back in those days, a quarter was worth a lot of money! Just see how many limes Amy could buy with 25 cents!)
"Thank you!" squealed Amy, jumping up and down and hugging her sister.

"A quarter will get me a bag of 25, maybe 26, if Mr. Peters gives me an extra. The girls will be so pleased!" Yelling her loud good-byes cheerfully to everyone, Amy dashed out the door, clutching the quarter tightly in her hand.
"What's made her so happy all of a sudden?" barked Jo, taking two stairs at a time.
"I'll tell you on the way," Meg smiled as she and Jo also left the house.
Before going to school, Amy raced over to Mr. Peter's, the grocer, and bought a big bag of limes. As Amy had hoped, he included one extra.

Carrying the limes to school made Amy feel powerful, since she could choose who would be her friend or not. Holding her head up high and proud, Amy walked into her classroom, deliberately rustling the paper bag so the sound would attract the ears of the other girls. As she expected, some girls ran over to her at once, complimenting her hair, her outfit, and anything else they could think of.
"Amy! Your hair looks so soft today!" shrieked one girl.
"Where did you get that dress? I want the exact same one!" cried another.
Soon Amy was surrounded by most of her classmates, each one trying to get a lime to prove they were her friend.
"Amy? Is that you?" asked a girl who walked over, wearing a pretty pink dress and matching ribbon. The crowd moved to make room for her. She glided lightly across and stood before Amy.
"Hello, Mary," Amy said cheerfully as she opened her bag and chose a plump shiny green lime to give to her. Accepting the lime with just a smile and nod, Mary glided past Amy and went to her desk.
"Hi, Amy! What's in the bag?" asked another girl walking over, wearing a green and white dress. It was Jenny, who had handed out limes last week, but didn't give one to Amy.
"How cheeky! She knows what I have," Amy thought to herself. Aloud she smiled and said in an extra sweet voice, "Oh, it's nothing special."
Jenny's eyes flashed and she was about to say something nasty when Kitty, Amy's best friend, grabbed her arm and said, "He's coming!"
The girls scattered to their seats. Amy shoved the bag of limes into her desk and sat up straight, trying to look innocent.

Mr. Davis, the teacher, a thin, balding man in his thirties, had only one complaint in life: that he was teaching a class of girls. With boys, all Mr. Davis needed to do was lift his stick, furrow his eyebrows and frown, and the class would do just as he instructed. With girls, Mr. Davis quickly learned, it was very different. Many tears, tantrums, and frequent silent treatments resulted if he tried to discipline them in any way. Still, Mr. Davis was very strict and stuck to his methods no matter what. That should have warned the girls since he had made it clear from the beginning that they were not to bring any limes to school.
"Good morning, class," Mr. Davis greeted the girls in his usual mechanical way. "We have a quiz this morning and I expect all of you to . . ."
His speech was interrupted by Jenny, who frantically waved her hand in the air.
Frowning, Mr. Davis asked, "Yes, Jenny?"
"Mr. Davis, I have an allergy and I think someone here has what I'm allergic to," she said in an innocent voice.
"What would that be?" Mr. Davis sighed.
"Lemons . . . ," she paused then continued, ". . . and limes."

Everyone gasped loudly. Amy felt her cheeks burn and her heart pump loudly. Mr. Davis did not say anything at first, but after what seemed like forever, he spoke in a calm but threatening tone. "Who has brought limes to school? Who has deliberately broken my rule?" Mr. Davis slapped his thin stick against the palm of his hand.
No one dared to speak, because everyone, including Amy, knew that Mr. Davis would surely use that stick on anyone who broke his rules.
Things were not going well for Amy March. "Oh, why, oh, why did I have to get these horrid limes," she lamented to herself.

It's true that Amy wanted to be popular or at least liked by the popular girls. She had always wanted to be the center of attention and experience what it would be like to have everyone look up to her. She would get her wish shortly, but not in the way she hoped.
"Miss March," Mr. Davis called to her, still hitting the menacing stick against his hand.
Amy felt her throat go dry, and the hairs on her neck stood up stiff.
"Stand up," the teacher ordered.

Next to her, Amy could hear Kitty whimpering and from the corner of her eye, she saw Jenny smiling wickedly at her. That did it. Amy had disobeyed Mr. Davis' rule, but she was not a coward; she would accept whatever punishment fit the crime. Her parents had taught her that when she misbehaved, she should confess and face the consequences with dignity and humility.
With shaking legs, and trying her best to hide her trembling hands, Amy stood up.
"Do you have a bag of limes in your desk?" Mr. Davis asked.
"Yes, sir, I do," Amy replied bluntly.
All the girls gasped loudly and some of them (Amy suspected Kitty was one) even began crying.
"Bring your bag and yourself up here." Mr. Davis tapped his desk at the front of the room with the stick.

Reaching into her desk, Amy grabbed the bag of limes (nineteen still remaining) and began the dreaded walk to where Mr. Davis stood. Amy could feel the eyes of her classmates burning the back of her head as she passed them, but she refused to look at anyone. All she could think about was how disappointed Mother and her sisters would be after they heard about this incident.
"Do you not know what I said about limes in my classroom?" Mr. Davis shouted suddenly, causing Amy to shrink back.

Grabbing the bag of limes, he walked briskly to the window, opened it with his stick, and to the horror of all observers, emptied the contents onto the streets below. Then, turning around, he looked at Amy and said: "Miss March, you have greatly disappointed me. I do not delight in what I am about to do, but I am a man who keeps his word."

He walked over to her and commanded her to open her hands, palms facing upward. Lifting the stick high above his head, he slapped her palms once, twice, then three times more. Each slap, painful as it was, was nothing compared to how the teacher hurt Amy next.

"To remind others who think they can get away with breaking my rules, you, Miss March, will stand here in front of the class for the remainder of the morning lesson, as a living example of what happens to those who disrespect, disobey, and disregard my words."
Mr. Davis positioned Amy in front of the blackboard so that everyone in the class had a clear view of her and would have to continue to look at her shame throughout the morning.

For Amy, this was the most humiliating, not to mention most heartbreaking experience she ever had in her life. She acknowledged her wrongdoing and willingly received the punishment of five slaps on her hands. This, however, to be displayed like a common criminal, was too excessive and unbearable for the young girl. Still, she kept her head high, refused to let the teacher or her classmates see her internal suffering, and did not shed a single tear. Even so, at that precise moment Amy resolved in her heart that she would never return to school again.
After Amy got home, she spilled her heart out to her family. Everyone, including Beth, who usually saw the good in all people and situations, agreed that Mr. Davis behaved inappropriately.
"Poor Amy. I wish I could have taken your place," Beth wept along with her younger sister.
"Take her place?" shouted Jo, who stopped pacing to throw her fist up and shake it vigorously.
"If it were me, I would have smacked him right across the jaw and knock him down! In fact, I think I just may do that! How dare he humiliate my sister in this way?"

For once Amy did not rebuke Jo for her unladylike behavior or her aggressive boyish attitudes. Mother, however, was concerned, although in her heart, she was in complete agreement with her short-tempered daughter.
"Jo, where will violence get you? Do you think taking revenge is the solution to this problem?"

Jo, cracking her knuckles, did not answer her mother. Mother continued in a patient yet firm voice: "Violent thoughts lead to violent acts. Your father and I do not want any of our girls to be revengeful. We must think with our heads; not react with our hearts."
"I agree with you, Mother, but I can understand Jo's point of view as well. I don't think we should allow Mr. Davis to get away with such maltreatment of his pupils," Meg unexpectedly spoke up.

Nodding, Mother soothed her youngest daughter's head which was lying across her lap. Looking down at her, "Amy, dearest, you are the victim of this distressing affair. What do you think should be done?"

Sniffing and hiccupping, Amy answered in a hoarse voice: "I want to forget everything that happened today. But I don't want to go back to school. I can't, Mother. I won't learn from him. I don't want to."
Mother continued to stroke her hair, considering Amy's request.
"Amy and I could homeschool together, Mother," suggested Beth.
"It will be so much nicer for me to have a fellow pupil than to do my lessons on my own."
"Please, Mother, may I stay at home with Beth and study here? Please don't send me back to that dreadful place," pleaded Amy.
"I can spare a few hours a week helping the girls with their lessons," offered Jo, who thought Amy's idea was an excellent one.
"And I can check their homework," proposed Meg.
Mother looked at each daughter with approval and appreciation.
"Yes, I think that will be the best for now. Of course after Father returns from the war, he will have the final say in the matter. For now, however, Amy, you may stay home and do your lessons."
Happily, Amy sprang up and hugged her mother and sisters.
"But you must promise to listen to your sisters and do your work. Studying at home will be no different from studying at school. Do you understand?" Mother asked in a warning tone.
"Yes, Mother, I promise to faithfully do my lessons. Beth and I will be model pupils. Just you wait and see," Amy replied in her usual cheery way.
Early the next morning, Mother paid a visit to Amy's school and teacher. She kindly thanked him for his efforts, collected Amy's belongings, and with a cool nod, left without a backward glance.

It took a few weeks for the family to adjust to homeschooling for Beth and Amy. Mother, Meg, and Jo all taught different subjects. With Beth, it was fairly easy, since they would each assign her a portion to study for the week, and she could do it at her leisure. Being an obedient and grateful girl, Beth never neglected her lessons, making sure she finished all the work first before she allowed time for herself. Even going to Mr. Laurence's every day, as well as playing on her own little piano, did not distract her from carrying on with her studies.
Amy, on the other hand, found out that she was not as disciplined as her sister. "Oh, Beth, can we please take a break? I'm exhausted!" she cried one afternoon as she struggled with a math problem.
"We just had a break, Amy, and besides, Jo wants us to finish this today," said Beth, pointing to the books stacked on the dining table.

Since Beth and Amy were studying together, Mother felt it best to set aside a certain period of time each day for the girls' lessons. Both Meg and Jo came home around the same time, so they took turns teaching the younger girls for a few hours every afternoon. Three times a week, Mother stayed home in the morning to help the girls with other subjects, and on the days that Mother went out for her volunteer work, Beth and Amy were given homework to do.

"I hope Jo never becomes a real teacher," complained Amy. "I would pity her students if she did. Just look at how much she gives us to do! How can I possibly read all that?" Amy spread her hand toward the books and dramatically flung her pencil down.

"Well, if you would stop wasting time complaining and actually start reading, then maybe you could finish your assignment by the time you're 20," joked Jo as she came into the room carrying more thick textbooks, which she threw on the table.
"Jo!" shrieked Amy. "What is that? Don't tell me we have to do more math problems?"
"You don't have to do all of them tonight," Jo reassured her sister, who let out a sigh of relief. Then Jo immediately added, "Some of this is for tomorrow night, since we won't be here."
Amy sat up straight and narrowed her eyes. "Why not? Where are you going? Is Meg going with you?" she questioned.
Chuckling to herself, Jo flapped a hand at her and said, "It's none of your business. Now have you solved that problem yet or not?"
Just then Meg rushed in, her cheeks flushed and eyes bright with excitement. She secretly whispered something in Jo's ear. Giggling and speaking in hushed tones, the two girls left the room swiftly.
"That's not nice! You shouldn't whisper in front of others!" Amy yelled after them. Frustrated, hungry, and cranky, Amy vowed to find out what her sisters were up to.
The March sisters rarely kept secrets from each other. No wonder Amy found it odd that her sisters would not share their news with her. She had no choice but to find out on her own.

The next afternoon, both Meg and Jo disappeared into their room as soon as they returned from work. Amy could hear a great deal of running around, closet doors opening and shutting, and worst of all, lots of laughter. Feeling particularly grumpy that day, Amy left Beth to figure out the math equation, and crept upstairs to her sisters' room. Luckily for her, the door was slightly open.
"Jo, can you help me with my hair?" Meg was saying.
"As soon as I tie this big Christmas ribbon around my waist," Jo replied, struggling with a satin sash that wound around her dark purple dress.
Giggling, Meg helped her clumsy sister, creating a perfect bow at the back of her dress.
"There, that's better," she laughed cheerfully. Then through the mirror, she caught sight of an uninvited guest. "I think we have a visitor," she remarked to Jo.
Jo swung around and caught Amy peering through the door. "What are you doing? And why aren't you downstairs doing your lessons?" she barked.
Amy stubbornly cocked her head and replied nastily, "Where are you going? Does Mother know? If she doesn't, I'm going to tell."

Jo pinched Amy hard on her arm causing her to squeal like a pig. "You nasty little worm! I told you to mind your own business! As for whether or not Mother knows, do you think we'd sneak around behind Mother's back without getting her permission to go out?" Jo shouted.
"You hurt me! My arm is bruised!" moaned Amy, rubbing the red spot on her arm.
"Serves you right!" said Jo sternly. "Now go downstairs and do your lessons!"
"Just tell me where you're going then," cried Amy.
"Jo, why don't we just tell her?" Meg said, trying to make peace.
"Fine, but don't start crying because you can't come!" Jo turned her back and continued to get ready.
Meg gently rubbed Amy's arm and began in her motherly way, "Laurie has invited us to―"
But before she could finish, Amy interrupted by screaming, "You're going to the theater! You're going to see that play! I wanted to see it! I'm the one who told you about it!"
Neither Meg nor Jo could deny it, for it was indeed Amy who had mentioned the very theater production a few weeks ago. She had heard about it from her friend Kitty.
"Well, darling, Laurie already saw it and he didn't think it was suitable for young ones . . ." Meg tried to reason with her frantic sister.
"That's not fair! I want to go! Please, I'm very mature for my age!" Amy continued to argue.
"Well, I know you are, but, well, maybe if we ask . . ." Meg struggled to find the right words to say.

"No!" Jo slammed the closet door and stamped her feet. "No, no, no! You are not coming with us because you are not invited! If you're as mature as you say you are, stop screaming like a monkey, and get back to your lessons!"

"I hate you, Jo March! I hate you!" Amy screamed at the top of her lungs. "You're going to pay for this! I swear you're going to be sorry!" Amy collapsed on the floor, wailing and throwing her fists around in frustration.

Jo, grabbing her bag, stepped right over her, and when she got to the door, turned around one last time and said in a spiteful voice, "You'd better not be in here when we get back. And you'd better have finished the work I gave you or else you're in big trouble, young lady!"
Meg, looking apologetically at her youngest sister, quietly followed Jo out of the room.
"I promise you will pay for this, Josephine March," sniffed Amy.

Mother enjoyed a quiet time with her two younger daughters that evening. She mended some old clothes to take to the Hummels, while Beth patched up her dolls to give to the little girls in that family. Amy was unusually calm and silent. She kept her nose in her book the whole time.
"Are you feeling all right, dear?" Mother asked worriedly.
"I'm fine, Mother. Just a little tired is all," was Amy's reply.
Beth glanced at her sister with concern but did not say anything.
At around 10:30, Meg and Jo returned from their evening out with Laurie.
"We're back!" Jo announced loudly, in case anybody didn't hear them happily chatting away outside the door.
"Come and tell us how your evening was," Mother called out warmly.
Meg and Jo entered the living room, their cheeks flushed with delight and their eyes sparkling like diamonds.
"Oh, Mother, it was absolutely beautiful," Meg praised, clasping her delicate hands against her chest.

"Well, I thought the costumes were a bit exaggerated," commented Jo critically, but then she started to laugh as she recalled a funny moment. "In one scene, the lights wouldn't come on so the characters didn't know who was standing where. Then finally, when the lights did turn on, well, they were all in the wrong place. So everyone kind of ran around trying to find their positions. We nearly fell out of our seats laughing."
Everyone except Amy thought Jo's description was funny.
