"Are you still mad at me, Amy?" Jo sat next to her sister and teasingly reached to touch her hair.
Moving her head out of Jo's reach, Amy replied coolly, "As you can see, we, too, have enjoyed a lovely evening at home. It was nice to be alone with Mother and Beth for a change."
"That's good. No hard feelings, then?" Jo held out her hand like a man.
Looking at her sister with disdain, Amy ignored her hand but said, "No hard feelings."
Mother watched the exchange between her two daughters uneasily. She could feel something was not right and wondered whether a major fight was brewing.
Yawning, Jo stood up and stretched. "I'm going to bed. Good night, all."
"I think I'll turn in as well," said Meg.
As they walked up together to their room, Meg turned to Jo and said, "Did you think Amy was acting strangely?"
Jo shrugged and replied, "It's obvious she's still mad at me. But she'll get over it."
With such an exciting evening, the girls had forgotten about Amy's threat. The next day, however, they would remember it all too well.
On Saturday mornings, Mother allowed the girls to sleep in while she and Hannah prepared their favorite breakfast. That day Meg was the first one to come down.
"Good morning. Did you sleep well?" Mother greeted her eldest with a kiss.
"Wonderfully, thank you. Last night was so magical," Meg replied dreamily.
"Is Jo still in bed?" asked Mother.
Shaking her head Meg answered, "She's up but she must be in the attic."

No sooner had Meg spoken these words when Jo burst into the room, in her writer's outfit─old red knitted hat, smelly oversized gray cardigan, and her gloves with the fingers cut out. Everyone would have laughed at her comical entrance but for the panic written all over her face.
"Jo, what is the matter?" Mother asked, alarmed.
"I can't find it. It's gone," Jo said in a trembling voice.
"What's gone, darling?" Mother tried to calm her shaking daughter.
"My story. The one I've been working on for the past two years. The one I was writing for Father," Jo replied, not sounding like Jo at all.
"What do you mean it's gone? Are you sure you didn't misplace it?" Mother asked.
"I keep it in my drawer upstairs. Everyone knows that. Why would . . ." Jo suddenly stopped abruptly, her face white and pained.
"Jo, Jo, please calm down," said Meg, who was thinking the exact same thing as Jo, but wanted desperately to prevent her sister from doing something drastic.
"That little witch," Jo muttered under her breath.

She pulled her hat off and threw it hard as she sprinted out of the kitchen screaming madly. At that unfortunate moment, Beth and Amy, awakened by the commotion, came down to see what was causing all the noise.
"What did you do with it?" Jo yelled as soon as she saw Amy.
"Jo! What is the matter with you?" Mother grabbed her wild daughter's arm.
Instead of denying she had anything to do with what was making her sister so angry, Amy pressed her lips together and remained silent.
"Amy?" Mother looked at her, puzzled. "Do you know what happened to Jo's story? If you do, you must speak now."
Wearing a nasty expression, Amy uttered, "I burned it."
The silence that followed was louder than if they had all been screaming at the top of their lungs.
"What?" Jo's voice cracked in agony.
"I burned your stupid story. I told you I would get you back," Amy spat.

Pulling away from her mother's grasp, Jo stomped over to Amy, and slapped her hard across the face. Then without another word, she ran blindly out of the kitchen, her cries of sorrow spreading throughout the house.
"Jo! Jo!" Mother ran after her distressed daughter.
Holding her red cheek, Amy burst into tears as well.
Wanting to shake her and comfort her at the same time, Meg pulled Amy close to her and said, "You have done a wicked thing, Amy. I don't know if Jo will ever forgive you."
That day, Jo locked herself in the attic, refusing to eat or even speak to anyone. No one had ever seen her so disheartened, and it worried everyone tremendously.
After Amy realized how grave her actions were, she quickly began to worry about how she could get Jo to forgive her. "Do you think Jo will come down for dinner?" she asked childishly.
"She has just lost the most precious thing in her life," Mother spoke to her sternly. "Do you think she would be thinking about food at this time?"
"I'm sorry. I wasn't thinking. I was just so angry at the time," Amy tried to explain.
"It's not me you should be apologizing to," was Mother's cool reply.
"Should I go up and see her?" Amy sniffed.
"Let her be, Amy. Just let her be," Beth said sadly.
"Do you think Jo will ever speak to me again?" Amy continued with her questions, hoping that someone would say something to ease her troubled heart.
However, no one could provide the words Amy wanted to hear, for what she had done was so horrible that no one blamed Jo for the way she was feeling.
Amy regretted it miserably. "What have I done?"

No one, not even Jo herself, could deny that she had a short temper. That however, normally meant that whatever angered her was quickly forgotten, and the good-natured Jo prevailed once again. But this time was a different matter. Nothing anyone said, not even Mother's tender comforting words, could soothe the burning pain in Jo's heart.
"I will never forgive her," Jo sobbed into Mother's arms.
"I know you are very angry at this moment," Mother sympathized, "but don't utter words you may regret later."

Inside, Mother's heart wept with her second child. Jo's beauty and charm, unlike Meg's or Amy's, was not immediately obvious to others. Her strength came from deep inside her creative soul and shone in her writing. This particular story was even more important to Jo because it was dedicated to her father. To Jo, taking and destroying her story was the same as cold-heartedly stabbing her in the back then cruelly laughing at her.
"Even if I forgive Amy," Jo sniffed, "I don't think I will ever forget what she did."
Mother held Jo close and silently prayed that this matter would not ruin the relationship between her two daughters forever.

For the next couple of days Jo avoided Amy altogether. When they happened to come across each other, perhaps at mealtimes, Jo stared at her coldly and moved away as if Amy had some contagious disease. Amy found this chilly treatment far more painful than being slapped or pinched by her sister.

On several occasions Amy tried to catch Jo off guard when she happened to be in a somewhat good mood or at least smiling. Each time, however, she was unsuccessful because Jo immediately stiffened and cooled when she saw Amy anywhere near her.

One afternoon, Laurie came over to cheer up his downhearted buddy. At first Jo refused to accept what Laurie called his "special remedy" for the troubled heart─a good cry, a good laugh, and a good friend. But later she changed her mind when she realized that Laurie did make her happier.
"See? It's not too difficult to smile, is it?" Laurie teased.
"I'm not smiling; I'm frowning because you're making my head ache," Jo muttered, turning her head away to hide the corners of her mouth turning upward.
"I have just the thing for headaches!" Laurie shot his finger up as if he had just thought of a brilliant idea.
"Oh no," moaned Jo. "With all your remedies, you should be a doctor; not an artist, when you grow up, dear boy."
Flapping his hand to silence her, Laurie simply said, "Fresh air."
"I beg your pardon?" Jo laughed.
"You need fresh air to get rid of that headache! And I know the best place for it," Laurie nodded knowingly.
"Whatever you say, Dr. Laurie," replied the obedient patient.
"Get your skates and meet me at my house," said Laurie, as he reached for the door handle.
"Oh, skating! Why didn't I think of that! I'll be over in two seconds!" Jo clapped her hands excitedly and ran out of the room.

If Jo had turned around as she crossed the living room, she would have caught sight of Amy, pretending to be interested in a book, but secretly listening to their conversation. Jo, however, was too excited to notice anything.
In the woods behind the March house and Laurence mansion was a pond that froze over every winter. Some years it was even safe to skate on.
"Brookes says the ice may not be thick enough in the middle but we should be able to skate along the edges," Laurie pointed out.
"I'm not afraid. Are you?" Jo asked.
"Of course not," Laurie replied hotly, "but we should be careful because the water will be freezing cold if you fall in."

Jo tied the laces on her skates and stood up. "I'll race you around the pond. Loser has to carry the winner home!" With that Jo sped off, letting out a loud yell. Laurie hurriedly tied his laces and shot after her.

Amy was relieved to see Jo behaving more like her usual self, though she still disapproved of her sister's tomboyish ways. Amy quickly put on her skates, determined to corner Jo while Laurie was around. She felt confident that this would be the day that Jo would forgive her so they could be at peace once again.
"Jo!" she called out to the small figures on the opposite side of the pond.
Hearing her name, Jo looked up but when she saw who was calling, her smile quickly turned into a scowl. She stopped abruptly, nearly causing Laurie to crash into her.
"What's the matter?" Laurie cried breathlessly.
"What is she doing here?" Jo pointed irritably to her sister who waved while trying to balance on her skates.

Amy wobbled on her feet and carefully stepped onto the icy pond. Unfortunately for her, she hadn't heard Laurie's warnings about the middle of the pond. Wanting to reach Jo and Laurie as quickly as possible, Amy began to skate toward them, cutting across the center of the pond.
"Oh no! Amy! Stop! Don't skate there!" Laurie shouted.
Amy could not hear exactly what Laurie was shouting. Her only focus was on reaching Jo.
"Amy! Stop! Go around the edge of the pond!" Jo cried, swinging her arms frantically.

What happened next occurred in a flash, but to Jo everything seemed in slow motion. Amy tilted forward as if she had tripped over something, then she glanced down and immediately jerked her head up, searching for an escape. Jo heard a slight cracking noise like distant thunder, followed by a splash.
"Amy!" Jo screamed as she saw her sister disappear rapidly beneath the icy waters.

Everything that had happened between her and Amy vanished from Jo's thoughts as the only fear that gripped her now was that she might never see her little sister again. Jo started to skate toward the hole Amy had fallen into, but Laurie grabbed her before she could go any further.
"It's too dangerous," he spun his head around and located a large fallen branch. "Help me with this!"
Laurie and Jo got the branch and carefully skated closer to where Amy's head was bobbing in and out of the water.
"Amy! Grab this! We'll pull you out!" Jo yelled as she and Laurie pushed the branch toward the hole.
Somehow Amy heard her sister's instructions and grasped the branch with her cold, weak hands.
"Hold tightly!" Laurie shouted, as he and Jo pulled Amy out of the freezing waters.
When they had gotten Amy to safer ground, Jo threw her own coat over Amy's shivering little body. Laurie did the same, even taking off his wool sweater and covering Amy's head with it.
"We have to get her home, now!" Laurie said in an unusually authoritative voice.
Jo was not about to argue with her friend. She was glad that someone was taking charge of the situation, because she had never felt so helpless in all her life.

Laurie carried Amy all the way home, talking to her, trying to keep her from falling asleep, because that would have lowered her body temperature even more. Jo was trying her best to contribute to the rescue mission but her whole body and mind were numb.
"What if she dies? It'll be my fault. How can I live with myself if Amy dies?" Jo repeated over and over again under her breath.
"She's not going to die, Jo. Just keep talking to her," Laurie panted.
Even though his main concern was Amy, Laurie's thoughts never left his best friend, who he knew felt guilty about the unfortunate accident.
"Mother March!" Laurie called out, kicking the door open with his foot when they got to the March home. Laurie was the only one who was allowed to call Mrs. March by that name.
"Heavens! What's happened?" Mother gasped as soon as she saw the three of them burst into the house.
Laying Amy in the chair closest to the fireplace, Laurie tried his best to explain.
For some reason, seeing her Mother's pale-white face made Jo feel even guiltier and she could not control the tears that started to slide down her cheeks.

Meanwhile, Mother was giving instructions to everyone. "Hannah! We need more wood. Meg, get some hot towels and boil a pot of hot water. Beth, go upstairs and grab every blanket you can find and bring them quickly. We need to keep her as warm as possible."

Laurie stepped back, letting Mother take charge of the situation. He shivered, not realizing until then how cold he was. Warming himself by the fire, he glanced over at Jo, who was shaking visibly from the cold, but did not seem aware of it. Wordlessly, he went over to her, putting his arms around her shoulders and patting her gently.
Jo, grateful for Laurie's kindness, leaned her head against him, and sobbed until no more tears would come out.

With the exception of a slight numbness in her hands and feet, Amy was going to be fine. Laurie and Jo had acted speedily and saved Amy before any severe damage had happened. Still, Jo could not help but feel that Amy's fall was her fault in the first place.
"Jo? Come here, dearest," Mother whispered when she saw Jo standing awkwardly at the doorway.

Mother had just come in to check up on Amy, who was sleeping soundly. Jo paced outside the bedroom but did not have the courage to go inside. Her mother's kind words, though, seemed a warm invitation.
"Amy is doing fine. She just needs to rest," Mother spoke softly. "You need some rest too."
Jo felt her throat tighten and the tears sting her eyes once again.
"Jo, whatever you are feeling, this was not your fault," Mother said, sensing Jo's painful guilt.
"But it was . If I hadn't been so mean, she . . . if only I hadn't lost my temper . . ." Jo choked.
Mother pulled Jo close to her and whispered, "I understand how you feel."
"How can you know what it feels like to be so angry, Mother?" sniffed Jo. "You're the most patient, kindest person in the world."
Mother smiled shyly and said, "I try very hard but, to be honest, I used to be exactly like you."

Jo stared at her mother unbelievingly. Mother was a role model for all her daughters. For her to admit that she had a temper like Jo's was too much of a shock. Shaking her head, Jo said, "No, I can't believe that, Mother. You're not like me at all."
Chuckling quietly, Mother replied, "You may think I am perfect and make no mistakes but Jo, I'm also human. I have many faults and weaknesses. I'm just better able to control them as I get older."
Jo, no longer crying, quietly contemplated her mother's words. "Do you think I will ever change and be like you?"

"That depends on whether or not you want to change. Some people feel that anger makes them stronger and more respected. Others see that anger, though sometimes unavoidable, can be controlled. That is what I am learning," said Mother.
Amy stirred and mumbled something softly in her sleep. Watching her, Jo confessed, "I thought I could never forgive her for destroying my story. I didn't want to forgive her."
"How do you feel now?" Mother asked kindly.

"I realize that I can always write another story. Amy might have ruined what I wrote down, but I still have it preserved in here." Jo tapped her heart. "And," she continued, "although stories may be replaceable, if I lost Amy, there would be no one to take her place."
Mother gave Jo a kiss and patted her hand, saying, "Yes, you can and will change, Jo. One day, that temper of yours will no longer control you." Mother got up and left Jo to sit with Amy for a while.
Jo started to feel better, knowing that perhaps she wasn't so hopeless. "If Mother can change, so can I. I am her daughter, after all," she said to herself.
"Jo?" Amy whispered weakly, her eyes half-opened.
"I'm here, darling," Jo replied warmly.
Amy stared at her for a long time before speaking. "Jo? I'm so sorry. Please forgive me."

Wiping her hand across her eyes, Jo, who had never cried so much in her life, took Amy's hand and held it close to her face. "Me, too, Amy. Let's forget all that's happened in the past and look forward. What do you say?"
Amy gave Jo a faint smile and squeezed her hand as she answered, "Thank you, Jo."

That evening, Jo could not sleep. Her mind was racing with thoughts about the events of the past few days. She suddenly found herself wanting to put everything down in writing because a story was forming in her head. When the other girls had gone to sleep, Jo crept up to her sanctuary, a place she had not visited since Amy had destroyed her story, and sat at the old familiar desk. She began to write, her pen flying over the paper, while she tried to jot down every word spilling out of her. In the end, Jo stayed up all night completing her story.

Finally, Jo leaned back in her chair and, stretching her neck and shoulders, thought of the perfect title for her story. Taking a clean sheet of paper, she wrote in big letters "Like Mother, Like Daughter—A story by Josephine March." Cradling her chin in her hand, Jo watched the sun rise, glad to be alive and to enjoy another beautiful day.
Although it was a long time in coming after an exceptionally lengthy and dreary winter, spring finally arrived.

For the March girls, springtime signaled new beginnings, new opportunities, and new dreams. Meg was already off to a good start that season, having been invited to several parties hosted by her wealthy friends. "What shall I wear?" was her most frequent complaint lately.

Looking through the closet, Meg pulled out a light green dress and held it up to her body. Through the mirror, she could see that it suited her complexion and enhanced the color of her eyes. But the dress was quite a few years old, and its hem was worn. "Oh, what should I do?" Meg let out a sigh of frustration.
"What's the matter, Meg?" asked Beth, walking in with an armful of folded laundry.
Relieving her of some of the burden, Meg explained, "Annie Moffat is having a party this Saturday and I haven't got anything to wear."
Beth replied thoughtfully, "You have many beautiful dresses, Meg."
"But they're so old!" complained Meg. "Annie and the others will all have new silk dresses in this year's style, and I'll be the only one wearing an old, ugly dress."
"I think you'll be the prettiest girl at the party, whatever you wear," Beth remarked. Cheering up a little at her sister's kind words, Meg continued with Beth's help to search for something to wear.
"What about this dress?" Beth asked, pulling out a white gown with blue flowers all over it.

Meg examined it closely for rips, holes, or stains but could not find any. In fact, the dress was in tip-top condition and it did flatter her a lot. "Thank you, Beth. This dress will have to do," Meg approved wholeheartedly.

The much-anticipated evening was soon upon them. Leaving Meg to get ready for her big night, Jo and the others amused themselves by doing what they loved most: Jo was reading a novel (another one "borrowed" from Aunt March), Beth was playing the piano, and Amy was drawing a picture of one of Mr. Laurence's horses.
"Has Meg come down yet?" Mother asked as she strolled into the living room, holding a velvet jewelry box.
Shaking her head disapprovingly, Jo replied, "I don't know why it takes so long to get ready. Just throw the dress on, slip into your shoes, and you're good to go."
Rolling her eyes, Amy said, "That's the difference between looking like a lady, and looking . . . well . . . just unladylike."
"How do I look, girls?" Meg floated in while her sisters were talking.
They all, including Jo, sucked in their breath, for Meg looked like an enchanted fairy princess.
"You look positively beautiful," complimented Mother, smiling approvingly at her eldest daughter.
"Oh, Meg, all the men at the party will want to dance with you," gushed Amy.
"Just be careful with your heels this time," Jo said jokingly, reminding Meg of the last party they attended together.
Laughing, Meg promised she would.
"I thought tonight would be a proper occasion for you to wear this," said Mother, opening the jewelry box and taking out a string of pearls. She put them around Meg's slim neck.
"Oh, Mother! They're perfect!" Meg's cheeks flushed with delight. "I feel like the most beautiful girl in the world."
Saying good-bye to her family, Meg left for Annie's house in high spirits.
When Meg got to Annie's house, however, her mood rapidly faded. At home, Meg may have been the radiant princess but among her friends, she felt like a farm girl on her way to milk the cows.
"Meg, you look . . . so charming," was Annie's forced comment when she opened the door.
"I like your hair. Did you do it yourself?" Sallie asked a little too sweetly.

Meg touched the curls on her head and nodded shyly, trying hard not to stare at what her friends were wearing. Just as she suspected, Annie, Sallie, and Annie's sister Belle were all wearing silk dresses in pastel spring colors. Their hair was perfectly pulled back into a high bun with two curls hanging down the side of each cheek. Meg also noticed that her friends wore make-up on their lips, eyes, and cheeks. They looked sophisticated and very elegant.
While Annie led her inside the house, Meg noticed Sallie and Belle whispering to each other.
"Meg," Sallie said in a cheery voice as she took Meg's arm. "You have the most beautiful eyes and I think if you had just a little bit of color there, they would stand out even more."
"I don't know," Meg said hesitantly. Mother did not approve of her girls wearing make-up.
"It'll be fun! And you'll look even prettier," Annie tried to persuade her.
"We're all wearing some. Don't you think we look nice?" Sallie pushed her face up closer to Meg.
Meg had to admit her friends looked very lovely.
"Well, maybe just a little then," she said, giving in.
Chattering excitedly, the four girls hurried up the stairs, giggling.
While Belle applied Meg's make-up, Sallie decided to change Meg's hair. Even before Meg could protest, Sallie swiftly pulled out the pins in her hair and brushed out the curls.
"Your hair was lovely, but a little old-fashioned. I think this style will suit you even better," Sallie said as she pulled, curled, and twisted Meg's hair into a bun.
"And your dress, which I love," Annie added rather hastily, "makes your skin look dull. But I think this one will make you glow!"
Meg immediately fell in love with the bright blue silk dress Annie held up, but pride stopped her from admitting it. "I think what I am wearing suits me fine, thank you," she replied graciously.
"Just try it on and see how it looks," begged her friends.

Not wanting to disappoint them, Meg changed out of her old cotton dress and into the shiny silk one. Almost at once, she felt the difference as the soft silk wrapped around her body. She suddenly stood up taller, held her head higher, and felt more confident.

After a few added touches to Meg's hair and make-up, Annie placed her hands on Meg's shoulders and turned her around to face the mirror. Meg gasped when she saw her reflection, for the face that stared back at her was not a farm girl's but a sophisticated young lady's.
"Oh, Meg, please wear this dress tonight!" cried Annie.
"Look at your amazing eyes and lips!" Belle pointed out.
"Meg, look at how your hair enhances your cheekbones!" said Sallie.
So finally Meg gave in to persuasion and agreed to wear the dress, make-up, and hairstyle her friends had chosen for her.

Grabbing hands, the four friends jumped up and down excitedly complimenting one another. Meg felt so proud to be a part of this exclusive group. Still holding hands, the girls walked down to the party that awaited them.

Not only did Meg look different at Annie's party, she acted differently, too. She walked with her shoulders pulled back proudly, coolly acknowledging people in an aloof manner as she passed them. When it came to dancing, Meg was selective, choosing only those partners who looked wealthy and handsome. She loved all the attention she was getting as she tossed her head back and laughed loudly (almost as loud as Jo) while dancing, quite aware that some of the other girls were jealously staring and whispering about her.
"Oh, I need to rest my feet," Meg gasped to her dance partner, who happened to be Annie's older brother Ned.
"Only if you promise to let me have the next dance," Ned said, leading her to some chairs.
Touching his shoulder lightly, as she had seen Sallie do, Meg said in a flirty voice, "I'll think about it. Now be a pet and get me a drink."
Ned happily obliged while Meg collapsed onto a chair next to Sallie.
"Meg, you are the darling of the party tonight," Sallie giggled.
Meg lightly touched her eyes with her handkerchief, being careful not to erase her make-up. "I have never had so much fun," she confessed.
"Well, I think Ned really likes you," Sallie whispered.

Meg looked over at Ned who was carrying two drinks over to where she sat. Ned was a tall, handsome young man, about two years older than Meg. She knew from Annie that their parents were hoping he would find a suitable wife and marry in the very near future. Meg hoped she might be that special someone he was looking for.
"Here you go," Ned said. As he handed the glass to Meg. However, he accidentally spilled some of the drink.
"My dress!" cried Meg, jumping up and trying to wipe off the mess with her handkerchief.
"I'm such a clumsy baboon!" exclaimed Ned.
"That's quite all right," reassured Meg, "I'll just step into the ladies' room and clean this off. Please excuse me." She left Ned standing there awkwardly with Sallie.

At the Moffats, even the ladies' room was a lavish affair. Massive gold-trimmed mirrors covered one wall above a solid oak rectangular table. Gold-plated brushes and hand mirrors, embroidered handkerchiefs, and fresh red roses in crystal vases adorned the table. Meg sat on one of the dozen plush velvet chairs set out along the table. On the other side of the wall were the toilets and wash basins.

Glancing at herself in the mirror and admiring her reflection, Meg proceeded to remove the stain on her dress. Luckily it came off and only needed to be dried. Meg pressed a handkerchief against the spot to soak up the moisture. Outside she could hear the faint sounds of a familiar tune. Humming along, she closed her eyes and imagined she was dancing with Ned.

"Did you see how she flirted with Ned?" came a high-pitched voice loudly from the washroom area. The wall blocked Meg's view of the speaker. For some reason, however, Meg knew the speaker was referring to her. Then another girl spoke in a lower voice but still clear enough to hear, "That's Belle's dress she's wearing."
"Of course it is. Her family can't afford anything like that. I heard she came tonight wearing a cotton summer dress."
Cruel laughter followed that remark.
"Does she think Ned Moffat will ask her out?" the high-pitched voice asked.
"Heavens, no! Annie and she are friends, but they would never allow her to become family."

Listening intently to their conversation, Meg did not realize that she had rolled her handkerchief into a tight ball and was clenching her jaw. Never had she been so humiliated. She lowered her shaking hands and slowly turned to look at the stranger staring back at her from the mirror. Until that moment, Meg did not realize how different she really looked. In fact, she was unrecognizable. "I hate you," she spat to her own pathetic face, which did not look so lovely any more.

Fantasies of marrying Ned Moffat and being the mistress of their impressive estate vanished into thin air. Delusions of being wealthy and sophisticated like Annie and Sallie faded even more quickly. Suddenly Meg longed for the comfort and simplicity of her family and home. Glittering gold and sparkling crystal no longer appealed to her, nor did the lovely silk and lace dresses of spring colors. Meg just wanted to be herself and be with those who loved her for who she was.

Blindly trying to find her way out of the Moffats' home, Meg was not looking where she was going. "Oh!" she exclaimed as she bumped into someone and fell to the floor. In her quest to locate the front entrance without attracting attention, Meg had run into someone heading toward the very festivities she was trying to escape.
"I beg your pardon, Miss," the young man apologized profusely, extending a hand to help her up.
"No, I should be the one apologizing, I wasn't looking . . . Laurie!" Meg shouted in relief when she saw who her victim was.

Laurie stared at her for a long time, obviously not immediately recognizing her. When he finally did, his jaw dropped, and he looked at her critically with a disapproving eye. "Meg? Sweet, innocent Meg? That can't be you!" were his first words.
"Laurie, I'm so happy to see you!" cried Meg. "I've been so miserable."
Laurie, who was still in shock, demanded, "What happened to you? What's that on your face? You look like a stranger to me!" He was very upset and did not hide the fact.
"Laurie," Meg pleaded, "please, I know I don't look like myself. I don't feel like myself either. But right now, I'm so miserable and I have to get out of here. Won't you please help me?"

Softening as he heard the desperation in Meg's voice, Laurie wrapped his arms around her and comforted her, saying, "I'm sorry for being so rude, Meg, but I was quite shocked. Of course, I'll help you. Come, now, let's get you home." Like a true gentleman, Laurie, without another remark about her appearance, escorted Meg home.

When Meg got home, she told her family what had happened. She spoke honestly about how she envied the wealth of her friends and their lifestyle. Then she told them about overhearing the conversation in the ladies' room that eventually opened her eyes to reality.
"I realize that what I have now may be simple to some, but it's very dear to me," sniffed Meg. "I wouldn't change my life now with any amount of money or pretty things."
"And we wouldn't want you any other way. You're our Meg and we love you," comforted Mother.
Hugging her mother and sisters, Meg gratefully accepted the precious life she had.

Anyone passing a certain smiling young lady skipping down the street would have assumed that she was happy. In fact, Jo was more than happy; she was ecstatic. She was sure to be spotted and gossiped about as she sprinted like a wild horse on a public street, but at this moment in time, she did not care. She felt like a free pony, released from captivity into the wild. Her captor: Grumpy, difficult Aunt March. Her release: Summer holidays.

Every summer Aunt March took a trip to Europe, often staying until the beginning of autumn. Although Jo secretly prayed that Aunt March would ask her to accompany her one day (as Jo had always longed to see Europe), still it was pure joy not to have to work all summer.

Jo pitied those poor souls who were trapped indoors on this glorious sunny afternoon. One of them, she noted when she got to her house, was probably sitting at the table with his books opened but his thoughts wandering off as he impatiently waited for his lessons to end. Turning toward Laurie's library, where the window was wide open, Jo called out in a teasing voice, "I wonder what I will do tomorrow since I can do whatever I want, unlike some people who must study their lessons."

Just as Jo had predicted, Laurie popped his head out the window and called out playfully, "Excuse me, would you mind keeping your voice down? Some of us are trying to get better educated, thank you very much."
Laughing loudly, Jo wiggled her foot at him, their signature greeting now.
Waving his foot back, Laurie called down, "Are you off now? Have your holidays begun?"
"Yes!" shouted Jo. "And I am ever so happy. I have so many things I want to do!"
"Well, I hope I am included in some of your plans. I have absolutely nothing to do this summer, so I'm counting on you girls to keep me entertained and out of trouble," Laurie said with a wink.

"Don't worry, friend, we'll have ourselves a ball," Jo promised. Waving at Laurie, Jo hopped and skipped up to her house and went in, but not before she heard Mr. Brookes reprimanding Laurie for interrupting their discussion on the French Revolution.

By coincidence Meg also got an early summer holiday because the Kings had unexpectedly decided to visit their relatives in California and were planning to leave shortly. Needless to say the girls were thrilled at the prospect of spending the summer without the burden of work.
"Then may Beth and I get an early holiday as well?" Amy had asked as soon as she heard her sisters' good news.

After much discussion with Mother, Meg and Jo decided the girls could have a few extra weeks to bask in the sun as long as they still did some homework every now and then. Content with that arrangement, Amy promptly shut her book and began working on her new art project, namely oil painting.
On the eve of their first day of summer vacation, the girls made many plans about what they were going to do with all that time.
"I want to go fishing," Jo started.
"I don't want to do anything at all; just go outside and paint, draw, and sleep," Amy said dreamily.

Mother, carrying in a stack of clothes to be mended, remarked, "We have plenty to do around the house and since Father isn't here, we need to make repairs before the winter and…" Mother stopped talking when she noticed the girls had long faces.
"Whatever is the matter, girls?" she asked.
Meg looked at Jo, who looked at Amy, who looked at Beth, who looked back at Meg.
Mother waited patiently, watching this wordless communication with amusement.
"Well, we thought, since it is our holiday, that—" Meg looked pleadingly at Jo.
"That we'd like a holiday," Jo finished for Meg, "Not just from work and school, but also from our chores and not to have to worry about repairs; just to be lazy."
"Do you think it would be relaxing if you did nothing at all?" Mother asked.
"We are going to do things," Amy stated, "just things that we want to do; not what we have to do."
The others nodded their heads in agreement.

"I understand," Mother said, "but I must warn you that being lazy and relaxing are not the same thing. But this may be a good learning experience for you girls. Let's try an experiment." Jo jumped up and cried passionately, "I love experiments!"

"Starting tomorrow, for one week," said Mother, "you girls can do whatever you want, whenever you want to do it. Hannah and I will continue to do our share of the housework and cook, but you will not have to do yours."
Here, Mother was interrupted by loud shouts of joy and clapping. She held up her hand to silence them and then continued, "But you must keep this up for one full week."
"That won't be too hard," giggled Amy.
"Don't be too sure, Amy," warned Mother. "Doing nothing is harder than you think. Now, what do you say?"
"Let the lazy summer experiment begin!" shouted Jo.

The first day of the experiment was just as wonderful as the girls imagined. They slept a lot, got up whenever they felt like it, and did whatever they liked. Beth, on an empty stomach, ran over to Mr. Laurence's house to play the grand piano. Meg chose the arduous task of sitting in the sun and doing nothing. Amy decided to paint Meg doing nothing and took all her oil paints outside to set up her easel. Jo, with one of her favorite books on hand, joined her sisters nearby, and soon the March girls, minus one, were enjoying their lazy summer morning.
"Ah, isn't this relaxing?" sighed Meg, turning her face up toward the warm rays of the sun.
"Hold still, Meg," cried Amy as she tried to capture her sister's face.
"Will you please be quiet so I can read in peace?" Jo called out from under a shady tree.
As the sisters soaked up the sun in serenity, they could hear the faint sounds of Beth playing the grand piano at Mr. Laurence's mansion.
Of course, even lazy people get hungry, so when Jo could no longer ignore the growling of her stomach she said, "I'd better eat something or my stomach will complain."
"Yes, I'm getting hungry, too," said Meg.
"I'll come as well," Amy said, abandoning her paintbrush and colors without a second glance.

The three sisters went inside to the kitchen expecting some food to be ready for them but they were startled to see nothing on the table. Laughing, Meg confessed, "I think it was my turn to make lunch and I forgot completely. I'm sorry."
"No need to apologize, my dear," Jo said graciously, "we're on holiday. I'm sure we can find something to eat."
Searching high and low, the girls finally found some stale bread and butter, which they washed down with cold tea.
"Let's go back to relaxing then," said Jo, patting her still growling stomach.
The girls did just that.

After a few days, the lazy holidays were turning into a nightmare. Since the girls were not allowed to do their chores—as part of the experiment—the house soon began to look and smell like a dumpster. The only tidy, well-kept part of the home was Mother’s bedroom and her spot in the living room where she had her chair and reading table. She sat there now, pretending to be interested in a book, but actually observing her girls.

Meg, Mother noticed, looked cross and agitated, traits her eldest daughter normally did not display. Her hair was carelessly tied up and her clothes had several stains, even a small hole under the armpit.
Jo looked like a volcano ready to erupt as she stomped around, shouting loudly at no one in particular, "Whoever took my book had better hand it over at once!"

Beth, the mildest and gentlest of the four, could be mistaken for a starved child because she was spending all her time playing the piano and forgetting a fundamental part of her well-being: eating. Glancing at Beth’s fingers, it was just as Mother suspected: they were swollen, stiff, and raw.

Of the four girls, however, Amy was clearly the messiest. Her paints and brushes were scattered everywhere, making it a challenge at times to walk without tripping over her art tools. Her usually curly bouncy hair was now oily and sticking to her cheeks like uncooked bacon. Specks of paint decorated her hair as if someone had stood over her and sprinkled it generously onto her head.
"Thank goodness, tomorrow is the last day of this experiment," Mother said to herself.

The next morning the girls reluctantly went downstairs expecting cold food at the table. During the week of the experiment, by the time the girls had got up, their breakfast was already cold. They were grumbling and complaining until Jo, who was leading the pack, stopped, sniffed, and smiled. "Girls! Can you smell that?" she asked.
"Mmm . . . smells like sausages!" said Amy, breathing in deeply.

Like a pack of famished wolves, the girls tore into the dining room, where they were greeted by Mother, who was just laying out a plate of sausages. "Good morning, my little daughters. Since the experiment ends today, I thought we’d celebrate with a late breakfast."
Gratefully, the girls sat down to devour their meal while Mother asked their opinions about the experiment.
"It was fun for one day," Jo said in-between bites. "But I got so bored! I actually wanted to clean up my room after a while."
Meg nodded and said, "I had such an ache to pick up a needle and mend some old clothes."
"Well, I didn’t realize how messy I was," cried Amy. "My hair, my clothes . . . I looked frightening!"
"I found that when I played the piano, I forgot about everything else," said Beth, blushing. "Sometimes I even forgot to eat."
"How lucky that we have you, Mother," said Amy dramatically. "Without you, we might have died!"
Mother was thoughtful for a moment before replying, "Well, actually I’m taking the day off tomorrow."
The girls stared at her, stunned.
"What do you mean?" asked Meg.
"Since you girls had one week to do as you please, I think I deserve one day all to myself," said Mother.
The girls looked at each other, at a loss for words, until Jo finally said, "Of course, Mother should have the day off. Don’t worry, Mother, we’ll manage fine on our own."

"Thank you, darling," said Mother with a smile, then added, "and by the way, Hannah is taking the day off too." With that Mother got up and left her daughters contemplating how to deal with the situation.
That day was a busy one for the March sisters. After they happily and eagerly performed their chores, they discussed how to divide Mother and Hannah’s workload between them.
"Since Jo and I get up early, we’ll make breakfast," said Meg.
"I can go to the grocer’s to buy our fruit and vegetables," offered Beth.
"I’ll do the wash and hang it outside to dry," said Amy.
"What else does Mother do?" Jo asked, tapping the pencil on her lips.
"Who’s going to make lunch and dinner?" Amy asked.
"Amy and I can make lunch if Jo and Beth take care of dinner," suggested Meg.
With everyone happy, Jo sat back with her hands folded behind her head and said in a relaxed, confident way, "Mother has nothing to worry about."

It was strange not to see Mother or Hannah in the kitchen the next morning, but Meg and Jo quickly got busy making breakfast. They decided on ham and eggs with fresh bread, since Mother always baked her breads early in the morning.
"Jo!" Meg cried, looking around, "we forgot to set the dough out last night for the bread!"

The girls had often watched Mother kneading the dough and setting it out to rise the night before so that she could bake it first thing in the morning. Enjoying a slice of warm fresh bread might not seem like much, but it brought great pleasure and comfort to the girls at the start of the day. Today, sadly, they would have to do without that morning ritual.
"Where are the eggs?" Jo asked, looking in the baskets and the pantry.
"Something’s burning on the stove!" Meg pointed to the smoke coming from a pan.

"Oh, the ham!" exclaimed Jo. Forgetting how hot the pan was, she grabbed the scorching handle then dropped the pan and its contents (four thick pieces of burnt ham) onto the floor. The girls ended up having fruit and milk for breakfast.
Just before setting out for the grocer’s, Beth realized she didn’t know what to buy, so she went to Mother, who was sitting in her chair reading.
"Darling," Mother interrupted, holding up her hand when Beth started speaking, "today is my day off. You must figure it out on your own."
A little while later, Amy also approached Mother for advice on what she should wash first. Mother simply repeated what she had told Beth and returned to her book.
The girls did not realize how dependent they were on Mother and Hannah. Sitting together for their dinner—a simple meal of meatloaf and bread—the girls talked about their day.
"I didn’t realize how much Mother and Hannah did for us," said Meg, resting her weary head on her hands.
"My hands are still hurting from doing the laundry," complained Amy.
"It was so hard to choose what to buy," said Beth.
"I wonder if Mother plans to take days off regularly," said Amy.
"I think Mother wanted to teach us a lesson," said Jo.
Nodding, Meg agreed. "Our experiment taught us to appreciate work."
"And Mother wanted us to see the importance of taking care of ourselves," added Jo.
"And of helping each other," said Beth.
"And supporting each other," said Meg as she tried to swallow a bite of dry salty meatloaf.
"And loving each other," smiled Amy, pushing her plate away.

Summer, was passing too quickly and although he was having fun with the girls, Laurie felt restless. He wanted to travel and visit his friends in Europe. Thinking about this, he sat on the window ledge, looking across at his unusually quiet neighbors one day.

"What is she up to?" Laurie wondered as he suddenly caught sight of Jo coming out of the house. He was about to call out to her when he noticed her acting very strangely. "Where is that girl going?" he asked himself.

Jo tiptoed out of the house, being careful not to slam the door, and quietly walked down the path. She was carrying a large envelope, which she held tightly as if her life depended upon it. She walked briskly down the street, looking behind her every few minutes.
"She’s sneaking out! Well, we can’t have that!" Laurie chuckled. He got up and hurried downstairs. Whatever Jo was trying to hide, he was determined to find out.

Laurie found Jo’s pace irregular. Sometimes she skipped, but other times she slowed to a crawl as if she were thinking about something. People like her were the most difficult to follow since you never knew if they would stop suddenly, turn around, and notice they were being followed. Still, Laurie thought his disguise was a good one. He wore his grandfather’s hat and walked with a cane.

Jo headed into town, passing the dentist’s office then the grocer’s, and walked toward the billiard room, but to Laurie’s great relief, she passed that disreputable place and went inside an office located next to it.
"Where on earth is she going?" Laurie was dying to know.
Positioning himself in front of a dress shop, he pretended to be interested in the latest colors of the season, while he waited for Jo to come out.
Laurie wondered how many more times he could raise his hat in greeting to each passing lady, as was the custom for gentlemen to do in those days.

"Good day, Madam," he said, imitating his grandfather’s voice as two elderly women approached the shop he was standing in front of. Keeping one eye on the office where his friend had gone, Laurie politely opened the door for the ladies.
To his delight, across the street, another door was opening at that moment, and soon Jo appeared looking excited, happy, and relieved. Laurie noted that she was no longer carrying the envelope.
Having successfully ushered the ladies inside the store, Laurie ran toward Jo. Raising his hat, he shouted, "Excuse me, Miss, one moment, please."
Jo turned around to see a gentleman running (quite quickly, in her opinion) in her direction. He looked very familiar and his voice sounded like . . .
"Laurie?" she asked, surprised to see her friend in town.
"Of course it’s me," he replied.
"What are you doing here?" Jo asked as she pulled the hat from his hand and tried it on herself.
"Never mind me, Jo March. What are you hiding?" Laurie demanded to know.
Flushing, Jo looked away and shrugged, "I don’t know what you’re talking about."
"Don’t deny it, Jo, I saw you. I followed you here, so I know you went inside that office. What is it? What is your secret? Tell me!" Laurie nearly shouted.
Jo crossed her arms stubbornly and said, "That’s very naughty of you to follow me, Theodore Laurence. And I don’t have to tell you anything if I don’t want to."
Laurie chewed on his lower lip then with a twinkle in his eye said, "If you tell me your secret, I’ll tell you mine."
Jo considered his offer then stuck out her hand. "Deal, but you must promise not to tell a soul."
Laurie swore he wouldn’t say a word.
Rubbing her hands together, Jo said breathlessly, "I sold two stories to the newspaper. They bought my stories, Laurie!"

Laurie stared at his friend, then let out a loud shout of joy and gave her a big hug. The two women who had entered the store now came out and seeing this public display of affection, covered their mouths and shook their heads disapprovingly.
Ignoring them, Laurie and Jo linked arms and ran down the street, still cheering and making a lot of noise.
As they got closer to their neighborhood, Jo turned to Laurie and said, "Now you have to tell me your secret."
Laurie covered his mouth and held back a giggle. "I don’t know . . ."
"Laurie! We had a deal!" Jo said, grabbing his arm. "What is it? Tell me!"
"Okay, but remember, you mustn’t repeat what I’m about to tell you," he said seriously.
"Laurie, tell me already!" Jo nearly screamed.
"Brookes has a crush on . . ." Laurie’s voice drifted off.
Jo, her eyes growing bigger and more alarmed, whispered, "Who? Meg?"
Laurie nodded, grinning. "It’s more than a crush, actually; Brookes is in love with your sister."
Jo stopped, her feet suddenly heavy and heart weighed down with this unexpected revelation. "No, that’s impossible." Jo shook her head.
"Why? Meg is a very beautiful girl and Brookes isn’t a bad chap," said Laurie.
Although she knew it would happen eventually, Jo refused to believe that one day her sisters would get married and have their own families.
"Laurie, are you sure?" Jo asked, hoping this was one of his pranks.
Laurie, however, nodded and said, "He wrote it in his diary, which happened to be open one day, and in passing, I . . ."
"You read his diary? You little crook!" Jo punched Laurie in the arm.
"I didn’t read the whole thing. I just glanced at it. Ouch! That hurt, Jo," he moaned, rubbing his sore arm.
Jo pushed him farther away; her once light and carefree steps were now burdened with what Laurie had just told her.

Two days later, Mother and all the girls, except for Jo, were sitting quietly in the living room, all occupied with their own work. Their peaceful afternoon, however, was suddenly interrupted by a noisy commotion in the foyer.
"My word," Mother exclaimed, putting down her sewing.
At that moment, Jo, the cause of the deafening sounds, burst into the room, swinging a newspaper in the air, and dashing around as if she were on fire.
"Jo! What on earth! Calm down, child!" Mother spoke sternly.
"Sorry, Mother," gasped Jo, as she ran past and pecked her mother on the cheek.
"Jo! What’s so exciting about that newspaper?" called out Amy.

Finally Jo collapsed onto the floor next to Beth, who gently took the paper from her. It was open to a particular page. "Like Mother, Like Daughter," Beth read, "by Josephine March. Jo! This is your story!"
Soon the entire house was filled with loud cheers and a great deal of shouting. Jo was now a published writer. As everyone came around to give her a hug, she held on more tightly and longer to Meg.
Now Jo’s secret was out of the bag but she wondered how much longer she could keep Laurie’s secret from being known. Jo hoped it would be a long, long time.

Time flew quickly and before long, Jo’s second story, entitled "Beautiful Strangers," was published in the Eagle (the name of the newspaper). The editor of the paper liked Jo’s stories so much that he bought four more of her works.
"The ending is so tragic, Jo," Beth remarked, pulling her sweater tightly around herself. The sudden drop in temperatures had brought about a colder winter than anyone anticipated.
"I felt this story should be more realistic; not so fanciful," the writer explained.

"Well, I think you should have made it happier," criticized the artist, as she thumped a lump of clay on the table to soften it. Amy had moved on to experimenting with clay, and was molding small sculptures of everyone and everything these days.

Mother’s familiar footsteps coming up the stairs outside sent the girls scurrying along to welcome her home. Tossing the newspaper onto the sofa, Beth raced to the door as Meg plumped up the cushions on Mother’s chair and Jo ran to warm her slippers by the fireplace. Amy wiped the clay muck off her hands and cleaned up her mess.
"Hello, my girls!" Mother came into the room, holding out her arms.
Her daughters embraced her, forming a circle so Mother would warm up quickly.
"I’d better see to dinner," Meg said, leaving her sisters tending Mother while she went to help Hannah.
"Do we have any letters from Father?" asked Beth.
Only Beth remembered that it was letter day and Father always sent a message, whether it was brief or detailed, to his family.
"I checked but there wasn’t anything today," Mother said in a gentle voice.
The girls grew silent, not wanting to ask questions that might result in answers they dreaded to hear.
Sensing their uneasiness, Mother said, "It’s not easy to write every week, especially when the soldiers are moving around so much. I’m sure your father is just fine."
A sudden knock on the door interrupted their conversation. Puzzled, Mother got up and opened the door to find a young man in uniform shivering in the cold. He held a thin square envelope in his hand.
"Mrs. March? Telegram for you," he said in an emotionless voice.
Mother took the envelope with shaky hands but held onto Jo for support as she made her way back to her chair.
"Jo, could you, please? I can’t . . ." Mother, who was usually calm and cool, sounded frightened like a little girl.
Impatiently ripping the envelope open, Jo read the message on the telegram, "Mrs. March, your husband is very ill. Must come at once."
Jo stifled a cry as the telegram dropped from her hands, falling to the floor. Mother sat erect but silent tears fell onto her lap while she tried to comfort Beth and Amy, who were wailing loudly.
"What’s the matter?" Meg ran into the room, Hannah close at her heels.
When Jo told them about the telegram, Meg collapsed onto the sofa, holding her head in her hands. Hannah cried, "Poor Mr. March. What are we to do?"
The grieving period for Father was short since time was running out and Mother had to leave immediately to be with him.
"Meg, pack extra socks and sweaters for Father. Beth, go downstairs and ask Hannah for my medicine bag."
At that moment, the doorbell rang and Amy went to see who it was.
When Mother and Meg came downstairs, they recognized the voices of Mr. Laurence, Laurie, and Mr. Brookes.

"Mrs. March, young Amy just told us the terrible news. We are at your service to do whatever is needed in order to help you and your girls," Mr. Laurence offered kindly, taking Mother’s arm as he led her into the living room.
"How did you know?" Meg asked Mr. Brookes, who also extended his arm to help her.
"Laurie saw a soldier walking toward your house, and we all know that the army only sends a soldier if something is seriously wrong."
Mother bowed her head in gratitude saying: "I am always grateful for your help, Mr. Laurence."
Shaking his head, he replied, "Please don’t mention it since it’s not only our duty but also our honor to help friends in their time of need."
"Would you allow me to go with you so that you’re not traveling alone?" asked Mr. Brookes.
Mother’s eyes filled with tears as she nodded, accepting his gracious offer.
"Now, Mrs. March, time is crucial," said Mr. Laurence firmly, "so I think you should prepare your things and leave as soon as possible."
"Grandfather, shall I ask Jenson to get the carriage ready?" asked Laurie, as he made his way to the door.
"Yes, and make sure Cook has prepared enough food and drink for the journey," Mr. Laurence called out as his grandson left to speak with the stable manager.
Within an hour Mother was ready to leave. Doing a last-minute check, she looked around to see if she had everything she needed. "Where’s Jo?" Mother asked, unable to see her second daughter.
"She’s somewhere, I’m sure," said Meg, helping Mother put her coat on.
"Tell Father we love him," said Beth, trying with difficulty to control her tears.
"We’re praying for his rapid recovery," said Amy.
"Girls, you must mind Meg and Jo, and don’t forget the Hummels, who need our help as much as anyone," said Mother.
"The carriage is ready," said Laurie, poking his head in the door.
As Mother turned to say good-bye, Jo, shoving Laurie forcefully, suddenly burst in through the door. She was wearing a bonnet tied carelessly around her head. "I made it in time," she gasped.
"Where have you been, Jo?" Meg asked in an annoyed voice.
"To get something to contribute to Father’s well-being," Jo answered in a trembling voice. She handed Mother some bills and continued, "It’s not much, Mother, but I don’t have anything else to give."
Counting the money, Mother questioned her daughter, "This is a lot, Jo. Where did you get it from?"
Untying her bonnet’s ribbons, Jo let the bonnet slide off her head as she stood in silence.
"Jo! Your hair!" screamed Amy.

"I had no choice," explained Jo, running her fingers through the short, boyish cut, and continued, "I remember that the barber said he bought hair and used it to make wigs. So . . ." her voice broke, but she bravely carried on, "I sold it."
Mother held Jo tightly in her arms and whispered, "Your father will know of your sacrifice and he will be so proud of you."
"I’m sorry, but you must leave immediately," Laurie interrupted gently, deliberately avoiding Jo’s eyes since he had not decided yet how he felt about her new haircut.
Not wanting Mother to worry, the girls forced themselves to smile and look hopeful. As soon as Mother had closed the door behind her, however, the March sisters all broke down weeping.
Although the house felt empty and dismal after Mother left, the girls did their best to remain positive and optimistic about matters, at least most of the time.

"If Aunt March makes one nasty remark to me today, I won’t tolerate it," Jo grumbled as her hand automatically reached back to pull her long hair into a bun; when she remembered it wasn’t there any more, she tugged at her short ends.
"Jo, you must be on your best behavior today since Aunt March may be willing to help Father . . . ," Meg remarked doubtfully.
"Aunt March never has and never will help our family until the day she dies," Jo snorted unkindly.
"Until who dies?" Beth inquired, walking toward her sisters with something steaming wrapped inside a kitchen towel.
Meg glanced sharply at Jo, "Never mind, Beth. What have you got there?"
"I thought you might need these," Beth said shyly, as she unwrapped two round (and slightly burnt) buns. "I baked them with old flour as Mother does, but they’re not as nice as hers."
Not only did the buns warm their hands, but Beth’s kindness warmed their hearts even more.
"Thank you, darling," said Meg, gently hugging her close.
Meg and Jo left the house and as they were about to turn the corner, they looked back as they always did. This time, instead of Mother, Beth stood at the window waving at her sisters.
"Sweet girl didn’t forget," Jo said, wiping a tear from her eye.
With lighter hearts and steps, the two March sisters proceeded to make their way to work.
The March sisters promised Mother they would write as often as possible to keep her up-to-date on their lives at home. For Meg, the best time for her to collect her thoughts was after dinner.
My Dearest Mother,
How happy we were to receive your last letter and to find it containing such good news that even Laurie shed a tear or two, though he insists something went into his eye.
We are so pleased that Father is recovering from his illness with your support and nursing skills to help him. Please send our love to him.
The girls are behaving beautifully and cooperating with us so that everything is in order and well taken care of.

Last night Amy decided she wanted to join the army when she was old enough but this morning she changed her mind and said she would be a better help for the community as a teacher or instructor of some sort. Jo unkindly laughed and the two of them exchanged heated words but they made up immediately and are now back to being friends.

Beth hasn’t been practicing the piano as often or as regularly because she feels that more important matters need her attention and it would be disloyal of her to do what she wants when everyone else is making personal sacrifices. We told her that you and Father both would want her to spend time for herself, but Beth feels that as long as you are away she must take on extra duties to make sure everything runs right.

Dearest Mother, we are so grateful to Mr. Brookes, who has been a great strength to you during this time. Please extend our greetings and best wishes to him as well and tell him that we are eternally in his debt.
We love you very much and anxiously await your return.
Your loving daughter,
Meg
Since Jo was accustomed to waking early to write, she used that time to compose letters to Mother instead.
To My Precious Mother,
I always knew Father was a brave fighter and each day he will grow stronger and healthier with your support and love.

We are very lonely without you, Mother, but I must say, the girls have been perfect angels. Meg watches over us like a mother hen (that’s her new nickname, though I don’t think she cares for it much), so Beth, Amy, and I, like meek chicks, obey her every word.

Yesterday I nearly ended my friendship with Laurie because basically he called me a liar (though he didn’t use those words exactly, it was what he implied). He said I agreed to go somewhere with him and I told him I did no such thing. Then we said some harsh words to each other and stomped off angrily. Then I remembered what you said about controlling my temper and I felt bad so I decided to apologize to Laurie, even though I still think I am right. But there he was, standing in front of our door, looking like a lost puppy. We both said sorry and are now best friends once again.
I’m getting accustomed to my new hair and others seem to be as well. I even heard old Mrs. Kemper say that the boyish cut suits me and I took it as a compliment.
Give my love to Father and greetings to Mr. Brookes.
All my love to you, Mother, until I write again.
Yours forever,
Jo
The two younger sisters wrote their letters whenever they felt like it, so theirs were shorter and more frequent than Meg’s and Jo’s.
Dear Mother,

I am sending some pressed pansies from the garden, as I am hoping that it will remind Father of home. I have also included a short note from the Hummels, though I wrote down what Mrs. Hummel said since her English is still quite poor. The children all seem to be well. They miss you almost as much as I do.
Please give Father a kiss from his Beth.
I love you, Mother dearest.
Little Beth
My Loving Mother,

You will be happy to know that I am doing my lessons faithfully. Jo was so cross with me the other day because I forgot (I really did) to write my essay. But today she seemed pleased with what I showed her. I’m back with oils now. I find that clay doesn’t allow me to express my emotions as clearly as oils do. I’ve inserted a picture I completed just this morning. Please tell Father it is drawn with love.
I am thinking about cutting my hair like Jo’s. I rather like that carefree style and feel that it would go well with my natural curls. What do you think, Mother?

Mr. Laurence visits us daily and every other day we are invited to dine at the mansion. His cook has excellent taste and prepares for us cuisine from the continent (which is Europe, in case you didn’t know). Just the other day she prepared a French meal for us. Mother, it was heaven. One day I must go over and learn her art.
Oh, it sounds like Jo is back home. I’d better get back to my lessons or else . . .
Please give my love to Father.
Affectionately,
Amy

Whenever or wherever the girls wrote their letters was up to them. When they received a letter from Mother, however, the sisters gathered closely together to listen and find comfort in Mother’s loving words, which helped them to have hope, joy, and faith for the future.

For the first week after Mother left, the March sisters did remarkably well with the housework. They took on additional chores and made time to help each other if needed. Once they were relieved to know that Father was recovering, a great burden was lifted from their heavy hearts, and soon the girls slowly began to return to their old habits.
Without Mother around to praise their hard work the sisters felt it only fair that they deserved a short break from their domestic chores.
Jo caught a bad cold and was not allowed to return to Aunt March’s until she was fully recovered. As Aunt March put it, she didn’t want Jo "spreading dirty germs around the house."

Jo had no complaints as she used the opportunity to catch up on some books that she had been aching to read. She soon settled herself on the sofa with a warm blanket, handkerchief, and cup of hot tea.

Amy found that additional housework had strengthened the muscles in her artist’s hands, giving her another chance to try her skills at clay sculpting. Without looking back, Amy abandoned her apron for her artist’s smock and before long was thumping, mashing, molding, and creating new pieces of art.

Meg, on the other hand, faithfully continued to write to Mother and Father, and more often to Mr. Brookes, who she said would appreciate a warm letter from time to time. In fact, her evenings with paper and pen took up so much time that she was soon neglecting her household duties.

"Amy! If you don’t stop that thumping I’m going to thump your head against that table soon," Jo shouted hoarsely at her sister, who had just destroyed a sculpture and was now trying to soften the clay to turn it into something else.
"You’re so violent and rude," snapped Amy, ignoring Jo’s threats by continuing to beat the clay harder. "Besides, shouldn’t you be in bed resting rather than down here anyway?"
"Girls, can you keep your voices down?" said Meg irritably. "I’m just finishing a letter to Mother and I can’t concentrate with your bickering."
Jo childishly stuck her tongue out at Amy, who returned the gesture.

While the others gradually ignored their chores, not to mention their consciences, Beth alone kept up her work. She would faithfully carry out her tasks as well as the ones her sisters had forgotten or postponed indefinitely. She tried to keep her spirits up by singing and humming to herself as she worked, imagining how wonderful it would be when Mother and Father returned home and they could be a family again. But as angelic as Beth was, she was also human. Sometimes she became so frustrated that she would seek solace in her parents’ room, lying on their bed and pretending they were hugging her. Doing this calmed her and gave her a sense of security so that she could continue her work cheerfully. Beth’s approach seemed to work because her sisters never saw her frowning, speaking insensitively, or acting rudely around them.

One evening, Beth, as usual, was in the kitchen preparing a food basket for the Hummels. She seemed unusually tired and sighed a great deal while she slowly filled the basket with bread, fruit, and hot soup. When her older sisters strolled into the kitchen, Beth looked at them pleadingly and asked, "Would one of you be able to visit the Hummels tonight? I don’t feel well."

Meg, washing her hands, shook her head and answered, "I would if I could, but I must finish this letter to Mother. Then I have to write a short one to Mr. Brookes because Mr. Laurence has an urgent message for him."
"And I can’t . . . ," said Jo, forcing a cough, "because I still have this nasty cold."
"But you seemed well enough to go out with Laurie this afternoon," Beth pointed out gently.
Jo’s face turned crimson as she replied with a chuckle, "I felt better then. But I think I should rest now."
"I’ve been going every night since Mother left, but I was hoping that one of you could go instead just this once," sighed Beth.

Meg and Jo both felt guilty that they hadn’t followed Mother’s instructions to visit the Hummels, yet they didn’t want to leave their warm home and walk in the freezing cold that evening. In order to ease her guilt, Meg suggested, "Darling, just stay in tonight. I’m sure the Hummels have plenty to eat for one evening, then tomorrow I’ll go and see them. I promise."
Beth smiled at her sister and said, "Thanks, Meg. But since I’ve already filled the basket, I’ll go and drop it off at their house. I’ll be back shortly."
Hugging their little sister, Meg and Jo went back to the living room to do their own thing. Sighing, Beth picked up the basket and got ready to leave.

That evening the others decided to turn in early, with Meg complaining of a headache, Jo blaming her cold, and Amy wanting her beauty sleep. Soon after Jo had fallen asleep, however, she was awakened by slow footsteps creeping up the stairs. Alarmed, she silently got out of bed, careful not to disturb her sleeping sisters.
The footsteps stopped in front of her parents’ room, so Jo cautiously tiptoed over and slowly opened the door. What she saw frightened her more than anything she could imagine.

"Beth! Beth! What happened?" she cried, seeing her sister spread out on their parents’ bed. Beth was breathing unevenly and her face was flushed with fever. Panicking, Jo looked around for a washcloth and water to cool Beth’s burning face.
"Jo?" Beth whispered weakly.
"I’m right here, darling," Jo replied, placing a wet washcloth on Beth’s forehead.
"Jo? She died . . . " Beth’s voice broke.
"Who, Beth? Who died?" Jo asked, startled at her words.
"The baby, Hummels’ baby . . . in my arms . . . ," Beth managed to say.
"Oh, my poor darling," Jo cried, holding Beth close to her.
"Doctor said . . . scarlet . . . scarlet fever . . . all the children have it . . . ," continued Beth. "Jo? I might be sick too."

Jo’s heart sank and she wanted to scream aloud with anguish. Scarlet fever, as everyone knew in those days before antibiotics and childhood immunizations, was often fatal. Both Meg and Jo had already had the disease and so their bodies were immune to the bacteria. Amy, on the other hand, had never had scarlet fever, which was both contagious and dangerous.
"I wish I knew what to do!" cried Jo, beating her fists against the bed in frustration.
"Please, Jo, my throat is so dry . . . my head hurts . . . ," Beth mumbled weakly.
Clutching her sister, Jo wept loudly, hating herself for allowing Beth to go to the Hummels when she should have gone, and at the same time, wishing Mother were there to tell her what to do.
"Jo? Keep Amy away. Keep her away . . . ," said Beth before she closed her eyes and became silent.

Meg had awoken when Jo crept out of the room but tried to go back to sleep until she heard a low moaning that sounded like a wounded animal coming from their parents’ room. She was uneasy about the strange noise but something told her it was important to check it out right away. What Meg saw as she opened the door would forever be branded in her heart.
"Jo! What’s the matter with Beth?" cried Meg, her knees buckling under her as she caught sight of her unconscious little sister.
Jo tried her best to explain in-between sobs while trying to move Beth under the bed covers.
"She has scarlet fever and it’s all my fault," wept Jo.
"Scarlet fever? How?" Meg asked, rising on shaky feet to help Jo lift Beth so they could make her more comfortable.
"I’ll explain later but for now, please call Hannah," gasped Jo, removing Beth’s clothes and shoes.
Meg could see the seriousness of the situation, so without another word she ran downstairs to wake Hannah up.

"There, darling. It’s going to be all right," whispered Jo. Brushing Beth’s hair away from her face, Jo felt Beth’s hot skin under her hand and heard her labored, uneven breathing. As frightened and shaken as she was, Jo heard approaching footsteps and knew instinctively that it wasn’t Meg or Hannah. Remembering Beth’s strong warning, Jo jumped up, flew out the door, and slammed it shut behind her before Amy could enter the room.

"Jo, what is going on? Who’s in there? Is it Beth?" asked Amy, launching one question after another. "I heard someone crying. Jo, was that you? Your eyes are all red and swollen. Where’s Meg? Can I go in there? Is Beth sick?"
"Amy, go back to the bedroom and don’t come out 'til Meg or I say so," ordered Jo.
Amy put her hands on her hips and said stubbornly, "No! I won’t! Not until you tell me what’s going on!"
Then she tried to reach for the doorknob, which Jo was covering with her back.
"Amy! Stop being so difficult! This is for your own good," Jo croaked hoarsely. "There’s no time to explain. Get back in the bedroom now!"
"You’re not Mother! You can’t tell me what to do! I won’t stand for it! What are you trying to hide?" Amy cried, wrestling with Jo to get into the forbidden room.

Left with no choice, Jo grabbed Amy forcefully and dragged her back to their bedroom, with Amy kicking and screaming at the top of her lungs. Then to ensure that Amy did not sneak out and expose herself to the disease, Jo locked the door from the outside and put the key in her pocket.
"Let me out! This is an outrage!" Amy screamed from inside, rattling the doorknob and pounding the door with her little fists.
"Amy, please, I’ll explain everything later," Jo said more gently, "but for now, this is for your own protection."

The short distance back to their parents’ room felt extremely exhausting and dispiriting as Jo contemplated the one sister locked up like a prisoner behind her while the other sister was imprisoned in her own sick body in the room ahead of her. Thank goodness Hannah finally appeared to take over the situation.
Though her face was tired, Hannah’s eyes were bright with anxiety as she searched for Beth.
"She’s in there," Jo said, pointing to her parents’ room, "and I’ve put her under the covers. She’s burning up, Hannah."
"I’ve called for Dr. Bangs," Meg told them as they entered the room together.

Wiping a tear with one large hand, Hannah put the other on Beth’s red, burning face, saying, "Until he comes, bring all the towels you can find and fill all the basins with cold water. We need to bring the fever down. Hurry, girls, go now!"
After the girls had taken numerous trips upstairs to bring cold water to the bedroom, Dr. Bangs finally arrived. He sent the girls out of the room but allowed Hannah to remain.
Exhausted and overwhelmed with guilt, Meg and Jo stood nearby, waiting for the latest news about Beth’s condition.
"I take full responsibility," whispered Jo. "I should have gone. I wasn’t even feeling sick, just lazy."
Meg shook her head and said, "No, the blame is on me since Mother left me in charge, which means I should have been the one to visit the Hummels, not Beth."
"Beth said the baby died of the fever, so the other children must have it too. I wonder how they are doing," Jo asked worriedly.

"Scarlet fever is infectious and spreads rapidly. You and I are immune, but what about Amy?" Meg looked toward their closed bedroom door. Amy had either given up or gone back to bed, but all was quiet from that part of the house.
"Meg? Jo?" Dr. Bangs came out from their parents’ room with a long, weary face.
"How is she, Doctor?" asked Meg, glancing at Hannah, who stood behind the doctor with her head lowered.
"Not too good, I’m afraid," the doctor said sadly. "This fever strikes quickly and although all of you did a fine job trying to keep her body temperature cool, the illness had already taken over."
Jo felt the room spinning as she staggered against the wall for support.
"Should we send for Mother?" Meg asked in a shaking voice.
"Not yet," said Hannah. "We won’t know how the little angel is until the morning, will we, Dr. Bangs?"

"That’s right," said Dr. Bangs. "I’ve given her some medicine to reduce the fever and I’ll return the first thing in the morning to check up on her. Meanwhile," he added as he headed downstairs, "all of you should try to get some rest."
"Dr. Bangs," called Jo, "the Hummel children have the fever, too. That’s where Beth got it from."
"I know, Jo. I’m just going there now," the doctor replied and smiled kindly. "I’ll let you know how they are."
Hannah followed him down, noting his instructions about what to do in an emergency. Meg and Jo went back inside to Beth, who was still red all over but now had a rash all over her face.
Her uneven breathing and the pain on her face broke their hearts.
"Oh, Beth. I’m so sorry," cried Meg, holding onto one of Beth’s hands.
"Beth, please get better. I promise not to be so selfish anymore. I’ll visit the Hummels every day from now on. Just get better," Jo said, her voice breaking with emotion.

They sat there like that for the whole night, neither wanting to leave their sister’s side. As the sun rose, Beth’s condition did not change, forcing them to face the unbearable question they had tried to avoid all night. With red-rimmed eyes, Jo turned to her sister and asked in a trembling voice, "What are we going to do, Meg, if our little Beth dies?"

The sun rose as it did every other day, promising light and warmth, but today, no amount of sunshine could brighten the March sisters’ darkened hearts. While Meg and Jo, who had not slept a wink all night, watched for any signs of change in Beth’s condition, they talked about what to do with Amy.
"Obviously she can’t stay here," stated Meg.
"Maybe Mr. Laurence and Laurie can look after her," suggested Jo.
"That wouldn’t be proper," Meg said, shaking her head. "Besides, they’ve done so much for us already we couldn’t burden them with anything more."
At the same moment the sisters thought of their only other solution, but both of them were hesitant to say it until finally Meg said, "We are left with no other choice but . . . "
"Yes, Aunt March’s," sighed Jo, finishing Meg’s words and already feeling sorry for Amy.
"If you can talk with Aunt March, then I’ll break the news to Amy," said Meg.

As the girls were agreeing to the plan, Dr. Bangs, looking as though he hadn’t had much sleep as well, returned to check up on Beth. Again, the kind doctor told Meg and Jo that he was concerned about them, and that they must look after themselves first in order to be better caregivers to Beth. Leaving Dr. Bangs to tend to Beth, Meg and Jo closed the door firmly behind them.
"We’d better go and talk to Amy," said Meg, holding out her hand for the key to the bedroom.

Although it was cruel to lock Amy up, it was the only way they could keep her away from Beth. Having unlocked the door, Meg and Jo expected Amy to come flying at them in a fit. However, they found her eerily quiet as she sat on the floor, hugging her knees close, her eyes swollen from crying.
"Is Beth dead?" was Amy’s first question. Although she did not know the details, Amy was extremely shrewd and could sense the seriousness of Beth’s illness without being told.
Meg squatted down beside her and said in a motherly voice, "It’s all right. Everything is going to be fine."
"Dr. Bangs is with her now. She’s stable for the time being, but there hasn’t been any improvement in her condition," Jo said truthfully.
"Beth has scarlet fever and that means you mustn’t be in the house or else you will catch it too," said Meg.
"But where will I go?" asked Amy.
"You need to go and stay with Aunt March," Meg said carefully.
After two seconds of stunned silence, Amy replied: "No! I won’t stay with that old lady. She gives me the creeps!"
"Amy!" Meg said sharply, "You must never speak about our relative in that manner. And you have no say in the matter, I’m sorry to say. Pack a few things, please, and get ready to leave immediately."
Amy argued, begged, cried, and shouted, but in the end, she saw her sisters’ decision was firm.

After a wearisome visit with Aunt March where Jo had to endure criticism of her parents and their upbringing of the girls, Jo’s relative finally agreed to allow Amy to stay with her. Laurie, on the other hand, proved his loyalty as a friend once again by wholeheartedly offering to do whatever he could to help.
"Laurie, can’t I stay with you and your grandfather?" Amy asked him as the Laurence carriage was taking them to Aunt March’s.
"I wish you could, Amy," Laurie answered, "but your sisters have made up their minds and you must honor their decision."
Amy crossed her arms and pouted.
Smiling at her childish gesture, Laurie said, "But I promise to visit every day as your messenger, and I’ll update you on Beth’s condition and other things happening at home."
