Amy’s eyes brightened and she flashed a big lovely smile, saying, "Oh, would you, Laurie? That would be grand. Thank you so much."
The remainder of the journey was filled with light talk and giggling as the two made an extra effort not to mention Beth’s illness.
Amy had been with her family to Aunt March’s house several times but had never been there by herself. She immediately felt intimidated, uncomfortable, and alone.
"Well, at least you’re not starving at home, as you seem to have grown since the last time I saw you," snapped the old woman, scrutinizing Amy from head to toe.

Aunt March was a critical, difficult, and stubborn person who usually got her way because she was very wealthy and powerful in the community. However, when it came to her only relative, her nephew Mr. March, she found that he would not give in to her even though she threatened to withhold any financial help he might need. Mr. March always kept his ground and never asked her for money. Even though Aunt March would never admit it, she respected her nephew’s sense of values and had a soft spot for her grandnieces. She loved Jo for her honesty and colorful character, which brought life to her otherwise boring existence; and Amy, for her beauty, good manners, and ambition.

"There are some rules you must obey in this house," Aunt March warned. "One, you must never shout or raise your voice. Two, you must never run around the house. If you break or damage anything, you will pay for it, even if you have to come work for me for the rest of your life. Three, meals are served at set times. If you are late, then you do not eat. Four, you will be given chores and expected to complete them by the time given."
"More chores," Amy sighed under her breath.
"What did you say?" Aunt March’s sharp ears picked up Amy’s mumbling.
"Nothing, Aunt March," muttered Amy, wishing she could calm her shaky legs.
"Five," continued the old woman, "you will sit and read to me every afternoon. "Your sister used to do that, but she got lazy, then she got sick. I don’t know what to do with that girl. Six . . . "
Amy sighed inwardly and wished she were at home with the others. Surely, getting sick was not as bad as having to listen to and obey all of Aunt March’s rules.
"How am I going to survive?" Amy wondered to herself.
Accepting her plight, Amy decided the only way she was going to manage her stay at Aunt March’s was to do exactly as she demanded.
"Don’t rub too hard or you might scratch my good silver," Aunt March snapped at Amy, who was polishing endless silver ornaments.
"Careful!" screeched Aunt March’s parrot, Polly.
"Yes, ma’am, I’ll be very careful," Amy answered dutifully.
While Amy carried on with her chores, Aunt March watched her secretly and thought, "Yes, this one has hope. She can be useful in society. This one is a lady."
"Careful!" Polly screeched again.

Back home, Dr. Bangs increased the dose of medicine, but Beth’s fever still persisted. Even though Jo felt totally hopeless and useless, she refused to give up. She continued to do everything she could to take care of Beth in the way she knew best. And so Jo opened an old book and began reading softly, "A beautiful dream was about to come true for Princess Anastasia . . ."

While she was at Aunt March’s, Amy felt as though she were trapped in a pitch-black tunnel with no light beckoning to her at the end. Until then, Amy had taken for granted the liveliness and warm affection of her family. How she missed the constant cheerful voices that seemed to fill the whole house all day long.
"Did I ask you to stop?" Aunt March snapped when Amy, who was reading to her, paused to think about her family.
"Stop!" screeched Polly as she took the cracker Aunt March offered her.
"Forgive me, Aunt March. I’ll continue . . . ," said Amy, returning her attention to the story.

Aunt March might have been a nasty woman but she was not heartless. She was also worried about the fate of Beth, who she thought was witless but pure-hearted and innocent. "What have you heard about your sister?" This time she interrupted Amy’s reading.
Fiddling with a corner of the page she was reading, Amy replied, "Laurie says that Beth is coping better but her fever still has to drop, and she remains stable but weak."
"And what of your Father? Will he be coming home soon?" asked Aunt March.
Shaking her head, Amy said tearfully, "According to the last message we got, Father doesn’t have the strength yet to make the journey home."
"Rubbish! Your sister needs your mother more than he does," Aunt March remarked in a gruff voice.
"Hannah says it’s best not to tell Mother just yet, since there isn’t much she can do here anyway," said Amy.
Aunt March felt a pang in her heart as she watched Amy struggle to control her emotions. "I have a gift for you," she said in a kinder voice.

Amy, wiping her tears (with a silk handkerchief, like a true lady), turned to her with curiosity. Aunt March held out a small green velvety box, which Amy slowly took from her. "Oh, Aunt March! I can’t accept this," gasped Amy, holding up an emerald ring that flashed brilliantly in the light.
"Yes, you can and you will, because I am giving it to you," Aunt March replied in a firm and strict voice that meant Amy should not try to argue with her.
"It’s beautiful," Amy said, her eyes dancing joyously as she put the ring on her middle finger.
"I’m glad you like it. Now get back to the story," snapped Aunt March as she fed Polly another cracker.

In addition to the ring, Aunt March promised Amy many more gifts as long as she remained obedient and found favor in the old lady’s eyes. Upon his next daily visit, Amy promptly told this all to Laurie, who looked doubtful as he listened patiently.
"Aunt March says emeralds are the most precious gems in the world," Amy said, sticking her hand out for him to admire.
"It’s very lovely, but don’t you think you’re a little too young for that?" asked Laurie with a frown.
"Age means nothing if you are a true lady," Amy said knowingly. "Aunt March says I have the potential to become a respected woman of society."
Laurie mumbled his opinion of Aunt March under his breath, but apparently Amy still had much more to say about material things.
"Aunt March says I’m to have her pearl necklace, earrings, and diamond brooch after she dies!"
"So you want her to die, do you?" Laurie asked nastily.
Reddening in the face, Amy stuttered, "No. What I meant was . . ."
"Do you want to know how Beth is or not?" Laurie asked rather harshly.
Caught up in her own fantasy world, Amy had forgotten at that moment why Laurie was visiting her every day. "Of course, Laurie," she said, shamefaced.
"Well, Beth is still . . . ," Laurie began more gently.

As he spoke, Amy looked down at the ring. It didn’t seem to shine as beautifully anymore, nor did the thought of a pearl necklace seem so appealing. The reality was that Beth was gravely sick, and death was no joking matter.

After Laurie had left, Amy had a lot to think about. She stared at herself in the mirror for a very long time. Speaking to her reflection, Amy said, "One day you’re going to die, too." "Can I take these things with me to my grave?" she wondered. Struck by the truth, she was forced to realize that her possessions would have no value to her once she were dead.

After much soul searching, Amy decided to write a will, reasoning, "I want the people I love to have my things so they’ll remember me by them." Armed with pen and paper, Amy began to write her last will and testament:
I, Amy Curtis March, being of sound mind, do give all my possessions to the following persons named:
To Father, all my drawings and sketches—those I kept since I was a little girl up to the ones he never saw.
To Mother, all my clothes, except for the blue dress with pink and white flowers. That one I want Kitty to have. See below.
To Meg, I give the emerald ring from Aunt March, because it is the perfect match for the color of your eyes. The velvet box I also give.

To Jo, I give you all my hair ribbons so that when your hair grows long again, you will have beautiful, colorful ribbons to decorate it with. I also give you all my pens for you to write more stories with.
To Beth (if she survives), all my dolls, my little play set of teacups, and pink slippers.
To Laurie, I leave you my handkerchiefs with my initials embroidered on them so you will always remember me as a true lady.
To Mr. Laurence, I give you my sculptures of your horses. I especially loved Harris, and there are two paintings of him that I hope you like.
To Kitty Bryant, my blue dress with pink flowers and my bead necklace, which she always admired.
To Hannah, my collection of seashells and the purple box I kept them in.

And now, after leaving my possessions in the care of those I love and trust, I want to say how much I love you all and that each one of you has a special place in my heart. I trust we shall meet again.
Signed: Amy Curtis March

When Amy finished writing her will, a peaceful calm came over her.She prayed, "God, if you allow Beth to live, I promise to be a better sister, daughter, and friend. Please give me the opportunity to prove that I have really changed."

The next day when Laurie came, Amy showed him the will and asked him to sign it as a witness. Amused yet touched by Amy’s maturity and thoughtfulness, Laurie agreed. Then he gave Amy the good news. "Mother March is coming home soon," he announced.
"Beth? Does that mean . . ." Amy couldn’t even say the words.
Laurie took a deep breath and said, "I don’t know, but Dr. Bangs said to send for your mother. The girls don’t know yet. I want it to be a surprise."
Amy was overjoyed that Mother was returning. She wondered whether her homecoming would be a happy or sad one.

The fever still had a strong grip on Beth, but like a little soldier, she fought it every step of the way. Meg and Jo tirelessly rotated shifts to care for Beth. Hannah also helped hugely by looking after all the household chores that the girls couldn’t do.

During Beth’s illness, Meg and Jo discovered many things about their sister that they hadn’t known before. For example, who would have known that shy little Beth had so many friends? When word got out that she was sick, every day someone would come by with a gift or flowers for her. The living room rapidly filled with beautiful blooms and lovely presents that Jo knew Beth would cherish.

"How kind. Everyone is thinking of our Beth," remarked Meg, folding some washcloths. Her eyes followed Jo as she carried to the table several loaves of fresh bread, courtesy of the baker, who had just come by to ask about Beth.

Jo, hands perched on her hips, stared at the large amount of food that neighbors and friends had brought over. "Meg, if you were Beth, what do you think you would do with all this food?" asked Jo, pointing to the overflowing table.
Meg, catching on to Jo’s line of thinking, replied, "I think I would share whatever I had."
Jo smiled at her sister, whom she was grateful to have during these painful times, and said, "Yes, I agree. That is exactly what she would do."
Meg and Jo generously filled a large basket with the food that had been kindly given to Beth.
"I hope the Hummel children aren’t too sick to enjoy this," said Jo as she placed the loaves of fresh bread in the basket.
"Dr. Bangs said that the Hummel children didn’t catch the fever as severely as our Beth," said Meg.
"That may mean our Beth will recover soon, too," Jo said hopefully.
Nodding but without commenting on her sister’s last remark, Meg said, "We should have done this sooner. I must confess all this to Mother when she returns."
"I wonder if we should send for Mother now?" asked Jo as she pulled on her coat.
"I don’t know. I just wish she were here right now," replied Meg, wrapping a scarf around her neck.
Clutching one handle each, the sisters carried the basket between them to divide the weight, but nobody could share the heavy burden of guilt on their hearts.

The visit to the Hummels wasn’t as horrible as Jo expected. Mrs. Hummel was still distressed over the death of her little baby, and although the girls tried to console her, she was too upset to be comforted. The other children, thinner from their illness, were extremely excited when they saw the large basket of goodies. After spending a fair amount of time with them, Meg and Jo returned home with lighter hands and hearts. Meg went upstairs to check up on Beth, giving Jo some time to spend alone. Jo went outside, hoping the cold air would clear her head.
"Jo? What are you doing out here?" Laurie had seen his friend sitting alone on a large rock in the yard and decided to join her.
"I just needed some fresh air," said Jo, putting on a brave face.
"How are you coping?" Laurie asked.
"Okay," said Jo meekly.
"No need to lie to me, friend," said Laurie, tilting Jo’s head upward to face him.
"You’re right, I’m not doing fine," said Jo before she burst into tears. "If Beth dies, I will never forgive myself."
"Stop talking nonsense. Dr. Bangs thinks Beth will recover soon; it’s just a matter of time. I know what will transform that frown into a smile," said Laurie, getting up and dusting off his bottom.
"Laurie, I don’t feel like laughing," Jo said wearily.

"Nonsense! Someone once told me that laughter is the best medicine. Now watch this." Laurie began to imitate his grandfather, then Hannah, Brookes, and finally each of the girls. Jo had to guess which person he was mimicking. Before she knew it, she was laughing happily, forgetting her troubles for just a moment.
"I just wish Mother were here. She would know what to do," said Jo after Laurie had finished his performance.
Laurie playfully pulled Jo’s short hair and said, "What if I told you that she’s coming home, as we speak?"
Stunned, Jo looked at him hopefully and said, "Mother is coming home? How? When?"
"Dr. Bangs told me to send for her. I didn’t want to tell you girls in case it worried you more. She should arrive here tonight," said Laurie.
Jo burst into tears again, sobbing loudly and hiccupping as she said, "Thank you, Laurie. Thank you."
Hugging his friend, Laurie sat with Jo until her tears stopped.
Jo did not tell Meg about Mother’s arrival, for fear her sister might think the worst.
"I wonder how Father is doing?" whispered Meg. "We haven’t had a letter in two days."
"Mother mentioned that he had such an appetite that he wanted to eat up her portion of their meals," Jo said smiling, as she recalled Mother’s last letter.
"Oh, that’s right. He’s even started to walk a little," said Meg.
"I never read that part. How do you know?" Jo asked, surprised.
Meg turned red and lowered her eyes before answering, "John said so."
"John? Who is John?" Jo asked rather loudly.
"Mr. Brookes. His name is John Brookes," Meg said in a dreamy voice.
Jo was beyond words because, with everything that had happened recently, she had forgotten about Laurie’s secret. Now it seemed as if the cat was out of the bag.
"Meg, have you been writing to Mr. Brookes? That’s very unladylike!" Jo scolded, borrowing Amy’s favorite descriptive word for her.
"Don’t worry, Jo. I only wrote a few times to thank him for his help. Besides, there is nothing improper about our writing," Meg said firmly.
Before Jo could speak her mind, the door suddenly opened and a familiar figure walked in, paralyzing the girls for a moment before they realized who it was.
"Mother!" Meg and Jo screamed together as they ran to hug her.
"We’re so happy you’ve returned," said Jo.
"Thank you, girls," Mother replied, kissing them. Then she knelt down beside Beth and said, "Don’t worry, love, Mother is here."

Meg and Jo confessed their wrongdoings to Mother, preparing to be disciplined for their selfishness. Instead, Mother just said to them, "Seeing your sister suffer like this is punishment enough. I hope you girls have learned a lesson from all this." Then Mother took them in her arms and hugged them and told them to continue praying for Beth.
The next day, Jo immediately noticed a change in Beth’s breathing. It was slower and more relaxed. The rash seemed to have faded and Beth looked more peaceful.
"The fever has broken," Mother said in a trembling voice.
Jo ran over and held Mother’s outstretched hand, asking, "Is she going to live? Will Beth be all right?"
With tears of relief streaming down her face, Mother replied, "Yes, our little girl is going to make it."

When Beth opened her eyes her first thought was that she had died and gone to heaven. Then she decided she was still dreaming because Mother was standing over her, smiling and calling her name. "No, it can’t be real," Beth said to herself. "Mother is with Father. She can’t be here with me."
"Hello, my darling girl," Mother said, stroking her cheek.
Beth tried to speak but didn’t have the strength to move her lips, so instead she made a tiny sound in her throat.
"I’m here, Beth," Mother said, "and so is Jo. She’s never left your bedside."

Seeing Jo’s weary face, Beth knew she was no longer dreaming. Holding out a weak hand to Jo, Beth parted her lips and whispered her sister’s name. Grasping her hand, Jo fell to her knees and cried tears of joy and relief.
News of Beth’s recovery certainly brightened everyone’s day. Jo, in particular, found herself smiling for no reason and doing out-of-the-ordinary things like singing aloud.
"When should we get Amy?" Meg asked as she and Jo helped Hannah prepare dinner that evening.
Meg seemed to be in an unusually cheerful mood herself, with flushed cheeks and sparkling eyes that gave her face a glow.

"I’ll go tomorrow morning. Maybe I’ll ask Laurie to come with me," said Jo, chopping some carrots and throwing them into the large pot where a special soup was boiling for Beth. Meg nodded dreamily as she crushed some peppers and added them to the soup.
"You’re awfully merry today," teased Jo.
Meg turned away but replied, "I’m happy that Beth is better."
"We all are, but there’s something else. Come, Meg, what are you hiding?" Jo persisted.
Meg looked over her shoulder to make sure that Hannah was out of earshot, then, pulling Jo to a corner, she pulled out a note from her apron pocket.
"What’s this?" whispered Jo, opening the note.
"Just read it, but promise me you won’t say a word to Mother or anyone else. It’s for your eyes only," said Meg in a hushed voice.
As Jo read the short message, her head began to spin and she felt a hot wave of anger rising up. It was from John Brookes, and the man was confessing his love for Meg.
"You’re too young!" were Jo’s first words, practically throwing the note back to Meg.
"I’m almost 18," Meg replied in a huff.
"You just turned 17!" Jo argued.
"It doesn’t matter. He loves me, Jo," Meg said, brushing aside Jo’s concerns.
"I think it’s scandalous! He’s too old for you and besides, why is he sending you a note like that at a time like this?" Jo nearly yelled.
"I think it’s romantic, and I thought you’d be more supportive and happier for me," Meg said in a hurt voice. Then she added, "He’s only 24."
"I’m disgusted with Brookes and with you!" Jo growled at her sister. With that, Jo yanked off her apron, stormed out of the house, and bumped into an incoming visitor.
"Do you think we might have telepathic powers, because I was just coming to see you," Laurie said when he realized who had just bumped into him.
"This is no time to joke, Laurie," said Jo, cracking her knuckles loudly.
"All right, then," said Laurie. "How’s our girl doing?"
"Thank you for asking, Beth is much better. Now, my question is: Are you available to help me get Amy tomorrow?" Jo asked in a very businesslike manner.
"I’m at your service anytime, anywhere," Laurie replied, bowing like a servant.
"Good. We’ll leave at 9 a.m. sharp," said Jo, turning around to go back inside.
"Wait! How’s your other sister doing?" Laurie asked slyly.
"She’s fine. Why?" suddenly Jo noticed something in Laurie’s mischievous eyes. "Theodore Laurence," she said sternly, "is there something you want to tell me?"
Laurie covered his mouth and let out a muffled shout, then he said in a low whisper, "Did she get a note from Brookes?"
Jo narrowed her eyes and answered, "What if she did? What do you know about it?"
Laurie slapped his knee and threw back his head, laughing loudly. "It was me! I wrote it! Brookes knows nothing about it!" the prankster admitted.
Jo could not believe her ears but worse yet, she could not believe that Laurie would play such a cruel joke on Meg.
"You . . . you . . . ," Jo stuttered. She was so angry that she could not even speak. Instead she kicked him in the shins with all her might.
"Ow! Why did you do that?" Laurie rubbed his sore leg, hopping on the other foot.
"What happens when Meg discovers that this was all a big joke? How will this affect her self-esteem and pride?" Jo spat at him.
"Brookes is in love with her, like I told you," Laurie said, massaging his leg. "I’m just helping the progress of this relationship."
"You march in there right now," Jo said, pointing toward her house, "and apologize to Meg for what you did before it’s too late!"
"Why are you really upset, Jo? Are you afraid that John is going to take away your precious sister?" Laurie asked. That question got him another hard kick in the other leg.
"Ow! You’re going to cripple me, Josephine March!" wailed Laurie.

"Apologize to my sister, though I won’t be surprised if she never speaks to you again. You’d better do it this instant, or else . . . ," Jo paused to form her words carefully, ". . . or else our friendship ends tonight." Jo turned her back on Laurie, who was rubbing both shins but staring up at her with a worried expression.
"Do you mean that, Jo?" he asked quietly.
Without looking at him, Jo simply replied, "Yes."

Frightened that Jo would carry out her threat, Laurie immediately went to see Meg and told her of his cruel joke. Meg, being so sweet and ladylike, forgave Laurie and told him that it was not important. In her heart, however, she was crushed.
Mother sensed right away how heartbroken Meg was. "It’s going to be fine, darling," Mother comforted Meg as she lovingly stroked her head.
"I thought he loved me. I . . . was so happy," sobbed Meg.

Mother thought for a moment before she spoke. "Meg, darling, I don’t know if I should say this, but both your father and I have grown very fond of John. He is a wonderful, kind, intelligent man. One day I’m sure he will make a fine husband."
"But not for me," wailed Meg.

"I wouldn’t say that," Mother said hesitantly. "I know for a fact that he thinks highly of you. He speaks with you in the warmest, most respectful way. I wonder if perhaps Laurie’s joke, bad as it was, may have some truth in it."
Meg sniffed but lifted her head and asked, "Do you think John likes me?"
Mother smiled and replied, "How could he not?"

On the surface, everything at the March home appeared to return to normal. Amy was back home, showing off her ring (not mentioning to Meg that she had left it to her in her will) and entertaining the family with funny episodes about Aunt March and her parrot, Polly.

Beneath the smiles and laughter, however, the sisters had changed considerably; they were no longer the carefree young girls they used to be before Beth’s illness. Perhaps the person who changed the most was Beth herself. Outwardly, she seemed to regain her health and sunny disposition. Her optimistic and innocent world, however, had been shattered when the Hummel baby died in her arms, giving Beth a close encounter with death. Beth withdrew even more into herself as if an inner light in her had been switched off. Seeing the change in Beth, Jo knew that she could never forgive herself for contributing to the loss of happiness in her sister’s life.
"Jo? Jo!" Amy called sharply.
Lost in thought, Jo did not even hear Amy speaking to her. "Sorry, Amy. What did you say?" she asked.

"I asked, ‘Where is Laurie?’ He was incredibly faithful," said Amy, "visiting me every day at Aunt March’s so I wouldn’t go insane with worry. Without him, I would have died!" Then realizing her poor choice of words, she quickly added, "I mean, it would have been just awful!"
"Am I his keeper?" barked Jo spitefully. "Frankly, Laurie is the least of my concerns now. My thoughts are occupied with far more important matters at the moment."

Meg, noticing Jo’s peculiar response, knew that her sister was not on speaking terms with Laurie because of the tasteless joke he had played. Meg also knew that Jo, although she was pretending to the world and herself that it didn’t matter, was deeply troubled by the rift in their friendship.
"I think we should have Laurie and his grandfather over for dinner tonight," Meg suggested while she looked away from Jo’s piercing glare.
"Why should we?" Jo asked sharply.
"Jo! You ought to be ashamed of yourself after all the Laurences have done for us," scolded Amy righteously. "We are indebted to them forever for their selfless deeds."
"I agree with Meg," said Mother, giving Amy a warning look to go easy on Jo. "We should invite them this evening if they’re available."
"Can I ask Laurie myself?" Amy jumped up, clapping her hands like a little girl.
Glancing at Jo, Mother replied, "Yes, you may."
When Mother and Amy left together with Meg trailing closely behind, Beth turned to her sister with worried eyes and asked, "Is everything all right with you and Laurie?"

Pressing her lips together, Jo forced a smile and took Beth’s pale, thin hand. "Friendships are forged through time, experience, and overcoming obstacles. Laurie and I have hit a barrier at the moment," Jo said truthfully, "but I’m confident that we will get over this."
Squeezing her hand gently, Beth rested her head on Jo’s shoulder.

On such short notice, a lot of tightly organized teamwork was needed to put together a meal quickly. For the rest of the day, everyone busily took charge of certain tasks to ensure a highly hospitable evening for their neighbors.
"It’s half-past six already! They’ll be here any minute!" Amy panicked as she set the cutlery on the table.
"Meg, did you check the potatoes?" Mother asked as she rushed toward the kitchen.
"They’re all done," answered Meg, careful not to collide with Mother as she carried out a large steaming dish.
While the others scrambled around the kitchen, Jo volunteered to help Beth downstairs so she could join the festivities.
"My legs feel like rubber," giggled Beth as she struggled to maintain her balance on shaky legs.
"Just hang on to me," said Jo, holding Beth around the waist and arm.

Her progress was painstakingly slow, but in the end Beth managed to seat herself on the sofa, then Jo wrapped a thick blanket around her for warmth. As Beth smiled up at her sister, there was a knock at the door, and Jo was the only one available to answer it.
"Good evening, Mr. Laurence," Jo greeted Laurie’s grandfather as she opened the door. She merely nodded to Laurie, who returned the curt gesture.
Mr. Laurence immediately made his way toward Beth, who welcomed her dear friend with a weak but genuine smile.
Standing together awkwardly, Laurie and Jo spoke at the same time.
"So how. . . ," "What did. . . ," "You go first," said Jo.
"It’s nothing," replied Laurie.
"Laurie!" Amy shouted cheerfully as she ran over to him and threw her arms around his neck.
Grateful for the interruption, Jo escaped to help Meg set the table.
Dinner talk was light and full of laughter—the main entertainment was Amy, who repeated her stories from Aunt March’s. If anyone noticed the tension between Laurie and Jo, they did not mention it.
"Jo, can you bring some more bread from the oven?" Mother asked kindly.
Jo stood up, grabbed the bread basket and was heading toward the kitchen when she overheard Mr. Laurence saying, "Laurie, can you bring me a glass of water?"
Even though Mother protested that one of the girls could get it, Mr. Laurence insisted his grandson should go, thereby driving Laurie into the kitchen where Jo was.

Trying to ignore him, Jo tossed the bread into the basket as quickly as she could without acknowledging his presence. But since they were thrown together in a situation like this, they couldn’t avoid talking.
"Jo?" Laurie spoke first.
She turned to him without speaking.
"I don’t know how to make things right," he said quietly. "Could you forgive me and accept me as a friend again?"
Jo felt a lump in her throat as she looked at Laurie bowing his head, staring down at his hands. All her animosity, anger, and hurt melted away in an instant.
"Silly boy," she mumbled, "of course I can."
Jo grabbed him roughly by the neck and playfully messed up his hair.
"I’m really sorry, Jo," Laurie said sincerely.
"Let’s just forget about it," said Jo.

The two friends smiled at each other and knew that everything was going to be fine. Suddenly a loud commotion arose from the living room, forcing Jo and Laurie to cut short their reunion. Meg and Amy were beside themselves as they ran toward a tall thin man standing in the doorway. "Father! Father!" they screamed, as Mother stood still at the table, wiping her eyes with her napkin.
"I’m home, my little girls," said Father happily as he hugged and kissed each of his daughters.
Behind him stood Mr. Brookes, quiet as ever, but staring at only one person in the room: Meg.
Lifting Beth from her chair and putting her on his lap, Father gathered his girls around him and said, "How I missed my little women."
When Mr. Laurence, Laurie, and Mr. Brookes tried to leave unnoticed, Father called out, "Please stay. Tonight we’re celebrating with both family and friends." And that is exactly what they did.

After Father returned home, Beth’s recovery took a turn for the better as she rapidly grew stronger. In no time she was climbing upstairs and downstairs on her own. Being with his family again seemed to have the same effect on Father’s health as well. True, he had lost a lot of weight and his body seemed stiff and sore, but his eyes remained as kind and watchful as ever.
"Shall I continue with the next chapter, or do you want a nap?" Father asked Beth, who was lying on the sofa listening to him read.
Jo, who was also listening, answered excitedly, "Please carry on. I want to know what happens!"
Laughing, Beth nodded and said, "I’d like to hear more, too, Father, but only if you’re not too tired."
"I never get tired of reading to you, my dear girl," Father said lovingly, as he turned the page and continued.
"Oh, this color is not right either!" complained Amy from the corner by the window, where she had set up her easel and was trying to paint a vase of flowers.
Mother and Meg, smiled at the peacefulness of their family at that moment. But the peace didn’t last long.
"Oh, I can’t believe she’s here!" Amy suddenly cried as she glanced out the window.
"Who, Amy?" asked Mother, standing up to look for herself.
"Aunt March! Thank goodness, she didn’t bring that annoying parrot," said Amy, screwing the lids back on her paints.

Unseen by their children, Mother and Father exchanged wordless glances that meant "get ready" for this unexpected visit. Mother opened the door for Aunt March as she strolled into the house as if she owned it.
"Oh, there you are," she said, catching sight of Father.
"How are you, Aunt?" he asked graciously as he stood to give her a kiss on the cheek.

"You go off to war at your age, get sick, take away the children’s mother, meanwhile your small one gets scarlet fever and nearly dies," snapped Aunt March, "so that the youngest, as adorable as she is"—here Aunt March nodded approvingly at Amy—"is sent over to my care despite my illnesses . . . and you ask me how I am!" she concluded.

While Father tried to explain his situation to Aunt March, who demanded that Jo bring a blanket for her cold knees and ordered hot tea from Meg, Amy announced more visitors to the house. "Here come Laurie and Mr. Brookes," she shouted, waving eagerly out the window.
Cheeks flushing, Meg quickly disappeared into the kitchen to get the tea.

Father stood up, relieved, even for a moment, not to have to listen to his aunt’s scolding, and welcomed the guests into his home. Father and Mr. Brookes had formed a close bond during his sickness, and since then Mr. Brookes had become a regular visitor to the March home. As much as Meg tried to appear cool, secretly, she was happy to see John so often.
Her pride might not admit it, but Meg’s heart could no longer deny her feelings for him.
"I have something to ask you, sir," Mr. Brookes said to Father, not realizing that Aunt March was there.
"Who are you?" asked Aunt March bluntly.
While Father explained, Meg entered with the tea, her hands shaking ever so slightly, causing the china to rattle on the tray.
"Child," Aunt March shrieked at Meg, "I swear you’re going to break that cheap tea set if you clink them any harder!"

Turning a deep red, Meg would have dropped the tray if Mr. Brookes hadn’t sprung up and taken it from her trembling hands. As Aunt March sipped her tea, she kept one eye on Mr. Brookes, sensing his obvious attraction to Meg, and the other eye on Meg, who undoubtedly shared the same feelings toward him.

Meanwhile Jo, oblivious to what was happening, caught sight of Laurie trying to get her attention. He motioned with his head toward the kitchen, so Jo cautiously got up and crept away. Laurie joined her a few minutes later.
"What is it?" Jo asked him.
"Something major is about to happen. I can’t tell you but . . . ," Laurie began excitedly.
"Then why bother calling me into the kitchen?" Jo asked irritably.
"To save you the shock," Laurie said.
"From what?" asked Jo.

"Something major is going to happen that will change your life forever," Laurie said firmly, looking deep into Jo’s eyes. Then grabbing her arm, he led her back to the living room, where to Jo’s horror, the big event was just taking place. Mr. Brookes was on his knee in front of Meg and he was holding her hand.
"Margaret March, will you marry me?" Brookes asked in a gentlemanly manner.
"What is the meaning of this?" Aunt March demanded. "This is an outrage! You are only a child!"
"Aunt March, I don’t think this matter concerns you," Father said firmly.
"Of course it concerns me! I am the head of the family. You belong to me! Therefore I have a right to speak!" she said haughtily.
"I love your grandniece, madam, and I promise to make her as happy and content as she is now," John said kindly.
Looking him up and down, Aunt March said disdainfully, "You’re nothing but a poor tutor. How can you make this girl happy?"
Poor Mr. Brookes flushed with embarrassment and anger, but he controlled it admirably.

Surprisingly, it was Meg who spoke up. "Aunt March! I will not allow you to speak to this man in that way. "He is a good kind person who has helped our family when we needed him. What have you done for us? You never offered to help Father when he lost his money or even when he was sick. You never came to visit Beth while she had the fever. And now you come here and tell me that I can’t marry the man who has done nothing but good for our family? No! I will not allow it!" Meg cried, not caring as tears rolled down her cheeks.
Everyone was stunned. They had never seen Meg react so strongly in her life.
Shaking with anger, Aunt March pointed her walking stick at Meg and threatened, "I warn you, Margaret, if you marry this man, you will not get a single penny from me when I die!"
Meg took a deep breath and turning her back on Aunt March, she grabbed John’s hands and said to him, "Yes, John Brookes, I will marry you."
Jo felt the ground drop from beneath her and before she knew it, she was lying on the floor with a circle of worried faces staring down at her.
"Are you all right, Jo?" Laurie asked, pulling Jo up and giving her a slight shake.
Nodding, Jo said, "Yes, I’m fine."
"Oh, Jo, isn’t this wonderful news?" Meg said in a breathless voice as she hugged her sister. "I’m getting married!"
Hearing those words again, Jo fainted. She hoped she would never wake up from the awful nightmare that was about to unfold.

Meg and John had a long engagement—three years to be exact—since her parents, though they accepted John as their future son-in-law, wished the couple to wait until Meg turned twenty before they married. Now Meg was old enough, and the happy but eager couple were free to take their vows.
"Can you believe that in one month I shall be Mrs. John Brookes?" Meg gushed to her fiancé one glorious spring day as they took a walk around the Laurence garden.
"I wish it were today, this moment," John said tenderly as he wrapped his arm around her waist.

During the three years of their engagement, Meg had grown from a sweet, mild-mannered girl into a capable, beautiful, young woman. "Well, I don’t," Meg said very unromantically, "because there is so much to do, I don’t have a moment to spare if I am going to get everything ready before we get married."
So John patiently listened as his soon-to-be bride told him about the countless number of things that needed to be done before their wedding day.
One person who still prayed that the wedding day would never come was Jo who, despite the past three years, refused to accept that Meg would become a wife very soon.

"Look at those two! It’s rather disgusting, it is," Jo mumbled miserably as she spied on her sister and Brookes from the safety of the March home. Jabbing more of the air than the potato she was supposed to be peeling, Jo carelessly tossed the vegetable into a basket of half-peeled other ones that she had butchered while watching Meg and Brookes wander through the Laurences’ garden.
"Jo? Are you done with the potatoes yet?" Beth asked as she and Amy walked into the kitchen wearing aprons.

It was clear that the other girls had also changed in the past three years. Jo, who had long thick hair again, had pulled it into a neat, ladylike bun. Her face had softened, and she seemed calmer, more comfortable with herself and her body. Beth was a little taller, though very thin and without the glow of health that her sisters had. Still, she always wore a smile on her face and never held back from saying a kind word or performing a good deed for others.

But the most remarkable change was in Amy. She had always been pretty, but now she had turned into the kind of stunning beauty that artists dream about painting, poets are inspired to create poems for, and singers are moved to write songs about. All traces of the old Amy, including her tantrums and whining, were replaced by a sophisticated, polished, well-mannered young woman.

"Jo! You’ve stripped half the peel off this innocent vegetable and turned it into some modern art sculpture!" Amy picked up a battered potato, part of its peel dangling loosely, as Beth giggled and picked up some others in similar shape.
"Huh?" Jo tore her eyes away from the window to see what Amy was talking about.
"We’d better decide upon an alternative for the potato pancakes then," sighed Amy, wrinkling her perfect forehead at her sister.
"It’s all their fault!" Jo pointed accusingly at Meg and John far off in the distance, unaware that they were being blamed for the state of the potatoes.
"Oh, Jo," Amy remarked, shaking her head as she left the kitchen.

Beth stood for a moment with Jo, wishing she could erase the pain on her sister’s face and the deeper one in her heart. "As much as we’d like it, nothing stays the same, Jo," she said softly. "Letting go of something doesn’t mean you’re going to lose it. It means you are allowing it to find another home," she added with wisdom beyond her years.

For Jo, Beth’s words rang true in so many ways, not only concerning Meg. Aunt March had taken such a fancy to Amy during the brief time she stayed with her while Beth was sick, that the old lady had replaced Jo with Amy as her companion. At first Jo was upset, but then she decided to view the matter positively and chose to use her time wisely by focusing on her writing.
"Is Laurie coming home this weekend?" asked Amy, tying her wavy blonde hair back in a green ribbon that matched her dress as she got ready to go to Aunt March’s the next morning.

"I hope not, but I wouldn’t be surprised," Jo answered. She knew that although Laurie was away now at college, he insisted on coming home every week to, as he said, "get away from those horrid books."
"Well, he’s promised to escort me and Aunt March to the theater and she’s hoping it will be this Saturday," said Amy.
Yawning, uninterested in the trivial worries of Aunt March’s life, Jo flipped through her book and replied sarcastically, "I’m certain that Laurie will be thrilled to oblige Aunt March’s every wish."

Thankfully some things hadn’t changed, such as Jo’s passion for writing and her favorite spot to do it in. Armed with her pen, Jo sat upstairs in her sanctuary, her hand flying over the paper as she tried to finish another chapter in the novel she was currently working on. With the confidence she gained from selling some of her short stories, Jo decided to move on to longer pieces of writing. She was about to complete the last page when someone knocked at her door.
"Whoever it is had better go away," Jo called out threateningly, as she refused to get up to see who it was.
The knocker persisted, this time with a series of short taps in the rhythm of a well-known children’s song.
"Argh!" Jo threw her pen across the room and stomped over to unlock the door and unleash her fury.
"Surprise!" Laurie shoved his face in as soon as the door was unlocked and tackled Jo with such a hug that she didn’t have a chance to react.

Laurie, now twenty, the same age as Meg, had indeed blossomed into a handsome young man. He was very tall with broad shoulders and wavy dark hair that constantly fell over his left eye, giving him a very romantic look. Many girls at his college worshipped him as if he were a Roman god, and Laurie did not discourage their attention. However, to Jo and the girls, he was still silly Laurie, which he did not mind, because he could comfortably be himself around them.
"Do they not teach you to read in college?" Jo asked, pointing to the sign she had hung on the door that read: Interrupt At Own Risk.
Shrugging his shoulders, Laurie swung a brown bag in front of Jo’s face. "You don’t want to be interrupted even for this?" he teased.

"Oh, Laurie! Thank you!" Jo snatched the bag from his hand. Like a hungry lion, she nearly ripped the bag open and shoved two candies into her mouth, sucking one in each cheek, making her look like an overgrown chipmunk.

Meg had put all the girls on a diet before the wedding, forbidding any sweets in the house. Jo seldom had cravings, but candies were something she could not live without. Thanking Laurie for sharing the forbidden treats, Jo was glad to have him to rely on when things got tough.

The weeks leading up to the big event passed like mere minutes and before they could catch their breath, the eve of Meg’s wedding day was upon them. The girls changed into their pajamas but nobody felt like sleeping because this was the last evening that Meg would spend with them.
"This time tomorrow, you will be a married woman," Amy stated as she brushed Meg’s hair.
"Are you nervous?" asked Beth, laying her hand over Meg’s.
"No," said Meg with a smile. "After such a long engagement, John and I can’t wait to be married."
"Have you already forgotten about us then?" Jo pouted childishly.
"Of course not, Jo," Meg said gently, extending a hand, which Jo diverted her eyes from and turned away.
"I’m going to miss you girls very much," Meg continued. "But since I’ll live just down the road, I’ll expect daily visits so that we’ll always remain in close touch."
The sisters, including Jo, encircled Meg and after many sniffles, cries, and loving words, they went off to bed.
Several hours later as Jo was lying wide awake in the dark, she felt a familiar hand on her shoulder.
"Jo?" whispered Meg as she slid over to her sister and held Jo’s hand as they did when they were little girls.
"I’m going to miss you, Meg," Jo whispered tearfully.
"Me too," replied Meg. "Take care of the girls, Jo."
Nodding, Jo squeezed Meg’s hand and the two sisters fell asleep side by side.
Meg could not have chosen a more perfect day for the wedding. The sun was out bright and early while a gentle, light breeze pushed away the heat to make the temperature ideal for an outdoor ceremony.

Due to their tight budget, Meg and John had planned a small, intimate wedding, inviting only family and a few close friends. Among the guests was Sallie Gardiner, Meg’s close friend, who had married Ned Moffat a few months before. Sallie had had a lavish, elegant wedding, but Meg’s simple yet warm ceremony was just as memorable.
"Look at your tie, Brookes! It’s a mess," Laurie cried, undoing the tie and re-doing it skillfully.
"Thanks, Laurie, I’m a bit nervous," admitted his former tutor.
"That’s understandable, considering today is the most important day of your life! But everything is going to be fine," reassured his grown-up pupil.

Beth came out wearing a light blue silk dress and pink flowers in her hair. She sat down at the piano that was brought out especially for the occasion and began playing. Although Meg had wanted all three of her sisters to be bridesmaids, Beth was too nervous to walk down the aisle and have everyone stare at her. Instead, she offered to play the music for the wedding. Taking her cue, the guests found their seats and waited for the bride to enter. First Jo and Amy walked in together, each carrying a small bouquet, and wearing identical dresses to Beth’s. The girls smiled as they walked down the aisle.
"She’s so beautiful," Laurie murmured as the girls passed him.
"That Amy is going to break many hearts," replied Sallie, thinking Laurie was talking about the youngest March sister.
Laurie, however, was not referring to Amy; his eyes and heart were set on the other sister.

Finally, the bride walked down the aisle with her father. Meg looked radiant in her white gown. She wore white daisies in her hair and held a simple bouquet of flowers in her hand. It was her smile, however, that lit up her face and illuminated her joy.
The ceremony was short. Once Meg and John had exchanged their vows and rings, Mr. and Mrs. Brookes presented themselves to their guests.

"Congratulations to you both!" Cheers and best wishes for the new couple were heard throughout the reception. Jo, having endured starvation for as long as her body would permit, could no longer neglect her rumbling stomach and purposefully made her way to the buffet table to indulge to her heart’s content. Following closely behind like a lovesick puppy was Laurie.
"Jo, you look amazing," he kept saying, much to her annoyance.
"If you wore this dress and put this paint on your face, Laurie," Jo said, indicating her gown and makeup, "you’d be gorgeous too. Now, stop embarrassing me and go away."
Laurie was not easily discouraged and would have gone on, if not for the entrance of an uninvited guest.
"Josephine!" Aunt March’s voice shrilled loudly, causing everyone to stop mid-conversation and frightening Beth so that she stopped playing her music.
Jo nearly dropped her plate because Aunt March was the last person she expected to see.
"Where is she? Where is your sister?" Aunt March demanded, briskly walking toward Jo and Laurie with determination.
"I’m here, Aunt March," Meg boldly called out and cautiously approached her aunt, while John followed closely behind.
Aunt March did not speak until Meg stood before her. When she arrived, the old woman scrutinized her from head to toe. "Yes, yes, all very simple like you," Aunt March snapped.

John opened his mouth to defend his wife but Meg gently placed her hand on his arm to silence him. Since their last encounter, which had ended so disastrously, Meg had not spoken to her aunt for the past three years. "What can I do for you, Aunt March?" Meg asked calmly.
"I’ve come to give you your wedding gift," Aunt March said, holding out a white envelope.
"Aunt March, it isn’t necessary for you to give a gift," Meg said graciously but firmly.

Aunt March peered at Meg, then softening a little she said, "I know I uttered words that I shouldn’t have and I regret them deeply. You are my only living relatives . . . ," she choked up but continued, "and I would like nothing more than to make the best use of my time on earth while I can."
Mrs. Brookes warmly embraced her old aunt and gave her a tender kiss saying, "Thank you, Aunt March, for helping my husband and me start our married life at peace with our loved ones."
Appropriately, Beth started up the music again and everyone laughed and danced merrily.
"Do you think they’ll be happy?" Jo asked Laurie as they watched her sister and brother-in-law dance.
"Naturally," Laurie replied. "They are, after all, in love."
Snorting, Jo remarked, "I think love is rather silly."
Laurie held his tongue, but he disagreed.
After hours of celebrating, Meg and John were ready to go to their new home, just down the street from her family’s house.
"Well, here we are," John said, stopping in front of their small modest house. "It’s not as cozy as your place or as grand as the Laurence mansion but it’s ours."
Taking his arm in hers, Meg smiled at him and said, "Yes, it’s our home, sweet home."

As Aunt March’s favorite grandniece, Amy received many favors from her rich relative, including art lessons at the finest institute in town. On the first day of class, she realized that she already knew some of her classmates from school. These were the girls whose parents had the wealth to send their children to this particular place.
"Amy? Amy March?" Christina cried disbelievingly on the first day of class.

"Christina! Mary! How lovely to see you again!" exclaimed Amy, genuinely pleased to see the girls, even though the memories of the limes incident still pricked her heart. Having survived many experiences, including almost losing a beloved sister, Amy felt life was too short to hold grudges. Instead, she chose to be friendly and kind even to those who had wronged her. Amy also tried her best to remain modest, even though Mrs. Meade, the art instructor, often showered praise on Amy’s talent.

"Lunch at my house this week, Amy," Mary informed her as the class was dismissed one afternoon. At some point during the classes, the girls had decided among themselves to take turns hosting a luncheon every Saturday. Amy had attended three so far, and it seemed to her that each girl tried to outshine the one before by preparing fancy feasts and desserts more suited for a ball than a midday meal. However, Amy doubted very much that the girls actually cooked the meals themselves; most likely they relied on servants to get the job done. After lunch, the girls would set out for some scenic place and spend the rest of the afternoon sketching, painting, and doing what all girls love best: gossiping.
Amy knew that after Mary, it would be her turn to host a lunch and so began her worries.

That evening, Amy drew up a schedule for her upcoming luncheon, including the menu and activities to follow the meal. She had checked her savings beforehand to make sure she had enough to finance the event. Fortunately, Amy received a generous salary from Aunt March, so she was able to put away a little extra each week for special occasions. Originally, Amy had wanted to save enough money to travel to Italy and paint to her heart’s content. Sighing loudly, she said, disheartened, "Italy will have to wait till after lunch."

Father, carrying a large basket of fresh, ripe vegetables, walked in as Amy was making her curious remark. Chuckling, he said, "I’m sure you know what you’re talking about, but I haven’t a clue what you mean."
Slipping the paper into her pocket, Amy gave her father a hug and said, "It’s nothing, Father, but I may ask for some of your vegetables next week."
"As many as you like, darling," he replied, tweaking her nose.

Amy spent a great deal of time (and money) making individual invitations for her lunch. Handing them out to the girls, Amy heard many compliments about her design and artwork. "I’ve hired a carriage that will take us to the most enchanting place in the world," she said as her old habit of bragging started to return. "I personally prefer oil paints but its beauty can be captured with any technique of your choice."

On the eve of the party, Mother and Jo watched Amy anxiously as she scurried around like a little mouse preparing things. They waited for her instructions since Amy had asked for their help, along with that of Beth, Hannah, and Meg (who had to decline because her husband’s friends were coming for dinner that very day).
"Do you know how much she’s spent so far?" Jo asked disapprovingly.
"It’s her money. She can do as she likes," Mother replied.
"But she’s blowing her hard-earned money on just this one day and for a bunch of whiny girls who don’t even care about her," Jo said critically.
"Jo, even though we may not agree with Amy’s idea, we have agreed to help her, so let’s keep our word," Mother said.

It was not easy to do even that, as Jo discovered, with Amy’s short temper, sharp reproofs, and constant corrections. "Jo, I said beat the eggs one at a time, not all together!" Amy shouted after she had asked her sister to help bake a cake.
"Jo, don’t slice the meat so thickly!" she corrected after asking Jo to help with the sandwich meat.
"Jo, must you sing while you wash the vegetables? It’s rather annoying!" she snapped when Jo started to hum aloud to entertain herself.
"It’s you who’s annoying," Jo wanted to yell back, but she bit her lip and did as Amy asked. Everyone fell into bed exhausted that night, looking forward to a restful sleep.
But a few hours later at the crack of dawn, Amy woke them up. After a poor attempt at an apology, Amy said to her sisters, "This house must sparkle and shine before the girls come."
The two sisters, yawning and rubbing their eyes, glanced over at the clock, which read 6:15 a.m. Groaning loudly, Jo murmured some unpleasant things about her youngest sister.

Unfortunately for Amy the weather did not cooperate with her plans. It was pouring cats and dogs while low thunder rumbled in the distance. Looking outside, Mother said, "Perhaps Mr. Laurence will allow you girls to paint in his conservatory."
"The rain may let up yet," Amy said hopefully, "so Father should still go and collect the horse and carriage anyway."

Ever the gentleman, Father put on his hat, found his umbrella, and set out to do as his daughter requested. Jo and Beth got to work cleaning every inch of the house, while Mother and Hannah finished preparing the meal. By the time they got everything ready, the March home looked quite presentable for a group of upper-class girls.
"Now I’m going upstairs to change so if anyone comes while I’m gone, please make them feel welcome," Amy said to her sisters while she went to make herself beautiful.

Around noon, when the guests were scheduled to come, Amy, looking very pretty in a green dress, stood waiting by the door like a good hostess. At the sounds of a carriage approaching, Amy excitedly opened the door. She discovered it was only Father returning, not with a grand carriage, but with an open wagon being pulled by an old, smelly horse. Running outside into the rain, Amy cried, "Father! This isn’t the one I hired!"
Trying to calm his daughter down, Father explained, "Mr. Glendale didn’t want his finest horse and carriage out in the terrible weather. He’ll give you a discount for these."
Amy’s neatly brushed and styled hair was soon dripping wet and her clothes clung to her like a second skin.
"Amy, you must change out of those clothes or you’ll catch a cold," Mother said, pushing her upstairs to her room.
Sniffing, Amy argued, "But this is my best dress. I don’t have anything else to wear."
"Don’t exaggerate," Mother said firmly. "You have a closet full of pretty things. Now go and change!"
Shuffling her feet, Amy cried, "Can the day get any worse?" It did for poor Amy.

Having changed into her old but still pretty blue dress and pulled back her damp hair into a tidy bun, Amy was once again the eager hostess ready to greet her guests. She waited and waited worriedly for any signs of the arrival of the girls. But an hour or so later, after the rain had stopped and short bursts of sunshine had broken through the clouds, not a single guest had appeared at the March home. Amy wrung her hands, her face crumbling in disappointment as she craned her neck for any familiar faces on the street. Her family stood a little behind her, aching to console her but letting her retain some dignity. It was obvious the party was ruined.
"Just wait till I get my hands on those sissy, prissy, no-good brats," Jo mumbled under her breath, cracking her knuckles as she pondered ways to get revenge on those who had hurt her sister.
"Jo! You’re not helping the situation," Mother whispered loudly.
"Well, I don’t think we’ll be having any guests today," Amy called out with forced cheeriness.
"Maybe they got lost," suggested Beth kindly.
Amy let out an ugly laugh and said, "I doubt it, dear sister. More likely they all agreed not to come to teach me a lesson."
"It’s because they’re jealous of you," offered Jo. "You’re beautiful and talented, and you have a family that adores you."

Shaking her head Amy said, "Thanks, Jo, but it’s plain to see that the girls want me to know my place . . . that I don’t belong among them. They let me visit their mansions and castles, as if they’re doing me a favor, but they won’t set foot in a humble home like ours."
Father wrapped his arm around Amy and said, "I’m not excusing those girls for how they hurt you today, dear, but whatever their reasons were, don’t lose your self-worth or your pride in who you are."
"Thank you, Father, and all of you, for your help and for bearing with me," Amy smiled sheepishly. "I know I’ve been such a bother this week."
"It was our pleasure," Mother replied, giving Jo a stern look before she could say anything. "Now, what are we going to do with all this food?"

Over at the newlyweds’ house, Meg’s day was not faring any better than Amy’s. John had invited some of his friends over for dinner that evening. Although Meg had felt confident when she had agreed to prepare a meal all by herself, she was wondering now how on earth she had gotten herself into such a pickle. "Two cups of butter, no, one cup butter and one cup oil, no, that doesn’t sound right . . . Oh! I don’t know. I can’t remember!" Meg cried as she tried to recall the ingredients in apple pie.

Frustrated, Meg decided to make the creamed chicken first but could not find a clean pot to make the sauce in, because all her dishes were either dirty or being used. At home, Meg had always relied on Hannah to wash the dishes while she cooked, and another person to help her prepare the vegetables or hand her the ingredients she needed. As the mistress of her own home and without a helper (John’s modest salary did not allow them to hire someone at the moment), Meg had to do everything on her own and it was driving her mad.
"Oh! I should just tell John to cancel tonight’s dinner. I can’t do it!" said Meg, dropping into a chair, where she held her head and began crying.

A light gentle rap on the window, then a louder one, forced Meg to look up with red eyes. Jo was peering in with a worried expression, mouthing something Meg could not understand. Wiping her tears, Meg stood up and opened the door to let her sister in.
"What’s the matter, Meg?" Jo demanded, taking hold of her sister’s hand.
"I’m so glad to see you, Jo," sniffed Meg. "How is everything going with Amy’s luncheon?"
Snorting loudly, Jo explained what had happened while Meg listened intently.
"Poor Amy!" Meg said, forgetting her own plight at once.
"Yes, but our Amy is a fighter," said Jo proudly, "and she’s already put this incident behind her. She’ll be fine. Now what is going on here?"
"I’m such a horrible wife!" Meg began, tears forming again.
"Don’t say such things. That’s not true. Tell me how I can help," said Jo.

Meg explained what she was doing and why things weren’t going as smoothly as she’d like. "I didn’t want to ask you or Mother since I knew Amy needed your help, and besides, I thought I could manage on my own," Meg said.
"Why doesn’t John help you?" asked Jo, still looking for an excuse to dislike the man who had taken Meg away from her.
"I’m afraid I’m to blame since I sent him out early this morning on a few errands because I didn’t want him to get in my way," Meg said, shamefaced.

As Jo sized up the situation, she realized that Meg was in trouble and desperately needed help. In a flash, Jo had a great idea. "Meg," she said excitedly. "Clean up this mess, clean yourself off, put on your lovely dress, and leave the rest to me."
"Jo, are you out of your mind? The guests will be here in two hours," Meg said impatiently.
"Please, Meg, I have an idea. Just trust me," Jo begged.
Meg stared at her sister warily.

Something about Jo’s voice and manner persuaded Meg to trust her, so she did as Jo asked. After cleaning up the kitchen and washing the dishes, Meg took a long bath and changed her clothes. With no sign of Jo, Meg anxiously tidied her small living room and set out the cutlery and china plates purchased with Aunt March's generous wedding gift. Then she paced the kitchen floor, her heart racing as her eyes skimmed the bare table. Meg was beginning to feel sorry for John, who would be coming home to find nothing ready for his guests, when her ears picked up the sounds of a horse trotting, then stopping in front of the house. Looking out, Meg burst out laughing at the comical sight. An old horse was pulling an older wagon with great effort while the passengersㅡher sistersㅡwaved enthusiastically from the cart.
"Delivery for Mrs. Meg Brookes!" Jo shouted as she jumped out and, grabbing a few baskets, headed toward Meg’s open door.
Amy and Beth followed suit and soon, after several trips, because there was a lot to carry in, Meg’s kitchen and dining room table were filled with the lavish food prepared for Amy’s party.
"Oh, girls! I don’t know what to say!" Meg cried, her eyes shining brightly.
"We can’t possibly eat all this food ourselves," said Amy.
"It looks like a feast fit for a king," Meg praised. "John will be so pleased."
"We make a good team, don’t you think?" asked Jo.
"We sure do," said Amy. "Through thick and thin, we March girls know how to stick together."

During the 1860s, the era the March girls lived in, it was the custom for ladies to make formal visits regularly to their neighbors and relatives as a courtesy and display of good manners. Amy, wanting very much to be regarded as a well-bred lady, eagerly planned such occasions with a keen sense of purpose.
"Jo, aren’t you going to get ready?" Amy asked her sister one Friday morning.
"For what?" Jo, sprawled out on the bed, didn’t even look up from the book she was reading.
Amy stopped brushing her blonde wavy hair and stared at Jo through the mirror in front of her. "Don’t tell me you’ve forgotten," she said in an exasperated voice.
"Okay, I won’t," replied Jo, turning a page.
"Jo!" Amy swung around this time and faced her sister. "We’re supposed to make our calls today. You promised me! Time is important since we have half a dozen homes to visit."
Slowly tearing her eyes away from the book, Jo looked at Amy with a blank expression. "Calls? I don’t remember promising anything of the sort, Miss Amy March," she said.
Amy narrowed her eyes and said accusingly, "Yes, you did. You said if I finished the painting of Beth playing the piano for Mr. Laurence, then you would come with me in making calls."

Jo grimaced but tossed the book aside, for now she clearly remembered the circumstances of her promise, though she obviously had not been paying attention to its conditions when she made it. "I’ll come with you but I won’t be happy about it," Jo said childishly. "I won’t sit there with a fake smile and pretend I’m having a jolly good time."
"Oh, yes you will," Amy said sternly. "You are not going to embarrass me or our family by frowning, making rude gestures, or saying scandalous things."
The sisters stuck their tongues out at each other like true ladies, then Jo reluctantly got changed into something more suitable for the occasion.

The first house they called on was the Tudors’ home. The Tudors were one of the founding families of their town. They had two daughters about the same age as Jo and Amy but the girls were obnoxious and snobbish, not to mention renowned for their lack of good looks.
"Jo, I want you to be on your best behavior here," Amy said, stopping in front of the Tudor home.
"I will be if those ugly witches are," Jo answered promptly.
"Jo! Please! It will benefit our family to be on good terms with the Tudors. Be nice and don’t speak. Don’t say a word, please," begged Amy.
"Miss Amy! Miss Josephine! How lovely to see you!"
Mrs. Tudor welcomed the girls in an exaggerated voice when they were shown into the house by one of their many servants.
"Mrs. Tudor, thank you for having us. It’s our pleasure and privilege to visit your beautiful home," Amy gushed.

Having been told to remain silent, Jo merely nodded and wordlessly followed Mrs. Tudor to their sitting room. Waiting for them were the Tudor sisters, sitting on matching velvet chairs as if they were royalty and expecting Jo and Amy to curtsy to them. Amy, being a good spirit, went over and asked about their health, and complimented their dresses and hair. Meanwhile, Jo sat in the farthest corner of the room not uttering a sound.

"Would you like Earl Grey tea, Miss Josephine, or Darjeeling?" asked Mrs. Tudor while one servant brought in a china teapot and cups on a large silver tray and two others carried in the biscuits, sandwiches, and chocolate.
"Could I have a glass of milk instead, please? Thank you," Jo said, avoiding Amy’s glare from across the room.
Startled, Mrs. Tudor took a moment before answering, "Yes, yes, of course. Liddie, bring Miss Josephine what she wants."

Jo had to endure an hour of listening to how many suitors the girls had and where they were traveling for their summer holidays. Amy, nodding at the appropriate times, seemed genuinely interested in their affairs, but Jo, trying very hard to bite her tongue and keep from speaking out, decided to turn her attention to the birds outside.
"Well, we don’t want to keep you any longer as I’m sure you have a lot to do before your trip," said Amy graciously, standing up to leave.

After another ten minutes just to say good-bye, Jo and Amy stepped outside the Tudor home. As soon as they had done so, they heard one of the girls say to their mother as the door shut, "What a horribly rude person that Josephine March is!"
The other girl spoke next. "She looks at us as if we’re rats and doesn’t say a word! I’ve never been so insulted!"
Grinning, Jo took Amy’s arm and led her away from the house.
"I have to agree with the girls, Jo," Amy scolded when they were far enough away. "What was the matter with you? You barely spoke two words."
"You told me not to say anything," Jo reminded her.
"I meant not to say anything rude," sighed Amy, "not to say nothing at all."
"Permission to speak at the next home then?" Jo asked teasingly.
"Yes, please speak. Be more cheerful and friendly," said Amy.

The next home on their list belonged to the Chesters, another wealthy, well-respected family. The Chesters had three boys and one daughter, Mary, who was Amy’s classmate both in school and in art class.
"Good morning, Mrs. Chester," Amy said warmly to a middle-aged woman who was wearing a large string of pearls with a diamond pendant.

"What a simply adorable necklace you’re wearing, Mrs. Chester," Jo said, pulling the pearls toward her to have a closer look and in doing so, nearly choking the poor woman. "Oh! Are these your adorable little boys?" Jo blew kisses at three big teenage boys, standing behind their mother.
Amy’s face flushed as she noticed Mrs. Chester staring at Jo with an odd expression and the boys making funny faces.
"Mary! You are simply the most adorable little creature!" Jo shouted at the young woman waiting for them in the parlor.
"We were so distressed when you couldn’t attend Amy’s little party a few weeks ago. We missed you terribly!" Jo continued in a phony voice.

Soon tea was served and before long, Jo was deep in conversation with Mary’s brothers. Meanwhile Mary was trying to explain why she hadn’t attended Amy’s party. Amy replied with understanding, "Not another word, Mary, for it was a dreadful day to travel and I . . ."
Suddenly, Amy was interrupted by a loud squeal, then a burst of laughter exploding from the other side of the room. Jo and the Chester boys were rocking back and forth clutching their stomachs.

Amy shook her head, having only herself to blame for telling Jo how she should act at other people’s homes. Clearly, Jo was having fun playing different roles, making a spectacle of herself, and not caring how others viewed her or her family.
The visit with the Chesters was even shorter than the one with the Tudors. Jo and the boys erupted in laughing fits several more times before Amy made her excuses to leave.
"Are you leaving already? The boys seem to be having so much fun with your sister," Mary remarked slyly.
"Jo has a natural way with children," replied Amy in a composed voice, but feeling ashamed. "We would love to stay, but I’m afraid our next appointment will require a little more traveling time."
"Of course, I forgot that you don’t have a carriage," Mary said innocently, but with a stab in her sentence.
Smiling sweetly, Amy thanked Mrs. Chester and Mary for their hospitality then called out to Jo.

As soon as the door of the Chester home had closed, Amy’s frozen smile melted, and she turned to Jo in anger. "Can’t you behave like a lady just for once? Why do you choose to make a fool of yourself, of me, of our family?" she practically yelled in the middle of the street.
"Lower your voice, dear, people are watching," Jo said mockingly.
"Jo! I’m serious! Why are you determined to ruin my life?" Amy cried passionately.
"Why should I pretend to be something I’m not?" retorted Jo, who was close to shouting too. "I really don’t like these people nor am I interested in their lives!"
Regaining her composure, Amy breathed deeply and said, "Because that’s how people will learn to respect us and treat us better."
Shaking her head, Jo said, "You’re wrong, Amy. No matter how nice we are to them, they won’t think of us as their equal. I thought you realized that after your party."
The two sisters walked in silence for a while, then Amy spoke up. "Maybe you’re right, but I still believe that good will come if we try to show kindness to others regardless of how they see us."
"That’s why you are a dreamer, Amy," acknowledged Jo, "and I love you for it. But me? I’m practical and realistic and I don’t believe that I have to change just to make another person happy."
"Then I won’t ask you to," Amy said. "You are you, Jo, and I love you for it too."
Stopping in front of Aunt March’s house, the two sisters gave each other a quick hug.
"Can I be me now?" Jo asked playfully.
"Of course," smiled Amy. "Besides, Aunt March knows your true colors anyway." Giggling, the sisters held hands as they walked up toward the large mansion.

Aunt March’s housemaid Esther brought the girls to the west wing sitting room. (Aunt March’s mansion was so gigantic that she had three sitting rooms, one in each direction except for east.) The old lady sat in her "throne," as Jo called her large velvet armchair with gold armrests and satin cushions. Aunt March was feeding crackers to Polly who, upon seeing them, screeched loudly, "Mind your mouth!"
"Hello, Aunt March," said Amy, walking over and kissing her on both cheeks.
Jo stood awkwardly because in all the years she had come to work at this house, she had never greeted her aunt with a kiss.
"What are you standing there for like a stone statue?" the old lady snapped at Jo. "Polly needs more crackers."
"Crackers!" screeched the parrot.

Without another word, Jo turned around and headed toward the kitchen to do as Aunt March told her. When she returned with the crackers and a dish of clean water for the bird, Jo saw a rare sight: the deep lines on her aunt’s face had softened and the corners of her mouth lifted upward in a smile.
"Now Aunt March, I insist that you let me adjust these pillows back here. You don’t look very comfortable sitting there," said Amy, carefully rearranging the cushions on Aunt March’s chair.
"I’m fine," Aunt March said in a much more tender voice than she had ever used with Jo. "Where is that sister of yours? Has she gone to make her own crackers? Polly is starving here."
"Here we go," said Jo in an overly cheery voice, as she pushed the crackers into Polly’s face.

"Let me do it, Jo," Amy said, taking the dish from her and expertly breaking off pieces to feed the bird. Jo had to admit that Amy excelled at her job. Even though Jo knew Amy was not fond of the bird, at that moment, you could not see Amy’s true feelings, because she treated Polly as gently as Aunt March did.
When Esther brought in the tea and biscuits, Jo wandered over to the bookshelves to see if Aunt March had gotten any new books since she stopped working for her.
"Josephine, I’d like to hear a story," Aunt March called to her. "Amy here is a darling, but no one can read a story like you can, dear."
Feeling touched, Jo selected a new book that she thought would be interesting and took it over to Aunt March.
"No. That one’s terribly boring. Bring Stories from the Garden ," said her aunt.
"But doesn’t The Pirate’s Treasure Box sound more exciting and adventurous?" Jo asked persuasively, since the title was especially appealing to her.
"I don’t care for that one, Josephine. The other one is better," Aunt March said firmly.
"Yes, Aunt March," Jo said, bringing the garden stories book and sitting down next to her aunt.
Amy poured the tea and chose some biscuits for Aunt March while Jo opened the book to read.
"Girls, there is something I want to discuss with you," Aunt March began as she accepted the teacup from Amy with one hand, while placing the other on Jo’s arm to stop her from reading.
The sisters looked at her expectantly, waiting for her to continue.

"As you know, every summer I travel to Europe for a holiday," said Aunt March. "This year I have chosen to spend the entire year abroad as my health has worsened and the warmer climates seem to improve it somewhat."
"Of course, Aunt March, your health is the main priority," said Amy.

Nodding at her, Aunt March continued. "However, the doctor recommends that I travel with a companion . . ." Aunt March chose to pause here, sip her tea, and adjust a cushion before continuing. Meanwhile, both Jo and Amy, realizing what Aunt March was about to announce, held their breath. Each girl hoped her heart wouldn’t jump out of her chest because it was beating so fast.

"I must confess it was a hard decision for me to make," said Aunt March. "Whether you believe it or not, I am fond of both of you for obviously different reasons. However, as I will be covering all expenses for this trip, I expect my companion to be someone who will do exactly as I say."
Jo could hardly sit still since her dream of traveling to Europe seemed about to come true in the next few seconds.
Then looking at each girl long and hard, Aunt March held out her hand and said, "Therefore, I’ve decided to take Amy to Europe with me."

For days Jo locked herself up in her sanctuary, telling everyone that she was working on a new novel, when in fact she was bawling her eyes out. She didn’t fool anybody, because it was clear from her puffy red eyes and swollen nose that she hadn’t spent the night writing.
Having decided it was time to face reality, Mother gently knocked on the door, and said, "Jo? May I come in?"
"Mmm . . . ," Jo said in a muffled voice. Seeing Mother’s kind, understanding eyes, Jo broke out in a new wave of tears.
"Shh, darling, just let it out," comforted Mother.

"It’s not fair," wept Jo. "She knew how much I wanted to travel to Europe. Every year she would make me believe that the next year I could come along, but now to choose Amy instead . . . it’s unbearable."
"Do you remember how you used to feel when you came home each day from Aunt March’s?" asked Mother.
Sniffing, Jo replied, "Yes. She annoyed me to no end."
"Now imagine if you had to spend all day and night with her for one year. Honestly, Jo, do you think you could manage that?" Mother reasoned with her.

Wiping her nose with the back of her hand, Jo thought about it but did not answer, so Mother continued, "You once told me about the hundreds of libraries and museums you wanted to visit. Do you think Aunt March would allow you the freedom to do that?"

Jo, who had stopped crying, shook her head and said, "I never thought about it that way. You’re right, Mother, Aunt March would never let me follow my own personal dreams. Instead I would be at her beck and call every moment of the day."

Patting Jo on the back, Mother said, "But Amy reacts differently as Aunt March rightly sees. Amy is quite happy going for tea, socializing, and taking strolls. That’s why she would be a better companion on this particular trip. Do you understand that now?"
Jo nodded heartily and said, "Yes, Mother. I’m still jealous that Amy is going to see Europe before me, but she deserves it. She is very good to Aunt March and to our neighbors."

Jo told Mother how well behaved Amy had been when they made their calls. Remembering how hard her sister worked to please others reminded Jo of Amy’s words on the road: "I still believe that good will come if we try to show kindness to others regardless of how they see us." Jo had to admit that she learned something quite valuable from her sister through this incident.

In the girls’ bedroom, Amy had a lot to do in preparation for her trip. "Aunt March says not to pack too many things since she will give me an allowance so I can get my dresses tailored in the European style," Amy said excitedly to Beth.
"Europeans are so cultured and stylish. I think you’re going to fit right in, Amy," said Beth.
"Thank you, Beth. You are too kind and I’m going to miss you terribly. I really am," Amy said, hugging her tightly.
"Have you packed away Mr. Huggie?" Jo called out loudly as she walked in. Mr. Huggie was an old stuffed animal that Amy used to sleep with when she was a little girl.
"Unfortunately there is no room for him in my suitcase," Amy said, pointing to her oversized luggage.
"But he’s going to miss you," Jo teased.
"I feel better knowing he’s here with you," Amy said in return.

After Aunt March announced that she was taking Amy with her, it put a strain on Jo and Amy’s relationship. Jo wasn’t angry, but under the circumstances, she found it hard, as anyone would, not to be resentful. Now, however, it appeared that the tension had lifted and life was back to normal.
"You deserve to go, Amy, and I hope you have the time of your life," Jo said sincerely.
"Do you mean that, Jo?" asked Amy.
"Yes, and I’m sorry for behaving immaturely," begged Jo. "Will you forgive me?"

Amy hugged her sister hard and cried, "Oh, Jo, there’s nothing to forgive. I’m just relieved that you aren’t upset at me. I’ll write as often as I can and tell you all about the places I see and the people I meet."
"I’d like that, Amy. I really would," said Jo.

Having accepted that she might never have a chance to visit Europe in her lifetime, Jo was busying her days with writing, but she could not shake a restlessness that had developed in her heart.
