Lying in the yard one afternoon, Jo looked up at the sky and saw a couple of birds swirling around. "I wish I could spread my wings and fly off like you," she said to them dreamily.
The dark shadow of a human face blocked her view just then, disrupting her daydream.
"If you had wings, how would anybody be able to catch you?" the face said, showing that he had clearly been listening to her private monologue.
"The whole point is never to be caught but to have the freedom to go wherever you choose," Jo replied. "And how rude of you to sneak up on an unsuspecting person."
Reaching out to the hand extended toward her, Jo sat up and grinned into the face of her best friend. "What are you doing home at this time of the week?" she asked Laurie.
He shrugged and changed the subject instead. "I hear Amy’s off to Europe with your old aunt."
"That’s right. She’s going for one year. Now back to you. Why are you home?" Jo smartly brought the conversation back to Laurie.
"I’ve been suspended," Laurie finally admitted.
"Why? Laurie, what happened?" Jo asked in an alarmed voice.
"I got in a fight with these guys and well . . . here I am," he said lightly.
"How long are you suspended for?" Jo asked.
"Maybe two weeks," Laurie replied.

Jo gazed at him with concern knowing that he was going to college to please his grandfather, but he hadn’t quite adapted to the life there. She wanted to scold him but something stopped her. Instead she said, "Well, I’m glad you’re here because after Amy leaves tomorrow, I’m going to be so miserable. You can be a good boy and get me through this."
Grinning mischievously, Laurie saluted her and said, "Yes, sir! I live to carry out your orders."

The next day bright and early, after Amy managed to fit all her suitcases, paint sets, easel, and other art supplies into Aunt March’s carriage, she said her farewells to her family. "Good-bye, everyone! I’ll miss you all very much," she cried out, giving each person a hug.
"Be careful not to catch a cold," Mother said tearfully.
"Remember to write often," said her father.
"Find yourself a handsome Italian prince," were Jo’s parting words.
"Please think of us because we’ll be thinking of you," pleaded Beth.
"Take care of yourself," cried Meg and John.
"I may make a surprise visit on you," Laurie called out.
"That would be wonderful, Laurie. I do hope you’ll come. Bye! Good-bye!" Amy shouted, as the carriage disappeared around the corner.

With first Meg and then Amy gone, the house seemed empty and desolate. Beth must have felt it too, Jo thought, because her younger sister seemed more subdued lately. Watching her now as they hung out the laundry on the clothesline in the yard, Jo sensed something was definitely amiss.
"Beth, how are you sleeping lately?" Jo asked, clipping two clothespins on Father’s undershirt.
"Fine, Jo. I’m fine," Beth answered breathlessly. Then looking out across the yard onto the Laurences’ garden, Beth let out a short sigh.

Laurie was kicking a ball around, probably imagining it was someone’s head. Jo smiled as she remembered how furious Mr. Laurence had been when he heard that his grandson had been suspended from college. It wasn’t a laughing matter, but Laurie had told her about his grandfather’s reactions so vividly, imitating his voice and gestures, that Jo couldn’t help giggling.
"Look at what a handsome man our boy has turned into," Beth said in a soft voice as she kept her eye on Laurie.
Jo, suddenly feeling uneasy, thought she might have figured out why Beth had been so quiet these past few weeks. "She’s in love with Laurie!" Jo screamed silently.

Around the same time but in an entirely different part of the world, Amy was walking arm-in-arm with Aunt March along the famous Piccadilly Circus in London, England. Amy was dressed smartly in a well-fitted stylish dress with matching hat and parasol and taking small dainty steps so as to keep pace with her elderly aunt. Looking very prim and ladylike, Amy was noticed by the gentlemen passing by, some of them even stopping to offer compliments.

"Did you know, Aunt March, that the name Piccadilly comes from a frilly collar called a ‘picadil,’ which was quite popular during the seventeenth century? That’s why there are so many dressmakers along this street," Amy said knowledgeably.

Glowing with pride, Aunt March said, "How clever you are, my dear." Then leading Amy to a very distinguished dressmaker’s shop, she said, "If Piccadilly is famous for its fashions, then that is what we must get for you while we are here."
Hardly able to contain her excitement, Amy followed her aunt into the shop.

Back home Jo was going into a shop of a different sort–the fruit and vegetable kind. Since Beth did not have much of an appetite these days (as Jo found out from Meg, many lovesick people suffer the same symptoms), Jo wanted to buy some of Beth’s favorite fruits and surprise her that evening. As she was choosing a couple of ripe apples, a familiar voice called to her from behind.
"Jo! Fancy meeting you here!" Laurie shouted so loudly that the entire shop could hear.
"Shush, Laurie! Everyone’s staring," Jo whispered, her face turning as red as the apple in her hand. "What are you doing here, anyway?"
"I felt like getting some fruit to munch on," Laurie said, tossing an apple into the air and catching it.
"Don’t be silly. You have servants to do your shopping," Jo said, pointing at the apple, "and besides, I happen to know that you don’t like apples."

Laurie held up both hands as if to surrender and said, "I’ve been cooped up in the house, bored out of my mind, and then I saw you leaving the house and thought to myself: That’s odd—the old girl hasn’t been around lately."
Jo placed a hand over his mouth to stop his rambling. "As you can see I’m very busy right now, but perhaps I’ll come over later, if I have time," she said.
Shaking his head, Laurie said, "Mmm . . . bloof . . . mmhffoo," through Jo’s hand.
Removing her hand, Jo said, "What?"
"I said no. You’ve been avoiding me and I want to know why," Laurie repeated more clearly this time.
"I haven’t been avoiding you," Jo said as she turned her back on him and walked away.
"See? You’re doing it again, Jo. I demand to know what I’ve done to deserve such treatment from you," he said, pretending to be insulted.
"It’s not you; it’s Beth," Jo wanted to say but instead she said, "Would you mind holding this basket like a real gentleman? By the way, when are you going back to school?"
With one hand, Laurie held the basket but with the other he grasped Jo’s hand tightly. "Jo, why do you keep running? I’m getting tired of chasing you," he said in a very serious voice.
As much as Jo had been trying to ignore the signs, there was no denying now that Laurie was indeed in love with one of the March sisters, but it certainly was not Beth.
That evening, Jo sat in the living room with Mother. Beth had already gone up to bed, saying she had a headache, and Father was visiting a farmer who had lost his son in the war.
"Is something troubling you, dear?" Mother always seemed to know when her girls were weighed down by problems.

Jo deliberated whether to discuss Beth and Laurie with Mother, then decided it would be for the best and told her everything. Mother listened without speaking. Then she said, "That’s the trouble with love; it’s uncontrollable. It never goes in the direction that you want it to."
"Everything would be solved if Laurie would love Beth," exclaimed Jo.
"Are you sure of Beth’s feelings for Laurie? Have you spoken to her? Perhaps it’s something else and you are jumping to conclusions," Mother said.
"I haven’t asked her about it, but what else could it be?" Jo asked in a frustrated voice.
"What are your feelings for Laurie?" Mother asked gently.
"I love Laurie with all my heart but not like that. He’s my best friend, my brother, but . . ." Jo paused. "I don’t love him like Meg loves John."
"Has Laurie told you how he feels?" asked Mother.
Shaking her head, Jo answered, "No, but I’m afraid he’s going to very soon and I will break his heart. And if Beth finds out, then her heart will be broken. Oh, what a mess."
Mother held Jo in her arms for a while and then said, "What do you think is the solution to this problem?"
"I was thinking," Jo began. "Your friend Mrs. Kirke wrote that she is looking for a governess for her two girls in New York, didn’t she?"
Mother nodded and told her to go on.

"Well, what if I could apply for the position, just for the winter for now and see whether or not it’s a suitable place for me. I have become restless and thought of traveling myself, so this might be the best time to do so," said Jo.
"Yes, it does sound like a good idea," said Mother. "But Jo," she added, looking deep into her daughter’s eyes, "running away from a problem doesn’t solve it."
"I’m not running away. I’m buying time so that I will know how to straighten out the situation best. And who knows, maybe while I’m gone, Laurie will fall madly in love with Beth," Jo said hopefully.
"I’ll write to Mrs. Kirke immediately," Mother said.

Mother’s friend Mrs. Kirke sent a telegram asking Jo to come right away, saying her room was ready and waiting for her. Now it was time for Jo to spread her wings and fly just like the birds she had always envied and admired. But having to explain that to Beth was harder than she thought.
"What if I never see you again?" cried Beth.
"I’m coming back after the winter, Beth," Jo comforted her sister.
"I’m sorry if I sound selfish, but I can’t bear it if you leave too," said Beth.
After Jo had made many more reassurances and promises, Beth finally gave in and wished her the best of luck with this new chapter in her life.

Upstairs in her sanctuary, Jo collected her writing materials and her writer’s smock. She intended to complete her novel during her "expedition," as she called it, since each day would be an adventure. Within a few days, Jo was packed and ready to depart for New York City. Her family and friends waited downstairs to say good-bye to her.
"Jo, be careful because John says New York is a very dangerous place, so you ought to walk with your head up and alert, never go out alone, and always carry an umbrella," warned Meg.
"An umbrella? For what?" laughed Father.
"For protection, just in case, you know . . . as a weapon," Meg stammered.
"We’re very proud of you, darling, and we want you to have lots of adventures, but we are counting the days till you return," said Mother.
Beth didn’t say anything. She just hugged Jo tightly for a long time.

"I’ll carry your bags to the carriage," Laurie said, picking up the light luggage before Jo could protest. Outside, Laurie waited for her while she said her final farewells to her family. Then when she approached, he burst out, "You’re not planning on returning, are you?"
"Don’t make a scene, Laurie. Of course I’m coming back," Jo said, glancing back to see if Beth was watching them.
"Well, I’ll let you go this time, Jo March, but if for some crazy reason you decide to stay in New York, I’m coming to get you," Laurie threatened.
Hugging her dearest friend, Jo whispered in his ear, "Look after sweet Beth, will you? You’re all she has now."
"I will, Jo. I’ll look after her," promised Laurie.
Jo stepped up into the carriage and soon she was on her way to New York.

Meanwhile, many exciting events were unfolding in the life of Amy March, as she continued her tour of Europe. Aunt March had rented a beautiful villa in Nice, France, where the scenery was breathtaking. Every morning, Amy had to pinch herself as a reminder that she wasn’t dreaming but was truly in the most romantic country in the world. While Aunt March napped in the afternoon, Amy went out by herself, carrying just a sketchbook and her parasol, which no European girl left home without. She would wander along the beach until she found a spot that she wanted to draw. With so many beautiful scenes everywhere, her sketchbook was soon filled.

One particular afternoon while Amy was drawing a little girl playing in the ocean, a well-dressed young man carefully approached her. Speaking in French, he asked, "May I see what’s making you smile so much?"
During the short time she had been in Europe, Amy had already learned a few expressions in French, German, and Italian. So she fluently answered the young man’s question and showed him her drawing.

He made all sorts of lovely compliments in rapid French that Amy didn’t understand, but she nodded and smiled as if she did. "I’m sorry," Amy finally admitted when she could no longer fake it. "My French is very limited."
"Oh! You’re American! So am I!" the young man exclaimed. "I’m Fred. What’s your name?"
Amy introduced herself, and soon the two of them were having a lively conversation.
Across the Atlantic Ocean, Jo had just arrived in New York City after an exceptionally tiring but fascinating journey, during which she’d discovered landscapes that she had never seen before.

"Oh, my gracious me!" Jo gasped as she gazed around at her surroundings. Nothing could prepare her for the experience of New York City, where swarms of people bustled about on busy streets lined with building after building. Jo felt dizzy with excitement just thinking about the opportunities before her to explore all that the city had to offer.
Mrs. Kirke’s home was on a quiet street with large trees planted in a row in front of each house.

"Jo! Welcome to New York!" Mrs. Kirke called out happily when she opened the door to let Jo in. Mrs. Kirke was a few years younger than Mother, but had the same warm, inviting smile, which instantly reminded Jo how much she already missed her family.
"The girls are at the park now and will be home in a few minutes, so I’ll show you around the house," Mrs. Kirke said, taking one of Jo’s suitcases.

Everything in the house was well organized and clean. Once Jo saw her room, she knew her stay at the Kirkes’ home would be a pleasant one. Located on the top floor of the house, Jo’s room had one large window that boasted a fabulous view of the city in the distance. In front of the window was a large oak desk, where Jo could work on her novel and look outside whenever she wanted. Just standing there inspired Jo to pull out her paper and start writing immediately.
"I hope you are happy here, Jo," Mrs. Kirke was saying. "We want you to feel as if this is your home."
"Thank you, Mrs. Kirke," Jo said gratefully. "I am already falling in love with it."
"Oh, before I forget," added Mrs. Kirke. "We have a tenant who rents the floor beneath you.
"I’ll introduce you later. His name is Friedrich Bauer but we call him Professor. Oh, I hear the girls returning. Would you like to meet them now, Jo?"
"Yes, I would," said Jo, following her downstairs.

Back at the March home, Laurie was keeping his promise to Jo by making sure that Beth did not get too lonely. They sat for a few hours while Beth played the piano and they laughed as they chatted about old times.
"I’m going back to school in two days, Beth," Laurie told her. "Will you be okay without your sisters and me around?"
Smiling, Beth reassured him that she would be fine. "I have Meg, Mother, Father, Mr. Laurence, and of course, my beloved piano to occupy my days," she said.
"Do you think Jo will come back a different person?" Laurie asked cautiously.
Beth thought for a moment then replied rather sadly, "Yes, but change is inevitable. We must all face the truth and accept that nothing can stay the same forever."
"I don’t want things to ever change," Laurie said childishly.
Neither one of them, however, could have predicted how much their lives were going to be transformed.

France is a country where artists, intellectuals, and philosophers find inspiration. For romantics, it is a place where hopes and dreams might come true. Many people fall under France’s enchanting spell, and Amy March was one of them.

Amy found Fred to be everything she had ever hoped for in a suitor: he was from a very wealthy family, and he was handsome, intelligent, charming, and well groomed. There was no question that he adored Amy, practically worshipping the ground she walked on. They went to parties together, walked in the gardens, visited museums, and attended the theater several times. While she was enjoying these activities and Fred’s company, Amy tried to convince herself that he was a perfect match for marriage (that is, if her parents allowed her to marry at 18, which would be in one year). But something kept tugging at Amy’s heart.
"Fred is perfect," Amy said to her reflection in the mirror as she got ready for a party that evening. "So why do I feel this way?"

Until then, Amy had regarded marriage as a way to secure her position in society. She did not really believe that love had to be involved. It was more important to her that she marry the right person rather than a poor artist. "Love will come later as I grow fond of my husband and respect him," she told herself over and over again.

However, after meeting Fred, Amy could not put into practice what she thought she had strongly believed all these years. "Could I have been wrong?" she asked the confused image facing her in the mirror.

For Jo, love was the last thing on her mind as she busied herself in her duties as a governess to the Kirke girls. Jo taught them how to sew, bake bread, whistle, play soccer, and love reading. Her days were so busy with the girls that she had no time to think about the problems at home, and she didn’t mind that. Evenings were trickier since Jo’s responsibilities ended officially at four o’clock, and she had the rest of the day and evening to do as she pleased. In order not to fret about Beth, about Laurie, about Amy off in Europe, and about Meg coping with married life, Jo would either work on her writing or shut herself in the library downstairs and escape into a world of fiction.

On one such evening Jo had gotten settled in the library and was about to begin reading chapter four of Jacob’s Mysterious Guest , when she heard a man come through the front entrance. She buried her face in the book, praying that whoever it was would take no notice of her, since she was not particularly in a sociable mood. As luck would have it, the man passed by the open library door without stopping to see who was inside. Jo, pulling the book away from her face let out a sigh of relief, but that quickly changed into a scream. For there was the man she thought had already gone, standing in the doorway.
"Forgive me, miss," the man apologized profusely. "I didn’t mean to frighten you."
Still shaking from the shock, Jo was unable to speak, but her eyes fell upon his stocking feet, more specifically upon his left sock, which had a rather large hole in it.

"You see, I thought you were one of the girls trying to hide so she wouldn’t have to go to bed so early. That’s why I took off my shoes so I could scare you, no, not you, but . . ." The man struggled for words in a very strong foreign accent. "Anyway, I’m very sorry."
Then he gave Jo the warmest and friendliest smile she had ever seen. By now Jo had caught her breath and was doing her best not to stare at his bare toe, which was wiggling as he spoke.
"I’m Friedrich Bauer," the man introduced himself.
"Oh, you’re the Professor," said Jo, recognizing the name. "I’m Jo March, the girls’ new governess."
"What a pleasure it is to finally make your acquaintance," he said kindly.

The Professor, according to Mrs. Kirke, was originally from Germany but had come to America a few years ago along with his two orphaned nephews. He used to teach at a famous university in Berlin, but now he made his living as a tutor while caring for his deceased sister’s two boys. Mrs. Kirke said the Professor came from a wealthy and powerful family in Germany, but in his new country, he was almost penniless.

"Yes, the girls speak of you all the time," the Professor was saying. "They even showed me what you have taught them. For example . . ." Then to Jo’s horror, the Professor began whistling a merry tune she had taught the girls.
Blushing with shame, Jo, who had warned the girls sternly not ever to whistle in public because it was not ladylike, stuttered, "Well, I . . . the girls . . . just having fun."
With a twinkle in his eye, he continued, "So I taught them a melody I am particularly fond of. It goes like this." The Professor began whistling another cheery tune.
This time, Jo could not help laughing as the Professor did a little dance to go with his song. When his performance ended with a little bow, Jo clapped politely.
"May I ask what you are reading?" he asked, peering at the book on her lap.
Jo held it up and said, "I know I should be reading something more educational, but I just love mysteries and adventures."

Shrugging, the Professor said, "No, you should read what you enjoy. You are the director of your life, not someone else. Live in a way that will bring you happiness, not in the way others expect you to live it."
Appreciating his words, Jo asked the Professor to join her for a cup of tea.

"Thank you very much," he said as he sat down in the chair next to Jo. When he crossed his left leg and saw the hole in his sock, he quickly switched to the other leg. Then he let out a loud, hearty laugh. "Rest assured, Miss March," he said. "It is not my habit to purposely show my toes to young ladies."

Laughing along with him, Jo took a moment to study the Professor. He was older than she expected, perhaps in his mid-thirties, which, in comparison with her twenty years, was quite elderly. Yet he had a youthful energy. He also had an inviting warm smile and soft, expressive eyes. He was not handsome, like Laurie, but his face was interesting, and Jo found herself staring at it longer than she should have.
"Well, Miss March . . . ," the Professor said in his strong German accent.
"Please, call me Jo," she interrupted. "And by the way, if I may say so, your English is excellent, sir."

"Thank you kindly, Jo," he said, pronouncing her name like "Cho." "Then you must call me Fritz, agreed? If you like, tomorrow I will prepare a special German hot chocolate drink. Shall we meet here in the library at the same time?"
"I would love to, Fritz," Jo replied, not understanding why her heart suddenly began to beat faster.

No one ever said married life would be easy, but Meg did not expect it to be so challenging. John was a kind, loving husband who helped Meg in every way possible, for which she was truly grateful. Still, Meg found the little chores in everyday life that she had taken for granted at home were now a huge challenge for her. Then of course there were new issues that Meg had never experienced at home but had to learn to deal with as a married woman.
One day, as she was doing the simple act of preparing a meal, Meg felt dizzy and sick to her stomach. Fortunately, John was in the kitchen at the time and carried her to the sofa.
"Can I bring you anything? Water? A blanket?" he asked in a concerned voice.
"Just some hot tea, thank you," Meg said faintly.
By the time John brought the drink to her, Meg had gotten worse.
"Darling, I feel very ill," she told her husband.
"Shall I fetch Dr. Bangs?" he asked, squeezing her hand tightly.
"No," Meg said. "I need my mother."
John raced out of the house and down the street to get his mother-in-law, who, along with Beth, was in the process of giving each window in the house a good shine before the winter set in.
"John! What’s the matter?" Mother asked him when she saw his worried look.
"It’s Meg," he said, gasping for breath. "She’s not well and I don’t know what to do."
Throwing down her cloth, Mother wiped her hands and said, "Let’s not waste another moment while the poor girl lies sick."
When they got to Meg and John’s house, Meg was sweating and looking very pale. Mother put her hand on Meg’s forehead, over her heart, then down on her stomach. Then, surprisingly, Mother smiled.
"What’s the matter with her?" John asked, his voice trembling. "Is Meg going to be all right?"
"She’s going to be fine," Mother replied, nodding. "Meg isn’t sick—she’s pregnant."
Upon hearing those words, John collapsed into a heap on the floor next to his wife.
Meanwhile, Jo, who was not yet aware that she was soon going to become an aunt, spent her days content to be a governess and her evenings very happy to be with a friend.

"Jo, this week you must try to read this thrilling adventure that will take you across the seas," the Professor said, handing Jo a thick, old book from his own collection. Since their first encounter a couple of weeks ago, Jo found that she had a lot in common with the Professor. They both loved to read and write, though she preferred writing fictional stories and he favored poetry.

When he had moved to America, the Professor was forced to leave behind many of his possessions but he could not bear to part with his beloved collection of books, which he now displayed proudly in his personal library. Jo considered it an honor that the Professor wanted her to read some of his dearest treasures (though at first when he offered her his favorite book, she did not have the heart to tell him that she could not read German). Fortunately, the Professor owned a series of books translated into English that Jo was able to enjoy thoroughly.

On the weekends, the Professor would invite Jo to go with him and his nephews to the park or to take a carriage to Coney Island, an amusement park where children (of all ages) could go on rides. Jo noticed that the more time she spent with the Professor, the broader her horizon became. There seemed to be no end to the amount of knowledge to be learned.

Because the Professor was teaching her so many new things, Jo wanted to show her thanks but she couldn’t find a way to do so. Then one evening, the opportunity arose as she was washing her clothes. She happened to find two pairs of his socks, which he had probably dropped without realizing, on the floor of the laundry room. They were still damp and as Jo laid them out to dry, she noticed they all had holes in them. Smiling to herself as she recalled the first time she met him, Jo was about to leave when it occurred to her that perhaps she could help the Professor by mending his holey socks.

"I’ll bring them back here after I do it so he won’t know it was me," Jo thought to herself. Putting the socks into her laundry basket, she quickly climbed the stairs to her room and took out her sewing kit.

While Meg had just found out she was soon to be a mother and Jo was experiencing feelings she had never felt before, Amy was also discovering something new about herself. She sensed that any day now, Fred was going to propose to her and she was prepared. Sure enough, one chilly evening, Fred made an unannounced visit to Amy and her aunt.
"Why, Fred," Aunt March said fondly, for she was sure that he would be a perfect match for her grandniece. "What a pleasant surprise! To what do we owe this honor?"

Amy sat quietly clasping her trembling hands while she waited for the now inescapable question to fall from Fred’s lips. As he spoke to Aunt March, revealing his love for Amy, she watched him, feeling horrible about what she was going to do but at the same time knowing it was the right thing. Before she knew it, Fred was on bended knee asking, "Amy March, will you be my wife?"
Aunt March relaxed in her chair, absolutely certain what Amy’s answer would be.
"I’m sorry, Fred, I can’t marry you," Amy said clearly.
"What?" Aunt March’s eyes bulged in shock. "Amy, did you hear what Fred said? He wants to marry you!"
"I know, Aunt March, but I don’t want to marry him," Amy said respectfully.
"But why not?" demanded the old woman.
Poor Fred was in a state of such shock that he was speechless.
"Because I don’t love him," Amy admitted honestly. "And I must marry for love or I won’t be truly happy. I know that now."

If only Jo could have heard Amy’s admission at that moment, she would have marveled at how her sister had changed. And if Amy, for her part, could have seen Jo secretly smiling as she tenderly placed the mended socks back in the laundry room, Amy would have been shocked at the difference in her sister as well.

Winter was coming to an end, which meant that this chapter of Jo’s journey would conclude shortly too. Jo’s stay in New York had exceeded all her expectations and more as she looked back on her six months away from home. Feeling stronger, more mature, as well as more fulfilled, Jo readied herself to make the trip home. At the same time, she felt a dull ache in her heart because that meant she would have to say good-bye to a dear friend.

Just a few days before Jo was to leave, she received a letter from Beth telling her about Meg’s pregnancy. Coincidentally it was the Professor who delivered the mail to Jo that day, so she shared the good news with him. "I can’t believe I’m going to be an aunt!" she shouted in delight. For some reason, the idea of Meg getting married had been hard for Jo to accept, but news that she was going to have a little niece or nephew completely thrilled her.
"You like children, don’t you?" the Professor asked.
Nodding enthusiastically Jo said, "I love their innocence, their curiosity, their energy, and their humor. That’s why if I don’t succeed as an author, I am going to become a teacher."

Jo remembered the strange look that the Professor had given her when she made that comment. He said, "Then perhaps our paths may cross again one day, Jo, because it is my dream to start a school for boys, and I could use a good teacher like you."
Suddenly feeling shy, Jo merely said, "I didn’t realize you had such plans. One day, I hope you see your dream come true."
Now, as Jo sat packing her bags, she wondered what her dreams were and how they had changed in these past few months. A light knock on the door broke into her thoughts.
"Come in if you can find room for your feet," Jo called out, trying to clear some space among all her belongings scattered everywhere.
"I thought you only had a few things," the Professor joked as he looked around the messy room.
"I guess I must have acquired one or two more things while I was here," Jo said, chuckling.
"Will your bag be able to hold one more small item?" he asked.
"I’m sure I can find some space somewhere," Jo replied.
"I want to give you this," the Professor said, holding out a wrapped parcel.
Inside was a leather notebook with her initials on the cover. "Oh, it’s beautiful!" exclaimed Jo.
"For you to record your dreams," the Professor said smiling.
Swallowing the lump in her throat, Jo placed the notebook inside her handbag.
"Also, I want to thank you for this," the Professor said as he took his shoes off and proudly wiggled his mended socks.
"How did you know?" laughed Jo.
"When I saw the girls sewing, I knew these stitches belonged to you," he said.
An awkward silence followed. Then the Professor finally said, "Will you be returning to New York?"
"I would like to, but I can’t say with certainty," Jo said honestly.
"I hope we will meet again, Jo March," the Professor said with feeling as he held out his hand.
Smiling as she took his hand, Jo said, "It’s been a pleasure knowing you, Fritz."
As Jo finished packing her belongings, Amy was almost done with gathering everything into her luggage.

The following day, she and Aunt March were heading toward their next destination: Italy. Amy could hardly sleep that night because she had dreamt about visiting Italy since she was a little girl. "I guess some things do remain the same," she thought, thinking of her longstanding dream to see that beautiful country.

But Amy had changed in many other ways as she was learning on this trip to Europe. Reflecting on the relationship between Aunt March and Amy’s own family, Amy appreciated the worth of close family ties and the values her parents had taught her. She concluded that it was love, not money, that bonded people closely. That was why she could not marry Fred: she didn’t love him, much to the disappointment of Aunt March.
"I have a feeling that something wonderful is waiting for me in Italy," Amy said to herself as she lay in bed.
Jo’s homecoming was so heartwarming that she forgot about her friends in New York for a moment.
"You look different somehow, darling," her mother commented.
"Like a lady," teased her father, playfully touching her stylish bun.
"Mrs. Kirke taught me how to do my hair up in different ways," Jo said proudly.
"I’m so glad you’re home," Beth said quietly. "It’s as if you never left."

In Jo’s eyes though, much had changed during her absence, most notably Beth. She looked thinner, paler, and lifeless; a total contrast from the sunny, happy girl in Jo’s memory. When Jo told her Mother her worries, Mother shook her head and just said, "She’s never really been the same since the fever."

Early the next morning, Jo decided to brave the cold and took her new leather notebook and extra sweater to the pond behind their house. She was looking forward to having a private moment to reflect upon her trip, but when she got to the lake, someone was already there.
"Laurie!" she called out excitedly, truly happy to see her best friend.
"Jo! What are you doing here?" he asked, alarmed.
"I’m back, you know," she laughed.
"I know," he smiled. "I was going to come see you later on in the morning."
"I never knew you came down here to the pond," she said.
"I walk down here most mornings," he said, adding, "You don’t know everything about me."
"Well, I’m so glad to see you and I have so much to tell you," Jo said, trying to change the subject because she felt uneasy tension between them.
"So do I, Jo," Laurie said quietly as he stared at her for a long time.
"Laurieㅡ" Jo began, thinking she knew what he was about to say but not wanting him to say it, because once it came out, their friendship would never be the same.

Laurie abruptly interrupted her. "This may not be the best time to say this but I don’t care. After you left, my life has been nothing but agony. I went back to college, and by the way, you’ll be happy to know that I received the highest marks in my class and will graduate with honors."
"That’s wonderful, Laurie! I knew you could do it! I’m so . . ." Congratulating him, Jo prayed she would be able to say a few words before Laurie went on, but he continued as if he didn’t hear her.

"From the first day I met you all those years ago until this very moment, my feelings for you have never changed and they never will," he said passionately. Taking her hand, Laurie said, "Jo, my life, no matter how good it is, will never be complete unless you are in it."
Feeling as though her heart was being broken, Jo somehow found the strength to say what she could no longer hold back.
"Laurie, please don’t do this," she begged him. "Our friendship is the most precious thing to me, and I don’t want it to change. I can’t be the kind of person you want me to be."
Laurie bowed his head, his face crushed with pain.
"I don't love you like that, Laurie. I never have," said Jo to her dearest friend in the most brutal yet truthful words.

Not even the impressive sunrise nor the chattering birds could bring any cheer to the two people standing in silence by the pond. Jo could sense Laurie’s pain, and it hurt her to know that she could offer him no comfort.
Finally Laurie spoke up. "Is it because of that old man in New York?"
While Jo had been away, she had sent letters to family and friends in which she wrote enthusiastically about episodes with the Professor.

"Laurie, you’re like a brother to me. You’re my best friend. Can’t you understand that?" Jo tried to explain, carefully avoiding the issue of the Professor because she was not certain herself what her feelings were.
"This is unfair, Jo!" Laurie suddenly shouted. "I can’t understand it at all! I won’t!"

With that, Laurie stomped off, leaving Jo standing alone watching him disappear into the woods. Jo remained like that for a while, trying to digest everything that had just happened and what the consequences would be.

When she got home, Mother and Father had just left to do some errands in town so Beth was alone. Although her younger sister was now nineteen years old, Jo still regarded her as a delicate child. The last thing Jo wanted was for Beth to know what had happened between her and Laurie that morning. So, she suggested with forced cheerfulness, "Beth, shall we visit Meg and see how the baby is doing?"
With arms linked, the sisters set out to visit Meg, who was overjoyed when she saw them walking down the path to her house.
"Jo! I’m so happy to see you!" she cried.
Right away, Jo noticed the size of Meg’s stomach. Resting a hand over it, she spoke to the baby, "How is my little niece or nephew doing in there? Is Mommy feeding you lots of yummy things?"
"Oh, Jo," giggled Meg, giving her sister a hug. "It’s so good to see you."
For the rest of the morning, the three sisters chatted, laughed, suggested possible names for the baby, planned its future, and finally discussed who would be next to have a child.
"Well, it won’t be me," declared Jo. "Maybe Beth or Amy."
Beth smiled sadly, then said softly, "Maybe Amy."

On their way to Meg’s house, it was clear that Beth was moving much more slowly than usual, as if each step she took was painful. Jo had mistakenly thought Beth’s sadness was due to her lovesick feelings for Laurie, but after seeing the physical change in Beth, Jo realized that it was something more. On their way home from Meg’s, Jo gently brought up the subject.
"Beth?" she began. "Is there something wrong? If there is, you must tell me."
Beth took Jo’s hand and squeezed it with the little strength she had. "Yes, Jo, there is something wrong."
While Beth was thinking of how to tell Jo her secret, Laurie was pouring out his soul to his grandfather, who patiently listened to the heartbreaking story.

"I’m sorry Jo does not return your affections," Mr. Laurence said after Laurie fell into silence. Even Mr. Laurence was devastated at Jo’s rejection of his grandson, because all these years he had secretly hoped the two would marry. "But you must respect her decision, dear boy," he continued.
"I can’t, Grandfather. I can’t imagine my life without her," Laurie said in a distressed voice.
Mr. Laurence thought for a moment then suggested, "Perhaps, it would be best for everyone if you left for a while, took a trip somewhere. You can have time to deal with your emotions, and so can Jo."
Laurie didn’t want to leave but after much persuasion, he reluctantly agreed that some time away would do him good.
On the street below, Beth, having thought of different ways to explain herself, finally decided that the straightforward approach would be the best. "Jo, I’m dying."
Stunned, Jo stopped in her tracks, her body stiffening and her head throbbing painfully. "What? How do you know, Beth?" she managed to ask.
"I’ve known for some time, Jo," Beth said calmly. "And I’ve come to accept it."
Shaking her head wildly, Jo cried, "No, Beth, you must be mistaken. You can’t die! Has Dr. Bangs diagnosed you?"

Suddenly becoming the older sister, Beth shook Jo’s shoulder gently and said in a clear strong voice, "Dr. Bangs already knows, and there’s nothing that can be done. We must all face reality, and you must get on with your lives."
"I can’t lose you, Beth. Please don’t say that," Jo wept openly, not caring if people stared at her or not.

Beth took Jo’s hand and began walking again as she comforted her sister. "I’m not afraid, Jo. In a way, I’m glad because I won’t have to suffer anymore. It’s been so painful, Jo, and I don’t want to hurt any longer."
Jo could not speak, because she was weeping so hard that she started to hiccup.
"Let’s go home, Jo," Beth said gently, leading her devastated sister back down the familiar road.

That night, Jo sat upstairs in her sanctuary looking out into the dark, seeing clear images of their childhood reflected in the moonlight. So many happy memories filled her mind as she laughed, then cried, remembering precious moments from long ago.
Mother found Jo sitting there like that the next morning. "Jo? May I come in?" Mother called softly from the door.
Jo turned to her and stretched out her arms, desperately needing to feel the warmth of Mother’s love.
"Beth told you," Mother said simply as she tightly embraced her inconsolable daughter.
"Why Beth? She’s done nothing bad in her life. Why not me?" Jo asked.
"I know it’s hard to accept, Jo, but we must try to make Beth as happy and comfortable as we can before—," her mother choked, "before she goes. For her sake, we must be strong."
"I’ll try," sniffed Jo. "But I’ll never understand why this is happening."
"Now wipe your tears, my darling. Laurie is downstairs and he says it’s urgent that he see you," Mother said, using her apron to dry Jo’s eyes.
Laurie was the last person Jo wanted to talk to at that moment, but she felt she had to see him since she had broken his heart only the day before.
When she got downstairs, Laurie didn’t turn around to greet her as usual. Dressed in his overcoat and gloves, he spoke up when he sensed Jo’s presence behind him. "I’ve come to say good-bye, Jo."
"Where are you going?" she asked carefully.
Perhaps it was something in her voice that made Laurie turn around and face her. "My God, Jo, are you all right?" he cried when he saw the state she was in.
"I’m fine, Laurie," she lied.
"I’m going to Europe for a while," he said.
Nodding, Jo said, "Say hello to Amy if you see her."
"I doubt it, but if I do, I will," Laurie said, moving toward her to hug her. Then changing his mind, he stormed out the door.

Living a life of luxury and comfort was very agreeable to Miss Amy March. Italy was also very agreeable to Amy, who found it even more beautiful and romantic than she imagined. Every afternoon, she explored the villages near the one where she and Aunt March were staying. Her sketchbook and paints were her constant companion in case she was inspired to capture a beautiful scene. As in France, Amy drew a lot of attention from passersby and even though she didn’t speak their language, her generous smile and friendly tone of voice were universally understood.

Yet as time wore on, Amy began to grow restless and wonder if perhaps there was something more to life than just being content with material things. She also became very homesick, wanting more than anything to see a familiar face, talk in her native language, and walk down a well-known road. She kept in touch with her family and friends through letters, but it was not the same as being with those she loved.

One day, finding an isolated shady spot under a large tree, Amy began to paint the charming local children playing a game in the field. Smiling to herself, she was reminded of how she used to play outdoors with her sisters at that age. Unknown to Amy, an old acquaintance was very close by. He, too, was unaware that, in trying to get away from one March sister, he was soon to encounter another one.

Laurie thought, or rather hoped, that a trip to Europe would cure him of his broken heart. He visited old friends, went to his favorite restaurants, and attended social events where he met many likeable young ladies, but he found that no one could ever compare with his Jo. So he decided to give in to his tormented heart and his self-pity. Wearing a long face (not to mention an equally long moustache and beard since he had given up on shaving as well), Laurie walked the streets of Rome alone and depressed.

Jo, on the other hand, had put aside her own sorrow over Beth’s tragedy to focus on how she could make Beth’s last days more meaningful and fulfilling. One day, when the two sisters were sitting outside in the yard, Beth had said dreamily, "I’ve never seen buffalo except in paintings. They are such majestic creatures, yet they seem so gentle. It’s a shame they don’t roam this part of the country."
"Would you like to see buffalo?" Jo asked, a little surprised at her sister’s interest in such a wild animal and not in something milder and tamer like a giraffe.
Beth smiled shyly, saying, "They live out west so it isn’t likely that I’ll ever see one, as much as I’d like to."

This conversation gave Jo an idea but she didn’t tell Beth because she wanted it to be a surprise. Knowing that the Eagle would buy her stories (if the editor liked them, of course), Jo decided to consider different publishers as well. She had a few completed stories along with the couple she was working on at the moment. "If I write three or four stories a week," she calculated, "then I could save enough money to take Beth to California, where she can see buffalo."

With that plan as an incentive, Jo spared no time for herself. Every free minute that she had was spent writing, then taking her stories to the publishers in town. Physically and mentally exhausted, Jo kept herself going by keeping Beth’s wish close to her heart.

On an exceptionally glorious day in Rome, Amy, equipped with her sketchbook and pencils, strolled down a quiet road, looking for a place to sit and have coffee. Her eye caught sight of two little children standing in front of a bakery eating ice cream on the other side of the road. "I think I’ll have one of those," she said aloud, then crossed over to the store the children had just left.

She noticed a man sitting at a table by himself, sipping coffee, with a raisin bun left untouched on his plate. At first glance he seemed shabby and dirty, so Amy quickly looked away. As she waited for the baker to scoop out her ice cream, however, Amy stole another glance because there was something oddly familiar about him. Thanking the baker, Amy paid for her ice cream and deliberately walked past the silent man, who did not even look up as she went by. When it suddenly dawned on her, Amy swung around in disbelief. "Laurie? Is that you?" she whispered loudly.
The man slowly lifted his eyes, which Amy noted were red and dull. Then, recognizing the young woman standing before him, he broke out into a big, wide grin.
"Little Amy March? I must be dreaming!" he yelled, knocking aside his bun and nearly upsetting his coffee in the process.
"Laurie? I hardly recognized you!" Amy said, trying hard not to stare at his strange appearance.
"Look who’s talking! You dress like a European now, and your hair . . ." Laurie complimented her, in a voice and manner more like the old Laurie she knew.
"Oh, Laurie! I can’t believe you’re here. I was getting so homesick and I thought about leaving Aunt March and returning home just to see a familiar face," cried Amy.
"Well, I don’t blame you. You’ve been away for almost a year now," Laurie said. "Now that I’m here, we have a lot to catch up on."

"I would really like that. Tell me everything about home: Meg’s baby, Jo’s New York excursion–" Amy stopped when she noticed Laurie’s face harden again. "But we’ll leave all that for later. First of all, let’s go for a walk," she said quickly to change the subject. And taking his arm, Amy chatted away as they walked the streets of Rome.
That evening, Aunt March noticed a change in Amy’s spirits as the young lady sang softly and smiled a great deal while getting ready to go out to a party.
"What put that smile on your face?" Aunt March said in her usual gruff manner.
"You’ll never believe who I ran into on the street today, Aunt," Amy said, accustomed to her aunt’s manner by now.
"I hope it was young Fred and you begged him to forgive you for your foolish mistake of saying no to his proposal," the old lady snapped, still angry about Amy’s refusal to marry him.
Amy brushed aside her aunt’s remark and said cheerily, "I ran into Laurie! What a coincidence! He’s here for a while so we decided to catch up and see some sights together."
"Humph," grunted Aunt March, thinking that Laurie wasn’t a bad sort but she still preferred Fred.

Shortly after, the servant announced Mr. Laurence’s arrival. To Amy’s immense relief, Laurie had shaven off his moustache and beard and looked very handsome in his coat and tie. After he had greeted Aunt March, he and Amy went out, laughing and talking, both of them delighted and comforted to be with an old friend.

Laurie and Amy spent every day together, both of them enjoying the companionship of an old friend and familiar conversation. However, Amy sensed that Laurie was holding something back, and she had a good idea it had to do with Jo. One afternoon, while the two friends were relaxing—Amy sketching a paradise-like scene of fruit trees and birds while Laurie flipped through a bookㅡshe decided to ask Laurie about it.
"Laurie?" Amy called in her most ladylike voice. "Did something happen between you and Jo?"
Shutting his book, Laurie said, "What makes you ask?"

Carefully choosing her words, Amy replied, "You used to be best friends, but I’ve noticed that whenever I mention her name or talk about something to do with Jo, you either change the subject or avoid the topic altogether."
Laurie looked out at the scenery Amy was sketching and said nothing at first. Then, he said quietly, "She broke my heart, Amy."
Setting aside her sketchbook, Amy walked over and sat next to him. "Sometimes talking about it can help," she said kindly.
So Laurie began to tell her everything that happened, and Amy listened sympathetically.

Back home, Jo knew from Amy’s letter that she had run into Laurie in Italy. But Jo did not have a clue the two of them were talking about her at that moment. Her thoughts were otherwise occupied as she worked frantically, her fingers numb and stiff, putting the finishing touches on the last paragraph of her story. Satisfied with the ending, Jo threw on her coat and headed toward the office of the Volcano magazine. The Volcano printed trashy stories, but Jo knew that’s what sold and she needed the money.

Upon returning from the Volcano , Jo put her recent earnings into the box she had been saving her money in. It was almost full. She emptied the box and began counting. "Three hundred and fifty-two dollars and twenty cents," she calculated. "That should be enough for our trip."
Suddenly feeling as though a large weight was lifted off her shoulders, Jo threw her coat back on. This time, she headed toward the coach office in town.

After his intimate conversation with Amy, Laurie also felt as though a burden was lifted from his heart. He still thought of Jo, but not as often, and he noticed that he had begun to enjoy life again. Laurie had already been in Europe for over two months but only then did he feel as though his vacation was beginning.

Amy was touched that Laurie had opened up and shared his heartbreaking experience with her. She knew–everyone did–that Laurie had had a crush on Jo for many years. She also knew that it was one-sided, and Jo never looked at Laurie as anything more than her best friend and a brother figure.
"Miss Amy? Mr. Laurence is here," the servant announced through Amy’s door.
"Thank you. Tell Mr. Laurence I’ll be right down," Amy called back, grinning at the thought of someone calling Laurie "Mr. Laurence."

Tonight Laurie was taking Amy to the opera, so she had made an extra effort to look her best. Laurie seemed to notice how beautiful Amy looked, because upon seeing her walking down the stairs, he remarked, "I’m going to need a stick to keep all the young men away from you."
Suddenly feeling shy, Amy blushed as she took his outstretched hand.

Beth and Jo were not looking as lovely as Amy, but they were having a fantastic time as they poked their heads out of the coach to catch sight of endless rows of cornfields in Kansas. Their journey to California had begun three days ago, and it would take another week to arrive at their destination. The girls, however, were enjoying every moment as they saw new scenery, met interesting people, and heard a variety of accents along the way.
"It’s a shame neither of us can draw like Amy," Jo kept saying, because she wanted somehow to preserve the memorable sights to remind herself of this trip in the future.

However, Beth’s reply made it clear why she was taking this trip. "If we spent our time concentrating on one sight, we might miss out on the others. I’d rather see everything once than see the same scene over and over again. Besides, the picture we take with our heart is always so much more precious than the ones we capture with a brush, don’t you think?"
Closing their eyes as the wind blew against their faces, Jo and Beth breathed the Midwestern air in deeply.
Back home, Meg and Mother sat having tea and knitting clothes for the baby. Meg’s stomach was big, bigger than Mother’s had been during each of her pregnancies.
"Meg, I don’t mean to alarm you, but has Dr. Bangs mentioned anything about your baby?" Mother said.
"Why? Do you think there is something wrong?" Meg asked worriedly.
"Dr. Bangs is much more knowledgeable in these matters, but I wouldn’t be surprised if you were carrying more than one," Mother said with a smile.
Meg dropped her knitting and stared openmouthed. "You mean twins? I might be carrying twins?"
Shrugging her shoulders, Mother replied, "It’s not so unusual, Meg, and you seem quite large to be having just one baby."
Rubbing her big belly, Meg repeated disbelievingly, "There might be two babies inside?"

Not realizing that she might become an aunt to two babies at once, Amy, after enjoying several evenings of dancing and partying, was becoming increasingly irritated at Laurie’s playboy approach to life. They sat in the sitting room of the villa Aunt March had rented having a serious chat.
"When are you returning home?" she asked.
"I haven’t really thought about it," he answered, shrugging.
"What about graduation? What about finding a job?" she continued.
"I don’t have to work, really. Grandfather can provide me with all that I need," Laurie replied as if he didn’t care.
Amy, who was also knitting (all the March girls enjoyed it as a hobby), began clicking her needles faster and kept her mouth shut.
"Are you upset about something?" Laurie asked, noticing Amy’s coldness.
"Yes," she replied curtly. "You are the laziest boy I’ve ever met."
Startled, Laurie asked her why she thought that.

Putting her knitting down, Amy said, "Just because you’re rich doesn’t mean you should waste your life away. There is so much more for someone clever like you to do in this world. Money isn’t everything, Theodore Laurence!"
With those words, Laurie, but more so Amy, was shocked to discover how much she had changed in the last year.
"Why, Amy March, I never thought I’d hear you say that," Laurie said nastily.
"Well, that’s how I feel, and shame on you for exploiting and wasting your grandfather’s money this way," Amy snapped at him.
Standing up, Laurie said, "I can and will do as I choose."
"Then do it," Amy said in a shaky voice. "But don’t do it around me, because I won’t stand for it."
Grabbing his coat and hat, Laurie said coolly, "Take care, Amy. It was lovely to spend time with you, but I’m afraid the fun is over." And he walked out the door.
It took almost two weeks by coach, but Jo and Beth finally arrived in California. Jo had reserved rooms in a small, unique hotel that also offered tours to see the wildlife, including buffalo.
"Oh, Jo," Beth’s voice shook with emotion when their tour group finally came across a herd of buffalo grazing on the fields.
Just as Beth had thought, the massive creatures were gentle and peaceful as they carried on with their business, paying no attention to the humans staring at them from a distance.
"Is this what you imagined them to be like?" Jo whispered to Beth.
Nodding, Beth said teary eyed, "It’s a dream come true. Thank you, Jo."
Putting her arm around Beth’s thin, weak shoulders, Jo took in every detail around her, for she wanted to remember this moment forever.

After the argument with Laurie, Amy found it hard to find joy in anything, even drawing and painting. Laurie came by once more to tell Aunt March and her that he was leaving for Spain and wished them the best on the rest of their trip.
"I think it’s time for us to depart this place as well," Aunt March had said when Laurie left.
"Where shall we go?" Amy asked, not really caring since she knew Laurie would not be there.
"Florence," stated the old lady.
But as Amy stood outside on the balcony of their villa in Florence, she felt no inspiration to paint one of the most beautiful cities in the world. All she could think about was Laurie.

On the way back home, Jo noticed that Beth seemed to struggle more with the strenuous journey. She got tired easily, didn’t have the energy even to look outside at the scenery, and mostly slept a lot. When they got home, Beth, barely able to stand, clung tightly to Jo’s arm and said, "This has been the best adventure of my life, Jo. I’ll never forget it."

Jo clutched her hands tightly and pressed her lips to stifle an agonizing cry. She would have collapsed into tears then and there if not for Mother’s next words, "There’s a letter for you, Jo. Actually two."

As Mother handed them over to her, Jo recognized the strong handwriting of the Professor. After putting Beth to bed, Jo took the letters upstairs to her sanctuary. As she read them, her spirits lifted. She even laughed as she imagined the Professor speaking aloud in his German accent and calling her "Cho." Holding the letters close to her chest, Jo found the strength to bear the pain that was ahead.
A few months passed with no hope of Beth getting better. Without strength to sit, Beth was confined to her bed, which was moved downstairs so she could look out into the street and garden.
"Jo, can you read me a story?" Beth would ask.
When Jo brought over a book, Beth would move her head from side to side and say, "Leave me alone."

Jo felt helpless, because she wanted to ease her sister’s pain but didn’t know how. Mother seemed to deal better with the situation, bringing things for Beth just when she needed them and leaving her in peace when she wanted to rest.
Meg, who now knew that she was indeed carrying twins, also spent every day by Beth’s side. "Feel the babies kicking, Beth," Meg would say, placing Beth’s limp hand over her growing stomach.
"I felt it, Meg," Beth would say, her eyes filling with tears.
"You’re going to be an auntie soon, darling," Meg would remind her.
But Beth would only smile weakly and say, "I hope they’re girls, and they’re as beautiful as you."
One afternoon, Jo, not wanting to disturb Beth, crept over to refill the water pitcher on the table next to Beth’s bed.
"Jo?" Beth called softly.
"Yes, darling? Did I wake you?" Jo asked.
Beth shook her head slightly as if to say no, then said, "Will you lie here with me?"
Jo carefully got into the bed next to her sister and wrapped her arm around her. "I’m here, Beth. Do you want me to tell you a story?"
Beth blinked her eyes once and sighed. "Jo? I’m ready to go now."

Jo, not wanting to part with her sister yet, gently squeezed Beth’s shoulders and said, "Hold on just a little longer, Beth. Meg’s babies are coming and Amy will be home soon. Be strong for just a little longer . . ."
But Beth turned her head, looked at her sister tenderly, then closed her eyes, and died in Jo’s arms.

When Beth’s funeral was held a few days later, almost everyone from the town was there. Although the family had sent a telegram to Amy about her sister’s death, they urged her to stay with Aunt March for the rest of the trip, because that was what Beth had wished.

At home the March family had to rebuild their lives after the loss of beloved Beth. Mother, who had been so strong throughout Beth’s illness, seemed to age decades in a matter of days afterward. Still, she found comfort in the loving arms of her husband. Both Mother and Father tried to give each other strength to cope with the loss of one of their children.

However, Jo was inconsolable. No amount of kind words or deeds could soothe the pain in her heart. Every day she escaped into the woods, taking long walks by herself with her memories of her sweet sister.
A few weeks after Beth’s death, Jo was just clearing up the dishes from dinner when John came running into the house.
"Please, come quickly," he said breathlessly. "Meg is having the babies!"

Mother, Father, Jo, and Hannah raced out, leaving the dishes and other worries behind. When they got to the house, Dr. Bangs and a midwife were already there with Meg. Mother went into the room with them while Jo, John, and Father paced the living room anxiously. A few hours later, they heard a baby crying.
"Oh John!" Jo cried, holding onto her brother-in-law’s hand. "Congratulations!"
Then shortly after, another cry erupted, and they could hear laughter and cries from behind the door.
"John?" Dr. Bangs called, opening the door. "Come in and see your babies. Come, Mr. March. You too, Jo and Hannah."

Everyone crowded into the room where Meg sat up holding one baby in the crook of each arm. "This is your new son," she said, looking at the bundle on her right, then pointed her chin toward the left, adding, "and your new daughter."

Everyone started hugging and crying as they welcomed the newest members of the family into the world. Jo looked lovingly at her niece and nephew and realized for a sad moment that they would never see their Aunt Beth. However, Jo promised to do what she could to help them get acquainted with the wonderful aunt who had died before their birth.
"What are you going to name them, Meg? John?" asked Father.
"Daisy and Demi," the happy parents said together.
"Welcome to your family," the new grandfather said proudly.

Daisy and Demi were the apple of everyone’s eye as they charmed whoever caught sight of them. Meg brought over the babies almost every day, knowing that their adorable faces would bring smiles to a mourning household.
"Our Daisy is a stubborn one," John said proudly to Mother and Father. "If her brother comes near her space, she kicks and screams until he moves away."
"Sounds like our Jo when she was a baby," Mother said with a wink.

Everyone laughed at the resemblance. It was true the twins could not have been more opposite in temperament. Demi, the boy, was mild, quiet, and obedient, while Daisy threw tantrums until she got her way. But both babies looked like perfect angels when they slept in their father’s arms.
"Brings back memories, doesn’t it, dear?" Father said tenderly, putting his arm around his wife.

Jo watched as Meg placed a loving hand on her husband’s arm and leaned her head on his shoulder, while their babies slept peacefully. Instead of being moved by seeing such a loving family, it made Jo feel tremendously lonely and sad. Making her excuses, she went upstairs, got her notebook, and walked out to the pond.

It was no fault of theirs, but Jo felt distanced from her parents, from Meg and John, and also from Amy and Laurie, knowing they were seeing Europe together. It wasn’t jealousy, but Jo felt as though everyone had someone special to spend time with except for her. "This is ridiculous," she said to her reflection in the water. "I’ve done well on my own till now. Why should I start feeling sorry for myself?"

No matter how many times she told herself that, however, Jo still felt the empty space in her heart gradually growing bigger. Sighing loudly, she opened the notebook the Professor had given her and began writing, escaping into the world of make-believe where no one suffered loneliness.

In Florence, Amy sat on the balcony of the villa, silent tears falling onto her beautiful dress. In her hand was the telegram from home telling her of Beth’s passing. She had known that Beth was ill and that eventually this day would come, but Amy thought she would be with her family when it happened. Now she felt as if she had betrayed Beth for not being with her during the last months of her life on earth. "I’m so selfish for being here. I should be with my family," she cried to Aunt March when she first received the telegram.
"Beth wished for you to stay here, so you shall. We must let go of the dying and hold fast to life and live," Aunt March said bluntly.

Clearly, if Amy wanted any comfort, she wasn’t going to get it from Aunt March. For days Amy did not eat, speak, or do anything but sit on the balcony and cry. One day while she was doing just that, clinging to the piece of paper from home as if it was her only link to her family, she prayed for Beth. When Amy opened her eyes, she couldn’t believe who was walking toward the villa.
"Laurie?" she cried in a little girl’s voice.

Amy could see Laurie’s distressed face looking up at her and she knew he had also heard about Beth. She ran downstairs and flung herself into his arms as soon as she opened the door. They stood there like that, holding each other and crying together.
"I’m so sorry, Amy," Laurie kept whispering. "We all loved her very much."
Nodding but unable to answer, Amy kept crying, yet she found a calming comfort in Laurie’s arms.

On a rainy afternoon too miserable to venture outside to the pond where Jo had been doing most of her recent writing, she decided, for some odd reason, to pay a visit to Mr. Laurence. Without question Beth had been his favorite girl, so her death had affected Mr. Laurence deeply. Because he wasn’t family, however, Jo failed to realize just how much the old man must have been missing her. She thought it was a good time to see how Mr. Laurence was coping.
"Jo! What a pleasant surprise, my dear," he said happily when he saw who had come to visit.
Jo had baked some oatmeal cookies, which she handed over with a smile. "I’m sorry I haven’t been here sooner," she apologized.
Holding up his hand, Mr. Laurence stopped her, saying, "Jo, under the circumstances, it’s understandable. But I expect you to come and visit this lonely old man at least once a day from now on."
"I will, and since I’m a lonely old woman we can be lonely together," she said miserably.
"Splendid!" Mr. Laurence roared as if he hadn’t laughed out loud in a while.
They talked about the babies, Amy and Laurie, and other things. Then Mr. Laurence said something very interesting. "You know, Jo, I’d like to do something to commemorate Beth’s life," he said.
"What were you thinking of?" asked Jo.
"Some kind of place that would bring good to the community, just as Beth always did kind acts for others," he explained. "What do you think Beth would like?"
Jo thought for a moment, then said, "Well, Beth always loved children, so perhaps something for little ones?"
Mr. Laurence stood up and began pacing the room. He said, "Yes, yes, a school for children would be a fine idea. A piano school?"
Jo nodded in agreement and said, "Beth loved music so that would be a wonderful memorial to her."
Mr. Laurence stopped suddenly and said, "True, but Beth would want children to learn so much more. Jo! What about a school that teaches academics and arts such as piano or painting?"

Jo sat up straight, remembering someone else who wanted to start a school. "Mr. Laurence, if you do open a school in Beth’s name, I already know the perfect person to be the headmaster," she said excitedly.
Grabbing her hands tightly, Mr. Laurence said emotionally, "Let’s make this work, Jo. Let’s do this for Beth."
Letting go of his hands and giving him a tight hug instead, Jo cried, "Thank you, Mr. Laurence. This means so much to us, and Beth would be so proud if she knew what you were doing for her."

That evening, Jo wrote a long, detailed letter to the Professor, telling all that had happened in the past few months and ending with Mr. Laurence’s proposal. "If you are interested in this position, you may wish to make a trip here and meet Mr. Laurence in person to discuss the details further," she wrote. Placing the letter in an envelope and sealing it, Jo said, "Now, we’ll just have to wait and see what happens."

Just a few days later, that same envelope was handed over to the Professor, who read the letter with much interest. "Hmm, this sounds very promising indeed and highly tempting. I must find out about a coach ticket."

Laurie found a place to stay in Florence, and for the next few days, he and Amy were inseparable. Amy noticed some changes in Laurie: for example, he wasn’t throwing money around like before, he showed more consideration for others, and he seemed to be more responsible, more mature. Amy mentioned what she had noticed to him.
"After what you told me in Rome, I did a lot of soul-searching," he admitted.
"I’m sorry if I was blunt," Amy began apologetically but Laurie stopped her.
"No, I should be thanking you," he said. "You were right. I was too engrossed in myself to realize it then."
"Well, if you feel that way, then I’m glad I spoke up," Amy said with a smile.

"After Beth died," Laurie continued in a softer voice, "everything changed. I didn’t want to waste another moment on anything insignificant or meaningless. I need purpose and direction to guide me through this life."
Laughing, Amy laid a hand on Laurie’s and said, "Oh no! I think I’ve made a philosopher out of you."
Taking her hand, Laurie looked into her eyes and said, "Not a philosopher but a real person."
They sat there like that for a while, looking into each others’ eyes, both of them realizing that their friendship had turned into something deeper.

Back home, loneliness was a word and a state that Jo had long forgotten as she threw herself into Mr. Laurence’s project. One day she and Mr. Laurence were visiting possible sites to build the school on.
"What is the school going to be called, by the way?" Jo asked.
"I thought I’d leave that up to you," Mr. Laurence replied.
Grateful for his thoughtfulness, Jo promised she would think about it and let him know.
"The school will be small, but I want the students to enjoy all areas of education: not just academic, but arts and sports as well," Mr. Laurence explained.
"It sounds like just the kind of place Beth would have loved," Jo said warmly.
They were standing in front of a large house that looked deserted, yet it was appealing to both Jo and Mr. Laurence at once.
"For starters, the roof needs repairing, and the exterior will need to be repainted," Mr. Laurence remarked, gently tugging his chin in deep thought. "What do you think, Jo?"
Jo placed her hands on her hips and made as professional a judgment as an amateur can make. She nodded agreeably and said, "It’s perfect."

Across the ocean, Laurie and Amy were also finding many things they agreed upon. From Florence they agreed, with the consent of Aunt March, of course, to travel next to Venice. Amy filled two sketchbooks in the first three days they were there, every street being more colorful and exotic than the one before. On the fourth day, Laurie treated Amy to a ride on a gondola that he steered himself. As they glided over the water, Amy sketched the unique architecture while Laurie watched her with a smile.
"Stop staring at me. You’re making me nervous," she teased.

"I can’t help it. You’re fascinating to watch," he said in return. Laurie steered the gondola toward a small bridge that led to a beautiful flower garden. "I want to show you this breathtaking spot," Laurie said as he stood up and pointed toward the garden with his oar.

No one really knew how it happened, but Laurie lost his balance. For a second, he looked like a tightrope walker at the circus, wiggling this way and that to stay standing. But in the end, the weight of the oar won, and down he went into the water.
"Laurie!" Amy shouted.
Laurie shook his wet hair as he pulled himself into the gondola. "My ego is bruised, but I’m okay. Where’s the oar?" Laurie looked around and saw it floating gently away.
"We have to get that back!" he said, panicking.
There was nothing in the boat to use except Amy’s sketchbook. Without a second thought, Amy rolled it up and used it to paddle toward the runaway oar.
"There you go," she said, snatching the oar out of the water when they reached it and shaking out her dripping, ruined sketchbook.
Impressed beyond words, Laurie stared at Amy with a strange look. Then he simply said, "We make a great team, you and I. Do you think we can do it forever?"
Understanding what his words implied, Amy smiled shyly and said, "Yes, I think we can."

Jo was unaware of the tremendous development that had just happened in Venice, but she was also about to embark on a life-altering course. She had finally completed her novel, the one she had recorded in the special notebook from the Professor. With mixed feelings, yet determined to move ahead with her goal, Jo put the notebook into an envelope, wrote a New York address on it, took it to the post office, and mailed it off.

While Jo was in New York, the Professor had helped her get the addresses of several publishers. Until recently, Jo had been content to sell her short stories to local newspapers and magazines, because she was reluctant to reach out to a bigger wider market. After her sister died, however, Jo felt less afraid of failure. She decided to take chances and to set her standards higher. Having faced so many obstacles in life, Jo now had the confidence that even if she did fail, she could get right back on her feet again.

A few days later, two urgent telegrams were delivered: one to the Laurence household and the other to the March family. Jo happened to be the one who received it at their home, so she read it aloud for her parents to hear. "It’s from our Amy," Jo said cheerfully. "It reads, 'Dear Mother, Father, and my darling sisters: I am delighted to tell you that I am engaged to . . .'" Jo paused as she read the name, "'Laurie.'"
"Jo, are you all right?" Mother said as she saw her daughter’s white face.

"Yes, I’m just shocked. I . . . I never thought . . . ," Jo stammered. "I need some fresh air." She staggered out the door and walked briskly to the pond. Jo wasn’t upset that Laurie had found someone else to love after she rejected him, but that telegram signaled another change in their relationship. For Jo, this was going to take a little time to accept.

Sitting alone looking out at the pond, Jo was reminded of Beth’s words on their last trip. She heard Beth’s voice say, "If we spent our time concentrating on one sight, we might miss out on the others. I’d rather see everything once than see the same scene over and over again. Besides, the picture we take with our heart is always so much more precious than the ones we capture with a brush, don’t you think?"

"You’re right, Beth," Jo said, looking up toward the sky. "Life is constantly changing, and so are relationships. We can’t expect things to remain the same when we ourselves are forever evolving. But we will always have the precious memories of the past to look back on with fondness."

Establishing Beth’s school was a family affair. Father worked all day on the roof repairs while Jo and Mother took charge of the painting. John, on the days he didn’t work, came to help with the floors, and Meg provided the refreshments while her babies entertained all the workers. Mr. Laurence, of course, was in charge of the entire project. The transformation of the old house was amazing, as each day, the place looked fresher and improved.
"Does anyone need a drink?" Meg called, holding up an inviting glass of cold juice.
"I think we all do," stated Mr. Laurence as he motioned for everyone to take a break.

While the workers were satisfying their thirst, a carriage slowly pulled up at the house. A tall, sturdy young man got out, then held out his hand to a stylishly dressed young lady. She kissed the young man. Then, looking at the crowd in front of the house, she yelled, "Mother! Father! Meg! Jo! It’s me!"

"Amy?" Mother called, not sure she could believe her eyes. Then she ran to meet her youngest daughter. She hadn’t seen her in a year. Amy, too, lifted her skirts, and forgetting her ladylike manners, ran to embrace her dear mother.
"I can’t believe you’re home!" cried Mother, showering Amy with hugs and kisses.
"Laurie!" shouted Jo when she noticed him lingering awkwardly by the carriage.
He lifted his head eagerly as he saw his best friend running toward him with outstretched arms. Giving her a big hug, Laurie said, "It’s so good to see you, Jo."
"I’m so happy to see you, Laurie," replied Jo, "even though your dashing clothes are now covered in paint."
Laughing, he said, "I don’t think my wife will object under the circumstances."
"Your wife?" Jo asked, stunned.
Amy walked over to Laurie and waited till the others had caught up before announcing, "We got married in Italy last week."
For a moment, no one said a word until Jo, recovering from the shock first, congratulated them sincerely. "I’m so happy for you both!" she said, her voice choked with emotion.
"Thank you, Jo," Amy said warmly as she looked deeply into her sister’s eyes.

"Not only do I have my sister back," said Jo, taking their hands, "but now I have a new brother. I’m so pleased." Soon everyone joined in congratulating the newly married couple, until Mr. Laurence decided to call it a day and invited everyone to his home to celebrate.
While Amy rode back with Mother, Meg, and the babies, Laurie decided to walk back with Jo. "I have so much to say, but I don’t know how," Laurie said to Jo.
"Then you don’t need to say it," Jo replied. "We mustn’t be burdened by the past but look forward to what lies ahead."
"I’ll always love you, you know," said Laurie. "But it’s a different love than the kind I feel for Amy."
"And you will always be my dear boy, my best friend," said Jo. "I will always love you."
Jo and Laurie found great peace knowing that despite the bumpy road, their friendship had survived.

At the Laurences’ a feast was under way. Mr. Laurence wanted to know why Laurie and Amy had gotten married so quickly. More importantly, he wondered why they chose to do so in Italy. "France would have been a more romantic location, I should think," Mr. Laurence said with regret.
Jo watched Amy place her hand on Laurie’s as he tried to answer his grandfather’s questions. "What a lovely couple they make," Jo thought, and she truly meant it.
Suddenly, the servant announced to Mr. Laurence, "We have a visitor, sir."
"A visitor?" Mr. Laurence looked around. "We’re not expecting someone else, are we?"
"The gentleman says he is a friend of Miss Jo's," the servant continued.
"A friend of mine?" Jo repeated as she stood up.
"Then show him in, by all means," said Mr. Laurence.
To Jo’s complete surprise, the Professor walked in, holding his hat nervously in his hand but with his head held up with dignity.
"Professor Bauer! Fritz!" Jo shouted, her voice giving away her delight in seeing him.
"Oh, Miss Jo." His features softened as he recognized a familiar face. "I apologize for the unannounced visit but . . . it is a long story."
"No need to explain," Jo said happily. "Everyone, this is Professor Friedrich Bauer, my dear friend from New York."

No other words were necessary for once they heard who he was, the Professor was welcomed like a family member. Jo made space for him at the table and soon they were all laughing and talking like old friends.
"Where are you staying, Professor?" asked Mr. Laurence.

When the Professor named a local hotel in town, Mr. Laurence shook his head and said, "That won’t do at all. You must be my guest here." Then he rang for his servant to collect the Professor’s belongings and bring them to the mansion.
Jo still could not believe how easily the Professor blended in with her family and friends, sitting at the same table and telling jokes and stories as if he had known them all his life.
"Jo?" Mr. Laurence had to call twice to get her attention. "Jo?"
"Oh, sorry," Jo said. "I didn’t hear you."

"Would you mind taking Professor Bauer to see the school tomorrow morning? I’ve formally asked him to become the headmaster but he hasn’t given me his answer. Make sure you get it from him tomorrow," Mr. Laurence said with a wink.
