Smiling at him, Jo said she would be more than happy to do that.
The next morning, true to her word, Jo escorted the Professor to the school site, asking him along the way about his life in New York.
"Never mind me, Jo," he said. "I am more concerned about you. How are you coping with the loss of your dear sister?"

As it always was with the Professor, Jo felt safe and secure showing him her deepest feelings. By the time they reached the school, the Professor had already offered his warm words of encouragement and hope to Jo.
"Well, here we are," Jo said as she stepped back for him to view the school. "It doesn’t look like much yet, but we hope to open it by the next school year."
"It exceeds all my expectations," the Professor said, his eyes watering with emotion.
"It will be smaller classes, but the school promises to look after the individual needs and talents of each student," Jo went on to explain.
"As all good schools should," the Professor agreed.
"As Mr. Laurence mentioned last night, he is eager for you to become the headmaster of the school," Jo said.
"And you?" the Professor asked Jo.
"I’m to be your assistant, organizing lessons, making sure the pupils are behaving, and mending socks," Jo said with a twinkle in her eye.
"Then," the Professor said, puffing out his chest, "I will gladly accept."
They shook hands wholeheartedly.

50.title: A New Chapter for the Little Women

paragraphs.text: Plumfield School, dedicated to the memory of Elizabeth March, opened its doors three months later. People came from town and from neighboring cities near and far to satisfy their curiosity about the new establishment.
"It’s a nice turnout, isn’t it?" Mr. Laurence said proudly as he waved at a few familiar faces and warmly greeted those he didn’t know as well.
Mother kept wiping tears from her eyes as she said over and over again, "Beth would be so happy."

Jo, along with Amy and Laurie, happily served drinks and snacks to the visitors and directed all those who had questions to Professor Bauer. Meg gave tours of the place while John minded the children and made sure they didn’t eat more cookies than they should.
"I desperately need a cold drink," the Professor gasped as he politely detached himself from a group of mothers who had gathered to pepper him with questions about the school curriculum.
Handing him a tall glass of lemonade, Jo asked, "Do you think it’s going to be a success?"

Looking at her tenderly, the Professor remarked, "Jo, whatever you do will succeed. Do you know why?" Without waiting for an answer, he replied, "Because you put your whole soul into it." Laurie and Amy exchanged knowing glances as they predicted another wedding in the March family soon. At present, however, the Professor’s very words, like a prophecy, were about to come true. A young delivery boy ran up to the refreshment table asking for Josephine March.
"That’s me," she replied.
"Package for you, ma’am," the boy said, handing her a thick envelope.
"What is it, Jo?" Amy asked curiously.
"I don’t know," Jo said as she ripped the envelope open. Inside was a bound book, and when Jo saw the title and author’s name, she let out a cry, "It’s my novel!"
The Professor caught her arm to steady her while Amy took the book from Jo’s hands.
"The Little Women: A Story About Life, by Jo March," she read. "Jo! This is your book! Your book’s been published!"
Hearing Amy’s excited voice and Laurie’s cheers, Meg came running, followed by their parents. When Laurie held up the book, everyone clapped and shouted their congratulations loudly.
"See, Jo, another success," whispered the Professor. "Your soul is in that book, just as it is in this school." Jo took his hand without saying a word, because he already knew what she wanted to say.

The grand opening of the school Academy brought greater results than anyone had thought. It was obvious that the upcoming days would be busy with accepting applications and planning lessons. John quit his job and took on a position as an English teacher. Amy volunteered to work part-time as the art instructor, and Meg said she would teach a sewing class. Aside from the other teachers who were hired, Plumfield School was the joint effort of the March, Laurence, and Brookes families uniting as one.
As she pondered that, Jo decided it would be a good chance for her to spend some private time with her sisters. They agreed to take a walk together, just the three of them, down to the pond.
"This has really been an eventful day," Meg said when they reached the pond and sat on a fallen log.
"My legs are killing me," said Amy, rubbing her sore feet. "But I’d gladly stand for weeks if it means making this school a success."
The girls sat together watching a few ducks swim around the pond as the sun was sinking in the sky.
"We used to come out here a lot when we were younger, but I haven’t been for so long," said Meg.
"Remember how we used to swim in the water, and Jo would grab our legs and try to pull us under?" giggled Amy.
"Then you’d run home and tell Mother or Father what I did and get me in trouble," Jo pointed out.
"We were so young and carefree," Amy said with a smile on her face.
"That’s why we did so many foolish things," Meg said, blushing at the memory of some of her embarrassing moments.
"But look at us now, girls," said Jo. "Meg is a mother with two children. Amy is married to Laurie and may soon start a family of her own."
"And Jo is an accomplished writer and headmistress of the most prestigious school in America," Amy added with pride.
"By the way, you never told us what your book is about, Jo," said Meg.

Looking out at the pond, Jo took a moment to gather her thoughts before answering, "It’s about dreams and failures, growing up and growing pains, love and heartache, opportunities and memories, regrets and hope, birth and death . . . It’s about life."
The sisters grew silent as they watched the sun slowly disappear below the horizon.
"I miss her so much," Amy said, choking up as her mind filled with memories of Beth.
As they used to do when they were younger, the girls wrapped their arms around each other and cried.
"Beth wouldn’t want us to cry every time we think of her," sniffed Amy.
"You’re right," Meg said, wiping her eyes. "Beth was always a positive, happy girl, and that’s how I want to remember her."
"Remember how she used to always get excited whenever we started a new chapter in a book?" asked Jo.
Giggling at the memory, Amy said, "She said new chapters are the best because there is so much to look forward to."
Jo dried her eyes and looked at her sisters. "What do you say, girls? Let’s tell each other about the new chapters in our lives that are about to begin," she suggested.
Meg started first. "My new chapter begins with Daisy and Demi starting school. While they learn how to become good citizens, I will learn how to be a better mother, wife, daughter, and sister."

"My new chapter begins with finding a house for me and Laurie to live in," said Amy, and laughed along with her sisters. "Then each day I want to do something that will touch the life of another person in some way, whether through my words, actions, instructions as a teacher, or even through my paintings."

Finally it was Jo’s turn. "My new chapter begins with the start of a new outlook on life, on relationships, on goals, and on myself. I hope to treasure each moment as it deserves to be valued and love each person as they deserve to be loved."
Hugging each other tightly, the March sisters were grateful for each other and for the chance to bond even more closely as they grew older together.
"Well, girls, it looks as if this day is almost over," said Amy, looking up at the darkening sky.
"A new day waits for us tomorrow," said Meg, standing up to leave.
As Jo followed her sisters back to the house, she added, "and a new chapter in this story called life."
